pools.covers: reading §6.1.7, §6.1.8, §6.1.9 · lecture 6.1 slides slivers_in_the_sea, parts_of_a_vertebrate_brain, new_structures_old_parts · lab Specimens, Plan

items.stem: What is a vertebrate?

options.text: An animal with a skull and a backbone, or at least the beginnings of a backbone.
options.why: Correct. The beginnings of a backbone are enough, which is why the jawless fishes, lampreys included, count as vertebrates.

options.text: An animal with jaws and paired fins, the body plan from which every amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal descends.
options.why: Jaws and paired fins came later. The first vertebrates had neither, and lampreys and hagfishes still have no jaws.

options.text: An animal with a large brain divided into distinct parts, and therefore among the most complex animals of its time.
options.why: Being a vertebrate is a matter of a skull and a backbone, not of complexity. The first vertebrates were small prey animals.

options.text: An animal with a stiff rod running along its back, of the kind it shares with its closest invertebrate relatives.
options.why: That rod is the notochord. The closest invertebrate relatives of the vertebrates have one too, so it does not make an animal a vertebrate.

items.stem: What is the name for the group of animals with a skull and a backbone, or at least the beginnings of one, a group that includes every fish, amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal?

options.text: Vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. Every fish counts, the jawless ones included, since the beginnings of a backbone are enough.

options.text: Jawed vertebrates.
options.why: Jawed vertebrates leave out the lampreys and hagfishes, which are fishes with a skull and the beginnings of a backbone but no jaws.

options.text: Arthropods.
options.why: Arthropods, such as insects, crabs and spiders, have an external skeleton rather than a backbone.

options.text: Bilaterians.
options.why: Bilaterians are a much larger group, including worms and insects, most of which have no skull or backbone.

items.stem: Early Cambrian rocks in southern China hold Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia, the oldest fossils most researchers accept as vertebrates. What were these animals like?

options.text: A few centimeters long, slender and toothless, and most likely prey for the arthropods around them.
options.why: Correct. The first vertebrates did not rule their seas. They were small, and the arthropods were the formidable animals.

options.text: Up to a meter long and covered in plates of bony armor, and too well protected for most predators to attack.
options.why: Armored jawless fishes up to a meter long came later, from the Ordovician onward, beginning about 485 million years ago.

options.text: Large hunters with jaws and rows of teeth, and the top predators of the seas in which they swam.
options.why: The first vertebrates had no jaws and no teeth. Jaws evolved more than 420 million years ago, long after them.

options.text: Anchored in place on the deep seafloor, filtering their food from the water through frond-shaped bodies.
options.why: Anchored frond-shaped organisms belong to the oldest Ediacaran assemblage, before the Cambrian. The first vertebrates swam.

items.stem: An octopus and a honeybee are both quite complex animals. How does the chapter use them to show what the word vertebrate does and does not mean?

options.text: Neither animal is a vertebrate, so being a vertebrate is a matter of a skull and a backbone, not of complexity.
options.why: Correct. Vertebrate is not another word for complex. It names a body plan, and some quite complex animals lack it.

options.text: Both animals are counted as vertebrates in a loose sense, since complexity is what the word vertebrate has come to mean.
options.why: No animal is a vertebrate in a loose sense. The octopus and the honeybee show that complexity and being a vertebrate come apart.

options.text: Both animals are less complex than any vertebrate, which shows that a skull and a backbone always bring complexity with them.
options.why: The chapter calls both animals quite complex, and the first vertebrates were small prey. A backbone brings no guarantee of complexity.

options.text: Neither animal is complex in the way a vertebrate is, since complexity requires a brain divided into distinct parts.
options.why: The chapter calls octopuses and honeybees quite complex. It does not define complexity by a divided brain.

items.stem: A documentary announces, “With the first vertebrates, the most advanced animals in the Cambrian seas had arrived”. Which point from the chapter corrects the announcement?

options.text: The first vertebrates were small prey in a sea full of very complex and very formidable arthropods.
options.why: Correct. This is Module 2’s warning against reading the tree of life as a ladder. The first vertebrates were not at the top of anything.

options.text: The first vertebrates did not appear in the Cambrian at all, but only after jaws evolved in the Ordovician period.
options.why: The first vertebrates are early Cambrian animals. Jaws came much later, more than 420 million years ago.

options.text: The most advanced animals were the Ediacaran grazers, which had already solved every problem a nervous system would ever face.
options.why: The Ediacaran grazers faced a small control problem, of still food and no hunting. The chapter ranks no animal as most advanced.

options.text: The first vertebrates were ahead of the arthropods in their jaws and teeth, but behind them in everything else.
options.why: The first vertebrates were toothless and had no jaws. In that sea they were most likely prey for the arthropods.

items.stem: What is the notochord?

options.text: A stiff rod running along the back, which vertebrates share with their closest invertebrate relatives.
options.why: Correct. The earliest vertebrates had one, and in most later vertebrates it is largely replaced by the backbone.

options.text: A cord of neural tissue running along the back, which carries signals between the brain and the body.
options.why: That is the spinal cord, which is neural tissue. The notochord is a stiff supporting rod, not part of the nervous system.

options.text: A population of cells that forms along the edges of the developing nervous system and then migrates through the body.
options.why: That is the neural crest. The notochord is a rod along the back, not a migrating population of cells.

options.text: A braincase of cartilage enclosing the front end of the nervous system, found in vertebrates and in none of their relatives.
options.why: A braincase belongs to the vertebrate new head. The notochord is shared with invertebrate relatives, which is why it does not make an animal a vertebrate.

items.stem: Worms and insects have heads, with sense organs and neurons gathered at the front. What, then, was new about the head of the first vertebrates?

options.text: A particular package of paired camera eyes, a nose, ears, and an enlarged front end of the nervous system, all inside a braincase.
options.why: Correct. Concentrating senses and neurons at the front was old, as Module 4 showed. What was new was this particular package, enclosed in a skull.

options.text: The fact of having any neurons gathered at the front at all, since no animal before the vertebrates had ever concentrated them there.
options.why: That is the easy reading the chapter refuses. Module 4 followed neurons gathering at the front of bilaterians long before the vertebrates.

options.text: A pair of jaws lined with teeth, which let the head seize prey instead of scooping or filtering food from the water.
options.why: The first vertebrates were toothless and had no jaws. Jaws evolved more than 420 million years ago, long after the new head.

options.text: A front end of the nervous system divided into three layers of neurons, where a worm’s had only a single layer.
options.why: Three layers describes a lamprey’s pallium, not what was new about the head. The new head was a package of senses in a braincase.

items.stem: A reconstructed early Cambrian fossil shows a small braincase holding paired eyes, a nose and ears, but no jaws and no teeth. Which phrase from the chapter names what the braincase and its contents make up?

options.text: The new head: the package that the anatomists Carl Gans and Glenn Northcutt picked out as distinctive of vertebrates.
options.why: Correct. Gans and Northcutt’s phrase names the package of paired camera eyes, nose, ears and enlarged front of the nervous system, in a braincase.

options.text: The neural crest: the braincase and its sense organs themselves, which only vertebrates have in full.
options.why: The neural crest is a population of cells that builds much of the new head. It is the builder, not the package.

options.text: The notochord: the stiff rod that vertebrates share with their closest invertebrate relatives.
options.why: The notochord runs along the back and is shared with invertebrate relatives, so it is not what was new about the head.

options.text: The brainstem: the stalk connecting the spinal cord to the front of the brain, enlarged to serve the senses of the head.
options.why: The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain together. The package of senses in a braincase is the new head.

items.stem: What is the neural crest?

options.text: A population of cells that forms along the edges of the developing nervous system, then leaves it and migrates through the body.
options.why: Correct. Only vertebrates have it in full, and much of the new head is built from it.

options.text: A ridge of neurons along the roof of the midbrain that holds a map of the space around the animal and turns its eyes toward events.
options.why: That describes the tectum, the roof of the midbrain. The neural crest is a migrating population of embryonic cells.

options.text: A stiff rod running along the back of the embryo, which is later replaced by the backbone in most vertebrates.
options.why: That is the notochord. The neural crest is a population of cells, not a supporting rod.

options.text: A crest of bone along the top of the skull, where the muscles that work the jaws attach in the jawed fishes.
options.why: The name suggests a bony crest, but the neural crest is a population of cells. It does help build the skull, as cartilage and bone.

items.stem: The invertebrate relatives of the vertebrates have cells with some of the neural crest’s features. How does the chapter describe the difference between those relatives and the vertebrates?

options.text: The relatives have cells with some of the features, and only vertebrates have the full set.
options.why: Correct. That is why the chapter calls the neural crest a population that only vertebrates have in full.

options.text: The relatives have the full set too, and vertebrates differ only in having more of those cells.
options.why: If the relatives had the full set, the neural crest would not be a vertebrate novelty. The chapter says only vertebrates have it in full.

options.text: Vertebrates have lost some of the features the relatives have, and gained others the relatives lack.
options.why: The chapter describes no loss. Vertebrates have the whole set of features that the relatives have only some of.

options.text: The relatives’ features arose independently, so the vertebrate crest owes nothing to any older cells or genes.
options.why: The chapter’s point runs the other way. The crest was assembled mostly out of old instructions the relatives already had.

items.stem: What is the hindbrain?

options.text: The rearmost of the three main divisions, continuous with the spinal cord, which controls breathing, the heartbeat and other jobs that keep an animal alive.
options.why: Correct. The spinal cord widens at its front into three divisions, and the hindbrain is the rearmost of them.

options.text: The front of the brain’s three main divisions, whose roof receives signals from the senses and sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.
options.why: That describes the forebrain and its roof, the pallium. The hindbrain is at the other end, joined to the spinal cord.

options.text: The middle of the brain’s three main divisions, whose roof holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and the eyes toward events.
options.why: That describes the midbrain and its roof, the tectum. The hindbrain lies behind the midbrain.

options.text: A large structure attached to the back of the brain, which in jawed vertebrates adjusts movements by learning from the errors they make.
options.why: That is the cerebellum, which is attached to the back of the hindbrain. It is not one of the three main divisions.

items.stem: What is the midbrain?

options.text: The middle of the brain’s three main divisions, lying in front of the hindbrain, with the tectum as its roof.
options.why: Correct. The midbrain sits between the hindbrain and the forebrain, and together with the hindbrain it forms the brainstem.

options.text: The front of the brain’s three main divisions, holding the hypothalamus, the thalamus, the basal ganglia and the pallium.
options.why: That is the forebrain. The midbrain lies behind it.

options.text: The stalk formed by the hindbrain and the forebrain together, which connects the spinal cord to the pallium.
options.why: The stalk is the brainstem, and it is made of the midbrain and hindbrain, not the hindbrain and forebrain.

options.text: The deep middle of the forebrain, where connected clusters of neurons determine which proposed action is released.
options.why: That describes the basal ganglia, deep in the forebrain. The midbrain is a division of its own.

items.stem: What is the tectum?

options.text: The roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears there.
options.why: Correct. The map is built from what the eyes and the other senses report.

options.text: The roof of the forebrain, a sheet of neurons that receives relayed signals from the senses and sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.
options.why: That is the pallium. The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, one division further back.

options.text: A structure in the forebrain that relays signals from the senses into the pallium and carries signals back out again.
options.why: That is the thalamus. The tectum holds a map of surrounding space and turns the head and eyes.

options.text: A large structure on the back of the hindbrain that adjusts movements by learning from their errors.
options.why: That is the cerebellum, found in every jawed vertebrate. The tectum is the roof of the midbrain.

items.stem: A small object moves into view off to one side of a frog, and the frog’s head and eyes turn toward the object. Which structure, the one that received most of the frog’s visual input in Module 2, carries out this turn?

options.text: The tectum, the roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal.
options.why: Correct. The tectum’s map is built from what the eyes and other senses report, and it turns the head and eyes toward what appears there.

options.text: The pallium, the roof of the forebrain, which receives relayed sense signals and sends commands down.
options.why: The pallium does receive sense signals, but most of the frog’s visual input went to the tectum, which does the orienting.

options.text: The thalamus, above the hypothalamus, which relays signals from the senses into the roof of the forebrain.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals into the pallium. The turn toward something in view is the tectum’s job.

options.text: The cerebellum, on the back of the hindbrain, which adjusts movements by learning from their errors.
options.why: The cerebellum tunes movements from their errors. Turning toward an object that has just appeared is the tectum’s job.

items.stem: What is the brainstem?

options.text: The midbrain and hindbrain together, forming the stalk that connects the spinal cord to the front of the brain.
options.why: Correct. The brainstem is two of the three main divisions, taken together.

options.text: The hindbrain and spinal cord together, forming the cord that carries signals between the brain and the rest of the body.
options.why: The spinal cord is not part of the brainstem. The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain.

options.text: The forebrain and midbrain together, forming the swollen front end of the nervous system that sits inside the skull.
options.why: The forebrain is the front of the brain that the brainstem connects to. The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain.

options.text: The thalamus and hypothalamus together, forming the base of the forebrain beneath its roof, the pallium.
options.why: Those two are forebrain structures. The brainstem lies behind the forebrain.

items.stem: What is the forebrain?

options.text: The front of the three main divisions, holding several structures with distinct jobs, among them the hypothalamus, thalamus, basal ganglia and pallium.
options.why: Correct. The forebrain is found in every vertebrate, lamprey included, and holds several structures.

options.text: The front of the brain’s three main divisions, which is found only in mammals and is made up entirely of the six-layered neocortex.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a forebrain. The neocortex is the mammalian form of just one of its structures, the pallium.

options.text: The middle of the brain’s three main divisions, whose roof holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears there.
options.why: That is the midbrain, whose roof is the tectum. The forebrain lies in front of it.

options.text: The swollen front end of the spinal cord, which runs the jobs that keep an animal alive, such as breathing and the heartbeat.
options.why: That describes the hindbrain, the rearmost division. The forebrain is at the other end of the brain.

items.stem: What is the hypothalamus?

options.text: A structure at the base of the forebrain that keeps temperature, water and energy near their set points, and drives the animal to act when they drift.
options.why: Correct. It sits at the base of the forebrain, below the thalamus.

options.text: A structure in the forebrain, just above the thalamus, that relays signals from the senses into the pallium and carries the signals that the pallium sends back out.
options.why: That describes the thalamus, and the thalamus lies above the hypothalamus, not below it.

options.text: A group of connected clusters deep in the forebrain that determine which of the actions being proposed at a given moment is released and which are held back.
options.why: That is the basal ganglia. The hypothalamus keeps internal conditions near their set points.

options.text: The rearmost division of the brain, continuous with the spinal cord, which controls breathing, the heartbeat and the other jobs that keep an animal alive.
options.why: That is the hindbrain. Both keep an animal going, but the hypothalamus is a forebrain structure tracking set points.

items.stem: A lamprey has not eaten for many days, and its energy reserves have drifted well below where they are normally kept. Which structure’s job is it to respond to the drift and drive the animal to act on it?

options.text: The hypothalamus, at the base of the forebrain.
options.why: Correct. Energy is one of the internal conditions the hypothalamus keeps near its set point, and it drives the animal to act when the condition drifts.

options.text: The thalamus, above the hypothalamus in the forebrain.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals from the senses into the pallium. Keeping internal conditions near set points is the hypothalamus’s job.

options.text: The hindbrain, continuous with the spinal cord.
options.why: The hindbrain runs breathing and the heartbeat. The drive to act on a drifting internal condition comes from the hypothalamus.

options.text: The tectum, the roof of the midbrain.
options.why: The tectum turns the head and eyes toward what appears around the animal. It does not track the body’s internal conditions.

items.stem: Signals from a lamprey’s eyes reach the roof of its forebrain, and a command goes back down to its spinal cord. How does the chapter divide that work between the thalamus and the pallium?

options.text: The thalamus relays the sense signals into the pallium; the pallium receives them and sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.
options.why: Correct. The thalamus is the relay, and the pallium is the sheet that receives what is relayed and sends commands down.

options.text: The pallium relays the sense signals into the thalamus; the thalamus receives them and sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.
options.why: That reverses the two. The thalamus relays into the roof, and the roof, the pallium, sends the commands down.

options.text: The thalamus both receives the sense signals and sends the commands down; the pallium only holds on to what the thalamus has sent it.
options.why: The pallium is the structure that sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord. The thalamus relays into it.

options.text: The pallium both relays the sense signals and sends the commands down; the thalamus only keeps internal conditions near their set points.
options.why: Keeping internal conditions near set points is the hypothalamus’s job. The thalamus is the relay into the pallium.

items.stem: What are the basal ganglia?

options.text: A group of connected clusters deep in the forebrain that determine which of the proposed actions is released at a given moment, and which are held back.
options.why: Correct. Every vertebrate has them, lamprey included.

options.text: A group of connected clusters of neurons at the base of the forebrain that keep temperature, water and energy near their set points and drive the animal to act.
options.why: That is the hypothalamus. The basal ganglia determine which proposed action is released.

options.text: A group of nerve cell clusters outside the brain, built by the neural crest, that carry signals from the body’s senses in toward the spinal cord.
options.why: The neural crest does build most of the nerve cells outside the brain, but the basal ganglia lie deep in the forebrain.

options.text: A loose network of cells running the length of the brainstem that sets how awake an animal is and takes it in and out of sleep.
options.why: That is the reticular formation. The basal ganglia are in the forebrain, and they release one proposed action.

items.stem: A lamprey senses food ahead and a predator’s shadow above, and two incompatible actions are proposed at once, approaching and fleeing. Which structure settles the competition, and how?

options.text: The basal ganglia, deep in the forebrain: one proposed action is released and the other is held back.
options.why: Correct. The lecture calls this the something-that-chooses from the argument about competing demands, now with a name.

options.text: The hypothalamus, at the base of the forebrain: whichever proposed action best restores the body’s set points is released.
options.why: The hypothalamus drives the animal to act when internal conditions drift. Settling which proposed action goes ahead is the basal ganglia’s job.

options.text: The tectum, the roof of the midbrain: the head turns toward whichever of the two objects appeared first.
options.why: The tectum turns the head and eyes toward what appears. It does not settle a competition between approaching and fleeing.

options.text: The cerebellum, on the back of the hindbrain: the action that has produced fewer errors in the past is released.
options.why: The cerebellum adjusts movements by learning from their errors, and a lamprey lacks one in the jawed-vertebrate form.

items.stem: What is the pallium?

options.text: The roof of the forebrain, a sheet of neurons that receives relayed sense signals and sends commands down to the brainstem and spinal cord.
options.why: Correct. Every vertebrate has one, thin and three-layered in a lamprey.

options.text: The six-layered roof of the forebrain that is found only in mammals, and that makes up most of the mammalian brain by mass.
options.why: That describes the neocortex, the mammalian form of the pallium. The pallium itself is found in every vertebrate.

options.text: The roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and the eyes toward what appears there.
options.why: That is the tectum. The pallium is the roof of the forebrain.

options.text: A structure just beneath the roof of the forebrain that relays signals from the senses up into the roof and carries signals from the roof back out.
options.why: That is the thalamus, which relays into the pallium.

items.stem: What is the neocortex?

options.text: The six-layered form of the pallium found in mammals, which makes up most of the mammalian brain by mass.
options.why: Correct. It is the mammalian form of a structure every vertebrate has.

options.text: The thin, three-layered pallium of a lamprey, which is the oldest known form of the roof of the forebrain.
options.why: That is the lamprey’s pallium. The neocortex is the six-layered form the pallium took in mammals.

options.text: A new fourth division of the brain, added in front of the forebrain when the first mammals appeared.
options.why: The neocortex is not a separate division. It is the pallium, the roof of the forebrain, in its mammalian form.

options.text: The large, layered structure on the back of the hindbrain that adjusts movements by learning from their errors.
options.why: That is the cerebellum. The neocortex is the roof of the mammalian forebrain.

items.stem: In recent experiments, researchers stimulated points on a lamprey’s pallium with a small electric current. What happened, and what does the chapter conclude from it?

options.text: The lamprey moved its eyes, mouth or body, much as a mammal does when the matching part of its neocortex is stimulated; its brain is not a rough draft of a mammal’s.
options.why: Correct. A thin, three-layered pallium still sends commands down in a mammal-like way, which is part of why the chapter refuses the rough-draft reading.

options.text: Nothing happened, since a thin three-layered pallium is too simple to send commands anywhere; the lamprey’s pallium is only a rough draft of a mammal’s neocortex.
options.why: The stimulation did produce movement, and the chapter draws the opposite conclusion: the lamprey’s brain is not a rough draft.

options.text: The lamprey turned its head toward the stimulated side, since the lamprey’s pallium holds the map of surrounding space; the pallium does the tectum’s job in lampreys.
options.why: Holding a map of surrounding space and turning the head is the tectum’s job, in the lamprey as elsewhere. The stimulation produced eye, mouth and body movements.

options.text: The lamprey’s heartbeat and breathing changed, since the lamprey’s pallium runs the jobs that keep it alive; its parts divide the work differently from a mammal’s.
options.why: Breathing and the heartbeat are the hindbrain’s jobs. The finding is that the lamprey’s pallium behaves much like a mammal’s neocortex.

items.stem: How closely do a lamprey’s basal ganglia resemble a mammal’s?

options.text: They match a mammal’s almost connection for connection, part of why the chapter says a lamprey’s brain is not a rough draft.
options.why: Correct. Wiring that close suggests the basal ganglia were already in place in the common ancestor of lampreys and mammals.

options.text: They share a name with a mammal’s but have none of the same connections, since the two lineages built them separately.
options.why: A lamprey’s basal ganglia match a mammal’s almost connection for connection. Nothing in the chapter says they were built separately.

options.text: They resemble a mammal’s only in their position deep in the forebrain, and not in how their clusters are wired to one another.
options.why: The resemblance is in the wiring, almost connection for connection, not only in position.

options.text: They are missing from the lamprey, since the basal ganglia arose with the jawed fishes after the lamprey’s lineage had split off.
options.why: That describes the cerebellum’s history. Every vertebrate has basal ganglia, the lamprey included.

items.stem: What is the cerebellum?

options.text: A large structure attached to the back of the hindbrain that, in jawed vertebrates, adjusts movements by learning from their errors.
options.why: Correct. Every jawed vertebrate has one, and lampreys and hagfishes lack one in that form.

options.text: A group of connected clusters deep in the front of the forebrain that, in every vertebrate, determines which proposed action is released.
options.why: That is the basal ganglia. The cerebellum is at the back of the brain, on the hindbrain.

options.text: The roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears there.
options.why: That is the tectum. The cerebellum sits behind the midbrain, on the back of the hindbrain.

options.text: The rearmost division of the brain, continuous with the spinal cord, which controls breathing, the heartbeat and other life-sustaining jobs.
options.why: That is the hindbrain itself. The cerebellum is attached to the back of the hindbrain and adjusts movements.

items.stem: What is the name for the large structure attached to the back of the hindbrain which, in jawed vertebrates, adjusts movements by learning from their errors?

options.text: The cerebellum.
options.why: Correct. It is the conspicuous absence in the lamprey’s brain, at least in the form jawed vertebrates have it.

options.text: The brainstem.
options.why: The brainstem is the midbrain and hindbrain themselves. The cerebellum is attached to the back of the hindbrain.

options.text: The basal ganglia.
options.why: The basal ganglia lie deep in the forebrain and determine which proposed action is released.

options.text: The tectum.
options.why: The tectum is the roof of the midbrain and turns the head and eyes. It does not learn from errors of movement.

items.stem: A news headline from 2026 reads, “Lampreys have a cerebellum after all”. How does the chapter state the finding behind the headline?

options.text: A small region, in the place where jawed vertebrates have a cerebellum, holds cells much like some in a fish’s cerebellum, and whether it counts as a simple one is debated.
options.why: Correct. The region lacks the layered structure and the characteristic cells of a jawed vertebrate’s cerebellum, so the chapter keeps the question open.

options.text: A full cerebellum, with the layered structure and characteristic cells of a jawed vertebrate’s, was found in that region, settling that lampreys have one after all.
options.why: The region found lacks the layered structure and the characteristic cells. The chapter treats the question as debated, not settled.

options.text: A small region was found, but its cells resemble nothing in a fish’s cerebellum, settling that lampreys have no cerebellum-like tissue of any kind.
options.why: The region’s cells are much like some in a fish’s cerebellum. The chapter settles the question neither way.

options.text: A cerebellum was found in the hagfishes but not in the lampreys, which shows that the two surviving jawless lineages differ on this point.
options.why: The 2026 study was about the lamprey’s brain. The chapter groups lampreys and hagfishes together as lacking the jawed-vertebrate cerebellum.

items.stem: After learning the parts, a student writes, “The tectum is the orienting structure: orienting is its one job, and every structure has one job like that”. What does the chapter say about job descriptions like this one?

options.text: Each is a first approximation: every structure does more than one thing, and most of what an animal does involves several of them.
options.why: Correct. The one-line descriptions are a starting point, and the chapter flags them as such before filling them in.

options.text: Each is exact: every structure does a single job, which is why each one can be named by the one thing it does and by nothing else.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite. Every structure does more than one thing.

options.text: Each is exact for the lamprey only: its structures do one job apiece, and only in mammals does a structure take on several.
options.why: The chapter’s caveat is not limited to mammals. Every one of these structures does more than one thing.

options.text: Each is a guess to be thrown out: brain structures have no characteristic jobs at all, so naming one tells us nothing about it.
options.why: The descriptions are first approximations, not empty guesses. They are a start, to be filled in rather than discarded.

items.stem: A student reasons, “The basal ganglia pick one action over another, and every vertebrate has basal ganglia, so picking one action over another began with the vertebrates”. What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Choosing one action over another is older than the vertebrates: animals far simpler than a lamprey already did it.
options.why: Correct. Vertebrates added a structure given over to the job, not the job itself. As the lecture puts it, the worm already chose.

options.text: Choosing one action over another is newer than the vertebrates: it began with the mammals, whose basal ganglia added a second output.
options.why: The capacity is older, not newer. Modules 4 and 5 showed it in animals far simpler than a lamprey.

options.text: The basal ganglia do not choose among actions at all: in every vertebrate that job belongs to the cerebellum instead.
options.why: The basal ganglia do determine which proposed action is released. The cerebellum adjusts movements by learning from their errors.

options.text: Not every vertebrate has basal ganglia: lampreys lack them, so choosing one action over another began with the jawed fishes.
options.why: Lampreys have basal ganglia that match a mammal’s almost connection for connection. The structure missing from them is the cerebellum.

items.stem: What does the chapter say vertebrates did and did not add to the nervous systems that came before them?

options.text: They added structures given over largely to one kind of job; the capacities those structures serve already existed.
options.why: Correct. The capacities are old and the structures are new, and even the structures were built from old material.

options.text: They added new capacities, such as learning from reward; the structures that serve those capacities already existed.
options.why: That reverses the claim. Learning from reward appears in Modules 4 and 5, in animals far simpler than a lamprey. What was new was structures for it.

options.text: They added new genes for every kind of cell in the brain; the structures built from those cells already existed.
options.why: The chapter says the kinds of cells neurons are, and much of the genetic material, were already present in invertebrate relatives.

options.text: They added nothing at all; the vertebrate brain’s structures are found unchanged in their invertebrate relatives.
options.why: The structures were new, assembled at or near the origin of the vertebrates. Only the material they were built from was old.

items.stem: The neural crest was new with the vertebrates. At the level of genes, what does the chapter say was actually new about it?

options.text: A further set of genes linking older sets: it switches on at the border of the developing nervous system, starts cells migrating, then hands over to an older set.
options.why: Correct. The crest is the clearest case of a new structure built from old material. Only the linking set was new.

options.text: A new set of genes for making cartilage, which no animal had made before, and which crest cells switch on as soon as they begin to migrate.
options.why: The sets of genes that make cartilage, or a pigment cell, are old. The chapter credits the vertebrates with a set that links them.

options.text: A new set of genes marking the border of the developing nervous system, which the invertebrate relatives lack, and where the crest cells arise.
options.why: The border set is old too; the invertebrate relatives have it. What was new was the set linking it to the others.

options.text: A new set of genes for making pigment cells, which let the first vertebrates change color, and which crest cells switch on once they settle wherever they end up.
options.why: The pigment-cell set is old. The chapter says the only new set is the one that links the older ones.

items.stem: Which one-line summary captures the chapter’s account of what the vertebrate brain added?

options.text: New structures, built from old parts: a new population of cells assembled mostly out of old instructions.
options.why: Correct. The structures were new. The genes, the kinds of cells and the ways cells behave were old.

options.text: Old structures, built from new parts: familiar brain regions rebuilt out of genes that first arose in the vertebrates.
options.why: That reverses the claim. The structures were new with the vertebrates, and the genes behind them were mostly old.

options.text: New structures, built from new parts: brain regions and the genes that make them both invented by the vertebrates.
options.why: The genes and kinds of cells were already present in the invertebrate relatives. Only the structures, and one linking set of genes, were new.

options.text: Old structures, built from old parts: nothing in the vertebrate brain arose after their invertebrate relatives.
options.why: The structures were assembled at or near the origin of the vertebrates, so they were new.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the chapter refuses to treat vertebrate as another word for complex, drawing on what the first vertebrates were like.
items.answer: A vertebrate is an animal with a skull and a backbone, or at least the beginnings of one, which is a fact about body plan, not about complexity. Octopuses and honeybees are not vertebrates, but they are quite complex. And the first vertebrates were not impressive: animals such as Haikouichthys were a few centimeters long, slender and toothless, and most likely prey for the arthropods around them, which were the complex and formidable animals of those seas. Reading vertebrate as complex is the ladder picture of the tree of life that Module 2 warned against.
rubric: Defines a vertebrate by a skull and a backbone, or the beginnings of one.
Names a complex animal that is not a vertebrate, such as the octopus or the honeybee.
Describes the first vertebrates as small, toothless, and most likely prey.
Names the arthropods as the formidable animals of those seas.
Connects the mistake to reading the tree of life as a ladder.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the chapter’s claim that the vertebrate brain added “new structures, built from old parts”, using the neural crest as the example.
items.answer: Vertebrates did not invent the capacities their brain structures serve: approaching and avoiding, arousal, learning from reward and choosing one action over another all appear in much simpler animals. What they added was structures given over largely to those jobs. Even those structures were built from old material. The neural crest is the clearest case. A crest cell becomes cartilage or a pigment cell by switching on a particular set of genes, and those sets are old, as is the set that marks the border of the developing nervous system, where crest cells come from. The invertebrate relatives have all of them. What was new was a further set of genes linking them: it switches on at the border, starts the cells migrating, and hands over to an older set wherever they end up. A new population of cells was assembled mostly out of old instructions.
rubric: Says the capacities, such as learning from reward or choosing an action, predate the vertebrates.
Says the structures were new but the material they were built from was old.
Says the gene sets for cartilage or pigment and for the border of the nervous system are old, present in invertebrate relatives.
Identifies the novelty as a further set of genes linking them: switching on at the border, starting migration, handing over.
Concludes that a new population of cells was assembled mostly out of old instructions.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the chapter says a lamprey’s brain is not a rough draft of a mammal’s, while still naming one way the two differ.
items.answer: The lamprey’s brain already has most of the parts a mammal’s does, and they behave in mammal-like ways. Stimulating a lamprey’s pallium makes the animal move its eyes, its mouth or its body, much as stimulating the corresponding part of a mammal’s neocortex does. And a lamprey’s basal ganglia match a mammal’s almost connection for connection. The two do differ. A lamprey’s pallium is thin and has three layers, while in mammals the same structure grew into the six-layered neocortex, which makes up most of the brain by mass. A difference of that kind is growth of a shared part, not a draft being finished.
rubric: Reports the stimulation result: the lamprey’s pallium produces eye, mouth or body movements, as the mammal’s neocortex does.
Reports that the lamprey’s basal ganglia match a mammal’s almost connection for connection.
Names a difference, such as the thin three-layered pallium against the six-layered neocortex, or the missing jawed-vertebrate cerebellum.
Treats the difference as a change along one lineage, such as the growth of a shared part, rather than as evidence that the lamprey’s brain is unfinished.

items.stem: The first vertebrates had a notochord and a neural crest. How do the two compare in what they say about vertebrate novelty?

options.text: The notochord was shared with the closest invertebrate relatives; the neural crest, in its full form, was the vertebrates’ own.
options.why: Correct. The notochord is shared with the relatives, while only vertebrates have the full set of the crest’s features.

options.text: The neural crest was shared with the closest invertebrate relatives; the notochord, a stiff rod along the back, was the vertebrates’ own.
options.why: That swaps the two. The relatives have a notochord, and they have only some of the crest’s features.

options.text: Both were shared with the closest invertebrate relatives, which is why neither one appears in the chapter’s account of the new head.
options.why: The neural crest builds much of the new head, and only vertebrates have it in full.

options.text: Both were new with the vertebrates, which is why each is counted as part of the package that Gans and Northcutt called the new head.
options.why: The notochord is shared with invertebrate relatives, and in most later vertebrates it is largely replaced by the backbone.

items.stem: The hindbrain and the hypothalamus both do jobs that keep an animal going. How does the chapter tell their jobs apart?

options.text: The hindbrain controls breathing and the heartbeat; the hypothalamus keeps temperature, water and energy near set points and drives the animal to act when they drift.
options.why: Correct. One runs the ongoing jobs that keep an animal alive; the other tracks internal conditions and drives action when they drift.

options.text: The hypothalamus controls breathing and the heartbeat; the hindbrain keeps temperature, water and energy near set points and drives the animal to act when they drift.
options.why: That swaps the two. Breathing and heartbeat belong to the hindbrain, and set points to the hypothalamus.

options.text: Both control breathing and the heartbeat, and they differ only in where they sit: the hindbrain at the back of the brain, the hypothalamus at the base of the forebrain.
options.why: They do sit in those places, but their jobs differ. Only the hypothalamus is described as keeping internal conditions near set points.

options.text: The hindbrain relays signals from the senses into the pallium; the hypothalamus determines which of the proposed actions is released and which are held back.
options.why: Relaying into the pallium is the thalamus’s job, and releasing one proposed action is the basal ganglia’s.

items.stem: The tectum and the pallium are both the roof of a division of the brain. How do they differ?

options.text: The tectum roofs the midbrain and turns the head and eyes toward events; the pallium roofs the forebrain and sends commands down.
options.why: Correct. Both are roofs, of different divisions, with different first-approximation jobs.

options.text: The tectum roofs the forebrain and sends commands down; the pallium roofs the midbrain and turns the head and eyes toward events.
options.why: That swaps the two. The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, and the pallium the roof of the forebrain.

options.text: The tectum is found only in the lamprey; the pallium replaced it in jawed vertebrates as the structure that turns the head and eyes.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a tectum. The pallium did not replace it; the two are roofs of different divisions.

options.text: The tectum roofs the hindbrain and controls breathing; the pallium roofs the midbrain and relays signals from the senses to the thalamus.
options.why: The tectum is the roof of the midbrain, and breathing is the hindbrain’s job. The thalamus relays into the pallium, not the reverse.

items.stem: Worms and insects have heads too. In a few sentences, explain what the chapter says was already old about the head of the first vertebrates, and what was new.
items.answer: Having sense organs and neurons concentrated at the front was not new. Worms and insects have heads, and Module 4 followed neurons gathering at the front of bilaterians, alongside the senses. What was distinctive was a particular package: paired camera eyes, a nose, ears, and a front end of the nervous system enlarged to serve them, all enclosed in a braincase or skull. The anatomists Carl Gans and Glenn Northcutt called this package the new head, and much of it is built by the neural crest.
rubric: Says that concentrating senses and neurons at the front was not itself new.
Gives the evidence: worms and insects have heads, or bilaterians already gathered neurons at the front.
Names the package: paired camera eyes, a nose, ears, and an enlarged front end of the nervous system.
Says the package is enclosed in a braincase or skull, and calls it the new head.

items.stem: The chapter gives each part of the vertebrate brain a one-line job, such as “the basal ganglia determine which proposed action is released”. In a short paragraph, explain how the chapter asks those one-line jobs to be read, and why a one-line job is not the whole story about a structure.
items.answer: The chapter calls every one of these job descriptions a first approximation. Each structure does more than one thing, and most of what an animal does involves several structures at once. So a line such as “the basal ganglia release one proposed action” names one thing the basal ganglia do, not everything they do, and releasing an action is not something the basal ganglia do alone. The one-line job is where an account of a structure starts, not where it ends.
rubric: Calls the job descriptions first approximations, or says so in other words.
Says each structure does more than one thing.
Says most of what an animal does involves several structures at once.
Applies the caveat to a named structure and its one-line job.

pools.title: The Wrong Question, and Two Levels of One Change
pools.covers: reading §6.2.1, §6.2.2 · lecture 6.2 slides the_wrong_question, doyas_question, two_levels_of_a_change · lab Bench

items.stem: What is reverse inference?

options.text: Going from “this region was active during the task” to “therefore, the task involved the process that region does”.
options.why: Correct. It runs backward from an activation to a process, and it licenses little when the region is active during many different things.

options.text: Going from a part that two species both have to the conclusion that their common ancestor most likely had it too.
options.why: That is the comparative inference the chapter uses to read a lamprey’s brain against ours. It concerns ancestry, not what an active region is doing.

options.text: Going from what a synapse needs before it will change to the place in a brain where that information actually arrives.
options.why: That is what Doya’s proposal supplies for each family of learning. Reverse inference is the move from an activation to a process, which is what made the question of what each part is for so hard to answer.

options.text: Going from damage to a structure to the conclusion that the structure is necessary for whatever the damage disrupted in the animal.
options.why: That is the logic of a lesion, which tests necessity. Reverse inference starts from activity recorded during a task, not from damage.

items.stem: A student reads that the cerebellum and the basal ganglia are both active when an animal moves, and concludes that both are movement structures. Which findings reported in the chapter tell against that conclusion?

options.text: Both are also active during perception, planning and thought, and damage to either affects more than movement.
options.why: Correct. Activity during movement is real, but it is not selective, and the effects of damage are not confined to movement either.

options.text: Both fall silent during most movements, and damage to either one leaves the animal’s movements untouched.
options.why: The recordings do find both active during movement. The trouble is that they find both active during a great deal else as well.

options.text: Both are active only while a movement is being learned, and damage to either affects learning but never movement itself.
options.why: The chapter reports activity during movement, perception, planning and thought, with no restriction to learning. Damage affects more than movement, not something other than movement.

options.text: Both are active during movement in mammals but not in fish, so the conclusion holds for some vertebrates and fails for others.
options.why: The chapter’s evidence is not a comparison between lineages. It is about how widely the two structures are active, and the conclusion fails because that activity is not selective.

items.stem: Researchers record from one small piece of the basal ganglia, and the activity they find looks much like the activity of the stretch of pallium that piece exchanges signals with. What does the chapter take this kind of finding to show?

options.text: A structure whose activity looks like whatever it is wired to is not telling us what the structure is for.
options.why: Correct. If a piece mirrors its partner, recording from it tells us about the partner’s traffic, not about a job of its own.

options.text: That piece and that stretch of pallium do the same job, since their activity looks alike, so one of the two is redundant.
options.why: Similar activity does not show that two structures do the same work. The chapter’s point is that the resemblance makes the recording uninformative about purpose.

options.text: That piece is only copying the pallium’s signal, which shows that the basal ganglia compute nothing of their own.
options.why: The chapter draws no conclusion about what the basal ganglia compute from this finding. It concludes only that the recording does not reveal a job.

options.text: The pallium must be the true source of every job the basal ganglia have been credited with doing.
options.why: The finding says nothing about where jobs come from. It says that a structure’s activity, when it mirrors its connections, cannot be read as its purpose.

items.stem: What question did the neuroscientist Kenji Doya propose asking about each structure of a vertebrate brain, in place of what each one is for?

options.text: How each one learns, so that each structure is specialized in a method rather than in a job.
options.why: Correct. On Doya’s proposal a structure is identified by the way it learns, and one method can serve many jobs.

options.text: How each one evolved, so that each structure is identified by the lineage in which it first arose.
options.why: Where a structure arose is the comparative question the chapter asks elsewhere. Doya’s replacement question is about learning.

options.text: What each one is wired to, so that each structure’s job can be read directly off its connections.
options.why: Reading a job off the wiring is exactly what fails when a structure’s activity mirrors whatever it is wired to. Doya asks how each one learns.

options.text: When each one forms in the embryo, so that each structure is defined by the stage of development that builds it.
options.why: Development is how the brain is built, not the replacement question. Doya asks what method of learning each structure is specialized in.

items.stem: What does the chapter mean by a division of labor?

options.text: An arrangement in which different parts of a system take on different work, rather than each part doing everything.
options.why: Correct. On Doya’s version of it, the parts differ in how they learn rather than in which job they do.

options.text: An arrangement in which every part of a system can do all of the work, so that any part can stand in for any other.
options.why: That describes interchangeable parts, the opposite of a division. In a division of labor different parts take on different work.

options.text: An arrangement in which one part of a system directs all the others and hands each of them its work in turn.
options.why: A director handing out work is a hierarchy of command. A division of labor needs only that different parts do different work.

options.text: An arrangement in which the work is split across time, one part doing everything early and another taking over later.
options.why: Splitting work by time is not what the chapter means. The division is among parts working at once, each on different work.

items.stem: By the chapter’s test, what makes a claim about a brain algorithmic rather than implementational?

options.text: It would hold of a system built out of something else entirely.
options.why: Correct. An algorithmic claim survives a change of material. An implementational claim turns on which cells, which chemicals, and where they sit.

options.text: It names the cells involved, the chemicals they use, and where they sit.
options.why: That is the mark of an implementational claim. An algorithmic claim would hold of a system built from something else.

options.text: It states what problem the animal had to solve in its world, whatever the method.
options.why: A statement of the problem is computational. The test separates the two lower levels, algorithm and implementation.

options.text: It can be checked by recording from the cells that carry it out in a living animal.
options.why: How a claim is checked does not settle its level. The test asks whether the claim would hold of a system built of something else.

items.stem: An engineer builds a walking robot whose motors are all braked by default, and which makes a move by releasing the brake on one motor. Which claim about vertebrate action selection does the robot share with a vertebrate?

options.text: Hold every action back and release one, since that claim would hold of a system built out of something else entirely.
options.why: Correct. That is why the chapter calls it algorithmic: a robot could work that way, and so could a simulation.

options.text: The basal ganglia do it with dopamine and two opposed pathways, since the robot also holds some motors and frees others.
options.why: The robot has no basal ganglia and no dopamine. That claim is implementational and holds only of a particular kind of tissue.

options.text: No claim at all is shared, since claims about vertebrate action selection are claims about vertebrate cells and do not apply to machines.
options.why: Only the implementational claim is tied to vertebrate cells. The algorithmic claim is exactly the kind that carries over to a machine.

options.text: The claims about releasing one action and about dopamine together, since a robot that chooses the same way must be built the same way.
options.why: Working the same way does not require being built the same way. The dopamine claim is implementational, so the robot does not share it.

items.stem: The four kinds of learning from Module 5 were sorted by what has to reach a synapse before it will change. What did that sorting leave open, which Doya’s proposal addresses?

options.text: Whether an animal has any way to deliver that information, and where in a brain it actually arrives.
options.why: Correct. A requirement is not a delivery. Doya’s proposal names, for each family, the place in a vertebrate brain where the required information turns up.

options.text: Which of the four families an animal is using at a given moment, which the proposal settles from its behavior.
options.why: The proposal is not about identifying the family from behavior. It is about where each family’s required information arrives.

options.text: How fast each kind of synapse changes once its information arrives, which the proposal settles by measuring rates.
options.why: Speed of change is not the gap. Knowing what a change requires left open whether and where the animal can deliver it.

options.text: Why the four families evolved in the order they did, which the proposal settles by comparing living species.
options.why: The proposal is not an evolutionary history. It fills the gap between what a synapse requires and what a brain delivers.

items.stem: The chapter warns that two different things get called learning and must be kept distinct. What are they?

options.text: What the whole animal ends up able to do, and the change at an individual connection.
options.why: Correct. A family of learning is usually named for the first, such as finding food or avoiding what hurt it last time, while the change itself happens at the second.

options.text: What the animal learns by itself, and what it is taught by another animal of its species.
options.why: Self-taught against taught is a distinction about sources of a target. The chapter’s two levels are the animal and the connection.

options.text: What the animal learns while young, and what it goes on learning once it is fully grown.
options.why: Age is not the distinction. The two things called learning are the animal’s new ability and the change at a synapse.

options.text: What the animal learns that lasts for life, and what it learns that fades within minutes.
options.why: Duration is not the distinction here. The chapter separates the animal-level ability from the connection-level change.

items.stem: An animal turned right when turning left would have found food. Why can no single synapse in its brain be told “the animal should have turned left”?

options.text: A synapse cannot understand the meaning of anything that complex; what reaches it must be about its own inputs and output.
options.why: Correct. The animal-level mistake has to be turned into information about one connection’s own activity before that connection can use it.

options.text: A synapse can be told only whether food arrived, and turning left and turning right would each have earned exactly the same food.
options.why: That describes a reward signal, which is one kind of information a synapse can use. The general point is that anything reaching a synapse must be local.

options.text: No such signal exists anywhere in a brain, since no part of an animal ever holds information about its own mistakes.
options.why: Parts of a brain can hold information about outcomes. The problem is that a single connection cannot use a message about the whole animal.

options.text: The signal would arrive too late to be used, since a synapse stops being able to change once the movement ends.
options.why: Timing is not the chapter’s reason. The reason is that a synapse can use only information about its own inputs and output.

items.stem: A young animal learns to keep its eyes on a moving target. Stated as the chapter’s pairing, what are the two halves of this family of learning?

options.text: Keeping the eyes on target, and the information that must reach a synapse for that synapse to help with it.
options.why: Correct. Every family is an animal-level problem paired with a synapse-level requirement, and both halves have to be named.

options.text: The eye muscles that follow the target, and the brain structure that sends those muscles their commands.
options.why: Muscles and a structure are parts of the body, not the two halves of a family. The pairing is a problem and a requirement at a synapse.

options.text: The learning the animal does on its own, and the correction that a watching parent provides whenever the young animal errs.
options.why: The pairing is not self-taught against taught. It joins an animal-level problem to what a synapse needs.

options.text: The part of the skill present at birth, and the part the animal picks up after it opens its eyes.
options.why: Innate against learned is not the pairing. The two halves are the animal’s problem and what must arrive at a connection.

items.stem: Someone sets out to find where reinforcement learning happens in a vertebrate brain by finding where the animal’s goals are represented. On the chapter’s two levels, what is wrong with the plan?

options.text: The anatomical question is where a verdict gets delivered to the synapses that produced the action, not where the goals are.
options.why: Correct. Anatomy answers the synapse-level half of the pairing. The lecture puts it outright: the question is not where the animal’s goals are.

options.text: Goals are represented throughout the whole brain, so the question has no single answer and should be given up as badly formed.
options.why: The chapter treats the question as well formed once it is aimed at the right half of the pairing, the delivery of a verdict.

options.text: The plan is sound, since reinforcement learning is defined by the goals the animal is trying to reach.
options.why: The family is named for an animal-level problem, but the anatomical question concerns what reaches a synapse. Goals are the wrong target.

options.text: Reinforcement learning happens nowhere in particular, since a verdict is not addressed to particular outputs.
options.why: A verdict not addressed to particular outputs still has to be delivered somewhere. Where it is delivered is exactly the anatomical question.

items.stem: Suppose we want evidence that one part of a brain is for moving. The usual proposals are to record from it, to damage it, and to trace its wiring. Which result would cast the most doubt on the claim?

options.text: The part is active during movement, and just as active during perception, planning and thought.
options.why: Correct. For the cerebellum and the basal ganglia, the chapter reports each of these doubts: activity during many other things, damage that affects more than movement, and activity that mirrors whatever the part is connected to.

options.text: The part is active whenever the animal moves, and it falls quiet whenever the animal holds still.
options.why: That pattern would support the claim, since the activity tracks movement selectively. The doubt comes from activity that is not selective.

options.text: Damage to the part leaves the animal unable to move, and it leaves perception and thought unchanged.
options.why: Damage confined to movement would support the claim. The real finding for the cerebellum and basal ganglia is that damage affects more than movement.

options.text: The part’s outputs run directly to the circuits that drive the muscles, and to nothing else in the brain.
options.why: Wiring confined to the motor circuits would count in favor. Doubt comes when a part’s activity simply mirrors whatever it is wired to.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the chapter’s two levels of a single change in learning, and use them to say what the question “where does reinforcement learning happen?” is really asking.
items.answer: Two different things get called learning. A family of learning is usually named for what the whole animal ends up able to do, such as finding food or avoiding what hurt it last time. But the change itself happens at individual connections, and a single synapse cannot be told what the animal should have done, since it has no way to understand the meaning of anything that complex. Whatever reaches a synapse has to be about its own inputs and its own output. So each family is a pairing: an animal-level problem, and the particular information that has to reach a synapse for the synapse to help solve it. Anatomy answers the second half. Asking where reinforcement learning happens is asking where the machinery is that delivers a verdict to the synapses that produced the action, not where the animal’s goals are.
rubric: Names the animal-level half: what the whole animal ends up able to do.
Names the synapse-level half: the change at an individual connection, which can use only information about its own inputs and output.
States that each family of learning is a pairing of the two.
Says the anatomical question concerns the second half, what has to reach the synapse.
Applies it to reinforcement learning as where a verdict is delivered to the synapses that produced the action.

items.stem: One team proposes that a brain structure is set apart by the job it does, such as timing movements. A second team proposes that each structure is set apart by how its connections change. How do the two proposals differ?

options.text: Both divide the labor, but the first divides it by job and the second by method, so one structure can serve many jobs.
options.why: Correct. On the second proposal, each structure is specialized in a method of learning rather than in a job, and that is still a division of labor.

options.text: The first is a division of labor and the second is not, since a structure defined by how it learns could do any job at all.
options.why: Both are divisions of labor, with different parts taking on different work. They differ in what counts as the work.

options.text: The first is an algorithmic claim and the second an implementational one, since how connections change is a fact about cells.
options.why: A method of learning could hold of a system built of something else entirely, so specializing by method is an algorithmic claim.

options.text: The two are the same proposal stated twice, since timing is simply the method by which that structure happens to learn.
options.why: Timing movements is a job. A method is how a structure learns, such as from an error delivered output by output.

pools.title: Learning Without a Teacher, from an Error, and from a Verdict
pools.covers: reading §6.2.3, §6.2.4, §6.2.5 · lecture 6.2 slides learning_without_a_teacher, error_output_by_output, learning_from_a_verdict · lab Bench

items.stem: A rat hears a tone, and food arrives a moment later. Why does the connection from the cells carrying the tone to the cells driving the response to food get stronger?

options.text: Food already makes the response cells fire, and the tone cells are firing at that same moment, so both ends of the connection are active together.
options.why: Correct. Both ends active together is the entire condition Hebb’s rule requires, and nothing else has to reach the connection.

options.text: The food releases a reward signal that reaches the tone connection and reports that the tone was the right thing for the rat to have heard at that moment.
options.why: A reward signal is what reinforcement learning uses. The tone connection strengthens simply because both of its ends are active together.

options.text: The rat notices that the tone predicts food and strengthens the connection because doing so will bring it food more quickly.
options.why: Nothing in the rat has to know that the tone predicts food. That is what makes the learning unsupervised.

options.text: An error signal reports that the response cells fired too late after the tone, and the tone connection is adjusted until the timing is right.
options.why: An error about timing is what the rabbit’s blink needs, delivered by a climbing fiber. The rat’s tone connection needs only co-occurrence.

items.stem: A tone is paired again and again with a second stimulus that produces no response of any kind in an untrained animal. On the chapter’s account of what happens at the synapse, what becomes of the connection from the cells carrying the tone to the response cells?

options.text: It does not change, since nothing makes the response cells fire and so there is no co-occurrence to detect.
options.why: Correct. That is what an unconditioned stimulus is for at the synapse: something has to make the postsynaptic cell fire, or nothing changes.

options.text: It strengthens, since the tone and the second stimulus arrive together in time on every single pairing.
options.why: Two stimuli arriving together is not enough. The rule needs both ends of the tone connection active, and the response cells never fire.

options.text: It weakens, since the second stimulus fails to produce a response and so counts as an error for the tone.
options.why: No error is computed in unsupervised learning. With no firing at the response cells, there is simply nothing for the rule to detect.

options.text: It strengthens slowly, since a weak second stimulus still adds a little activity at the response cells each time.
options.why: The second stimulus produces no response at all, so it adds no activity at the response cells. There is nothing for the connection to pair with.

items.stem: Run the co-occurrence rule across everything an animal senses. What do its connections come to mirror, and how does that relate to learning the statistics of its input?

options.text: Which things in its world turn up together; learning that and learning the statistics of the input are one event described at two levels.
options.why: Correct. What goes with what, at the level of the animal, is the statistics of the input, at the level of the connections.

options.text: Which things in its world were followed by a reward; learning that and learning the statistics of the input are two separate processes at work.
options.why: Reward plays no part in the co-occurrence rule. What the connections mirror is simply what turns up together.

options.text: Which of its movements succeeded; learning that and learning the statistics of the input happen in two different structures.
options.why: Success of a movement needs an error or a verdict. The co-occurrence rule mirrors only which things turn up together.

options.text: Which things the animal attended to; learning that and learning the statistics of the input compete for the same connections.
options.why: The rule needs no attention; it strengthens whatever is active together. The two descriptions are of one event, not two in competition.

items.stem: What did the blocking result show about actual conditioning, and what does that mean for the co-occurrence rule as an account of conditioning?

options.text: Conditioning tracks only what was not already predicted, so the rule is the beginning of an account rather than the whole.
options.why: Correct. A bare co-occurrence rule would strengthen every cue that co-occurs. Real conditioning does not, so something more is at work.

options.text: Conditioning tracks every co-occurrence equally, so the co-occurrence rule is a complete account of conditioning.
options.why: That is exactly what blocking ruled out. Conditioning skips cues whose outcome was already predicted.

options.text: Conditioning is blocked whenever no teacher is present, so the co-occurrence rule needs a teacher to supply the part that is missing.
options.why: Blocking has nothing to do with teachers. It shows that conditioning tracks what was not already predicted.

options.text: Conditioning blocks background sounds such as a ventilation fan automatically, so the fan problem never arises in practice.
options.why: Blocking concerns cues that add no new prediction. It does not rescue the rule from strengthening the fan’s connection.

items.stem: Co-occurrence-sensitive synapses are found throughout a vertebrate brain. Why, then, does Doya single out the pallium as the place where unsupervised learning is particularly important?

options.text: Because nothing else arrives there, not because coincidence detection happens only in the pallium.
options.why: Correct. The case is an argument from absence: with no teaching pathway, the statistics of the pallium’s own input are all it has.

options.text: Because coincidence detection happens in the pallium and nowhere else, so the pallium is where this learning must occur.
options.why: That gets the argument backwards. Coincidence detection happens everywhere; the pallium is singled out because nothing else arrives there.

options.text: Because the pallium is the newest structure in the vertebrate brain, and newer structures are the more flexible learners.
options.why: The pallium is present in every vertebrate, including the lamprey. Its claim rests on what does not arrive there, not on its age.

options.text: Because a teaching pathway into the pallium has been traced, and it carries a signal reporting what went together.
options.why: No dedicated teaching pathway into the pallium has been found. That absence is the whole basis of its claim.

items.stem: A rabbit hears a tone, and a quarter of a second later a puff of air is delivered to its eye. After training, what does the rabbit do?

options.text: It closes its eye at just the right time, so the eye is already closed when the puff arrives.
options.why: Correct. The rabbit predicts the puff from the tone and times its blink to meet it.

options.text: It closes its eye as soon as the tone begins, and keeps the eye shut until the tone has stopped.
options.why: Closing at the tone’s onset would not be timed to the puff. What the rabbit learns is exactly when to blink.

options.text: It blinks only after the puff lands on its eye, but a little faster than it did before training.
options.why: A faster reflex after the puff would still leave the puff landing on an open eye. The trained blink comes before the puff.

options.text: It stops blinking to the puff altogether, having learned that the puff does it no lasting harm.
options.why: The rabbit learns to meet the puff, not to ignore it. Its eye is closed when the puff arrives.

items.stem: The rat’s tone and food, and the rabbit’s tone and puff, are both classical conditioning at the animal level. What does the chapter say differs between them?

options.text: What had to change: an association between two events for the rat, and the timing of one output for the rabbit.
options.why: Correct. A co-occurrence rule can deliver the association but not the timing, so one animal-level name covers two synapse-level requirements.

options.text: The animal-level name: the rat’s case is classical conditioning, but the rabbit’s is really reinforcement learning.
options.why: The chapter says both are classical conditioning at the animal level. The difference is in what had to change at the synapse.

options.text: The sense involved: the rat hears its signal while the rabbit feels one, and different senses learn by different rules.
options.why: Both animals hear a tone first. The difference lies in what had to change, not in which sense carried the second event.

options.text: The species: rodents learn by co-occurrence and rabbits by error, so the same task is learned differently between the two.
options.why: The difference is in the task, not the species. A task needing an association and a task needing timing make different demands.

items.stem: Two prediction problems both produce a guess about what comes next. The chapter still assigns them to different structures. What principle does it use to sort them?

options.text: The sorting goes by what has to be delivered to the synapse, rather than by what is being computed.
options.why: Correct. Two problems can compute the same kind of guess and still differ in whether an error has to be carried from elsewhere.

options.text: The sorting goes by which sense the prediction concerns, since each sense has its own structure for predicting.
options.why: The chapter does not sort by sense. It sorts by what has to be delivered, which is why prediction splits between two structures.

options.text: The sorting goes by what the animal is trying to achieve, since problems with different goals need different structures.
options.why: Goals belong to the animal-level half of the pairing. The sorting into structures uses the synapse-level half, what has to arrive.

options.text: The sorting goes by whether the prediction was learned or inborn, since learned predictions need a structure of their own.
options.why: Both problems are learned. What separates them is whether anything has to be carried between structures.

items.stem: Which part of prediction learning is the cerebellum’s share?

options.text: The part where the animal’s own output is what the prediction is about.
options.why: Correct. Predicting the next sensation is prediction learning too, and it stays in the pallium. The cerebellum takes the output-bound part.

options.text: All of it, since the cerebellum is the structure where prediction learning happens.
options.why: Predicting the next sensation involves no output and happens in the pallium. The cerebellum’s share is limited to predictions about output.

options.text: The part that concerns sensations from the eyes, such as a drifting leaf.
options.why: A drifting leaf is the chapter’s example of prediction with no output, and it stays in the pallium.

options.text: The part that is learned from rewards, such as food after a lever press.
options.why: Reward-driven learning is reinforcement, delivered to the striatum. The cerebellum learns from errors about output.

items.stem: A young songbird that has heard an adult sing practices against its memory of the song. Why does the chapter not count this as a true teacher?

options.text: No part of the bird holds the right motor command; it compares each attempt with the remembered song and works from the mismatch.
options.why: Correct. The target is one the bird manufactured from memory, not a correct output handed to the connections that got it wrong.

options.text: The adult is no longer present during practice, and a teacher counts as one only when it is present during each of the learner’s attempts.
options.why: Presence is not the chapter’s criterion. Even with the adult present, no part of the young bird would hold the right motor command.

options.text: A songbird has no cerebellum, so there is no route by which an error about its singing could be delivered at all.
options.why: Songbirds are jawed vertebrates and have a cerebellum. The problem is that nothing holds the correct command, not that no route exists.

options.text: The remembered song fades from one day to the next, so the target keeps changing and never settles into one answer.
options.why: The chapter says nothing about the memory fading. The bird has a target; what it lacks is anything holding the right command.

items.stem: Why can a synapse on a cerebellar output cell not tell prediction learning apart from supervised learning?
