options.text: What arrives on the climbing fiber is an error for that one cell, and the fiber does not report who supplied the target.
options.why: Correct. The two families do differ, in where the target comes from. The synapse cannot see that difference, so the two share a structure.

options.text: The two families differ in nothing at all, so there is no difference for the synapse, or for anything else in the brain, to detect.
options.why: They differ in where the target comes from, the world or a teacher. The point is that the synapse cannot tell which.

options.text: Both families arrive by dopamine, and the dopamine signal is the same whichever family produced it.
options.why: Neither family arrives by dopamine; both arrive on climbing fibers. Dopamine carries the reinforcement verdict.

options.text: The synapse can tell them apart, but the cerebellum as a whole ignores the difference when it adjusts the output.
options.why: The chapter’s claim is about the synapse itself. The fiber carries only an error, with no mark of who set the target.

items.stem: Prediction learning and supervised learning share the cerebellum. Where do most of the targets the cerebellum learns from come from?

options.text: From the world: a slipping image, a reach that missed, a swallow that went wrong.
options.why: Correct. A teacher is the exotic case, so most of the cerebellum’s errors come from targets the world supplies.

options.text: From a teacher: an instructor’s correction, or a parent guiding the young animal along.
options.why: Teachers almost never exist inside an animal. Most of the cerebellum’s targets are the world’s.

options.text: From the body: a full stomach, an injury, or a sudden change in temperature.
options.why: A full stomach or an injury is the kind of verdict reinforcement learning uses. The cerebellum learns from errors about output.

options.text: From the pallium: the statistics of whatever the senses happened to bring in.
options.why: Input statistics are what the pallium learns from, with nothing delivered. The cerebellum’s errors come from the world’s targets.

items.stem: When the rat eats the pellet, what arrives at a synapse?

options.text: A broadcast signal reporting only that things went better than expected, addressed to no particular output.
options.why: Correct. It says nothing about what would have worked instead. The animal-level problem is rich; the synapse-level signal is thin.

options.text: A signal telling the cells that produced the lever press that pressing was the right action to take.
options.why: A signal like that would be addressed to particular outputs, and the reward signal is not. It reports only how things went.

options.text: An error for each cell that drove the press, reporting how far each movement was from the ideal press.
options.why: An error per output is what climbing fibers deliver in the cerebellum. The reward signal is not addressed cell by cell.

options.text: Nothing at all, since the pellet is eaten too long after the press for any signal to reach the right synapses.
options.why: A signal does arrive; the gap in time is what Module 5’s traces bridge. The signal itself is a broadcast verdict.

items.stem: On its way to the lever, the rat groomed and sniffed. The reward signal is addressed to no particular output. What sorts the grooming and sniffing from the lever press?

options.text: The traces and estimates of future outcomes described in Module 5, since the signal itself cannot say which action earned it.
options.why: Correct. The verdict does not pick out the press. Module 5’s traces and estimates do the sorting.

options.text: The reward signal itself, since it is delivered only to the synapses that produced the press and not to the others.
options.why: The reward signal is not addressed to particular outputs, so it cannot pick out the press. Something else must do the sorting.

options.text: The climbing fibers, since they report an error to the cells that drove the grooming and to the cells that drove the sniffing.
options.why: Climbing fibers carry errors in the cerebellum for prediction and supervised learning. They do not sort actions by reward.

options.text: Nothing does, so grooming and sniffing are strengthened exactly as much as the press, and the rat grooms more from then on.
options.why: The chapter names what does the sorting, the traces and estimates of future outcomes. The problem is real but it is handled.

items.stem: What is the striatum?

options.text: The input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium arrive and the dopamine fibers meet them.
options.why: Correct. It is where the reward signal meets the pallium’s report of the situation, which is what makes a thin signal useful there.

options.text: The roof of the midbrain, which holds a map of the space around the animal and turns the head and eyes toward what appears.
options.why: That is the tectum. The striatum is in the forebrain, at the input stage of the basal ganglia.

options.text: A large structure attached to the back of the hindbrain, which learns from errors delivered to it one output cell at a time.
options.why: That is the cerebellum, which receives climbing fibers. The striatum receives dopamine fibers.

options.text: A structure above the hypothalamus that relays signals from the senses into the pallium and carries signals back out.
options.why: That is the thalamus. The striatum is where the pallium’s signals enter the basal ganglia.

items.stem: At the algorithmic level the reward signal is usually written as a single number. The dopamine cells, though, are a population, and what they report differs from one target to another. What survives either description?

options.text: The signal is not addressed to particular outputs, so it cannot say what any one of them should have done.
options.why: Correct. The chapter qualifies the single number and then keeps what matters for the argument: the signal is unaddressed.

options.text: The signal is identical everywhere it lands, since a population of cells can still report one shared number.
options.why: The chapter says what the dopamine cells report is not identical everywhere. The single number is an idealization.

options.text: The signal tells each striatal cell which action was right, since a population can address each target separately.
options.why: Differences across targets do not make the signal an instruction. It still cannot say what any output should have done.

options.text: The signal carries a separate error to each output cell, much as a climbing fiber does in the cerebellum.
options.why: An error addressed to each output cell is the climbing-fiber arrangement. The dopamine signal is not addressed to outputs.

items.stem: The reward signal is thin: it says only that things went better than expected. Why is so thin a signal useful at the synapses where the pallium meets the striatum?

options.text: Those synapses join the pallium’s report of the situation to units that propose actions, so strengthening one makes an action likelier to win there.
options.why: Correct. Strengthening there corrects no output, and it does not need to, because the rat’s problem was only to press more often in that chamber.

options.text: Those synapses drive the muscles directly, so strengthening one corrects the movement the pallium has just commanded.
options.why: The striatum does not drive muscles directly, and the signal corrects no output. It shifts which action wins.

options.text: Those synapses also receive climbing fibers from below the cerebellum, which add the detail about what should have been done that the reward signal lacks.
options.why: Climbing fibers arrive in the cerebellum, not the striatum. The reward signal is useful without any added detail.

options.text: Those synapses are so few that a single number is enough to address each of them separately in turn.
options.why: The signal is not addressed to particular synapses at all. Its usefulness comes from what the synapses connect.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how a rule that needs nothing but the two cells a connection joins produces classical conditioning in a rat that hears a tone before food, and say why the chapter calls that rule only the beginning of an account of conditioning.
items.answer: Food already makes the response cells fire without training. The cells carrying the tone contact those same response cells and are firing at the same moment, so both ends of the tone connection are active together, which is all Hebb’s rule requires. The tone connection strengthens, and after enough pairings the tone alone drives the response. This is unsupervised, because nothing in the rat had to know the tone predicted food. But the same rule strengthens the connection carrying the sound of a ventilation fan that happened to be running, and blocking showed that actual conditioning tracks only what was not already predicted. So a co-occurrence rule is the beginning of an account, not the whole of one.
rubric: Says food already makes the response cells fire, and the tone cells fire at the same moment.
Says both ends of the tone connection being active together strengthens it, until the tone alone drives the response.
Says the learning is unsupervised because nothing in the rat had to know the tone predicted food.
Gives at least one limit: the fan’s sound is strengthened too, or blocking shows conditioning tracks only what was not already predicted.
Concludes that the rule is the beginning of an account of conditioning rather than the whole.

items.stem: Prediction learning and supervised learning are different families, yet the chapter assigns both to the cerebellum. In a short paragraph, say how the two families differ, and explain why they nonetheless share a structure.
items.answer: The two differ in where the target comes from. In prediction learning the world supplies it a moment later, as when the puff tells the rabbit its blink was mistimed. In supervised learning a teacher that already knows the answer supplies it, and at the level of the animal such a teacher almost never exists. But both need the same thing at a synapse: an error computed for one output. In the cerebellum each output cell gets a single climbing fiber that reports the error for that cell. The fiber does not report whether the world or a teacher set the target, so a synapse cannot tell the two families apart, and they share the structure. Most of what the cerebellum learns from is the world’s targets, such as a slipping image or a reach that missed.
rubric: States that the families differ in where the target comes from: the world, or a teacher that holds the answer.
States that both need an error for one output delivered to the synapse.
Names the climbing fiber as delivering one error to one cerebellar output cell.
Explains that the fiber does not report who supplied the target, so a synapse cannot tell the families apart.

items.stem: A rat learns to press a lever that delivers food. In a short paragraph, state this case as the chapter’s pairing of an animal-level problem with what reaches a synapse, and explain why a signal that corrects no output is still enough.
items.answer: At the animal level the whole of the problem is that the rat has to end up pressing that lever more often in that chamber. At a synapse, what arrives when the pellet is eaten is a broadcast signal reporting only that things went better than expected. It is addressed to no particular output and says nothing about what would have worked instead. Dopamine neurons of the midbrain carry it to the synapses where the pallium meets the striatum. Those synapses join the pallium’s report of the situation the animal is in to the units that propose actions. So strengthening one of them corrects no output, but it makes one action more likely to win in one kind of situation, which is exactly what the rat had to end up doing.
rubric: States the animal-level problem as pressing that lever more often in that chamber.
States the synapse-level signal as a broadcast report that things went better than expected, addressed to no particular output.
Places its delivery at the synapses where the pallium meets the striatum, carried by midbrain dopamine neurons.
Says those synapses connect a report of the situation to units that propose actions.
Concludes that strengthening there makes one action more likely to win in that situation, which is all the problem requires.

items.stem: Supervised learning, with a teacher supplying the correct output, was ranked as the exotic case of learning. Yet the cerebellum learns from errors all the time. How do the two fit together?

options.text: A teacher almost never exists at the level of the animal, and most of the cerebellum’s errors are supplied by the world instead: a slipping image, a missed reach.
options.why: Correct. The cerebellum’s machinery would serve a teacher, but what actually reaches it is mostly error the world supplies, which is prediction learning.

options.text: A teacher exists inside every vertebrate, and the cerebellum is that teacher, holding the correct motor command for every movement in advance.
options.why: No part of the animal holds the correct output in advance. That is why a teacher is the exotic case, and why even the songbird manufactures its own target.

options.text: The cerebellum learns only in the rare cases where another animal demonstrates a movement, so its errors are rare in practice as well.
options.why: The cerebellum learns constantly, from a slipping image, a reach that missed, a swallow that went wrong. Those errors come from the world, not from a demonstrator.

options.text: The cerebellum learns without any error at all, from co-occurrence alone, so neither teachers nor errors bear on what it learns.
options.why: Learning from co-occurrence alone is unsupervised learning. The cerebellum is where errors delivered output by output arrive, along the climbing fibers.

pools.title: Three Structures, and Working Together
pools.covers: reading §6.2.6, §6.2.7 · lecture 6.2 slides four_families_three_structures, maps_and_loops · lab Bench

items.stem: Module 5 described four families of learning, but the chapter assigns them to only three structures in a vertebrate brain. Why are three enough?

options.text: Prediction learning and supervised learning differ in where the target comes from, but both need the same thing at a synapse: an error for each output.
options.why: Correct. Two of the four families make the same demand of a synapse, so one delivery route, the climbing fibers of the cerebellum, serves both.

options.text: Unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning both need a single number reporting how things went, so one structure can deliver it for both.
options.why: Only reinforcement learning needs a verdict. Unsupervised learning needs nothing delivered at all, since both quantities it uses are already at the connection.

options.text: Supervised learning almost never happens in vertebrates, so the chapter drops that family and gives one structure to each of the remaining three.
options.why: A teacher is the exotic case, but supervised learning is not dropped. It shares the climbing fibers with prediction learning.

options.text: Prediction learning happens everywhere in the brain rather than in one place, so it needs no structure of its own, and each of the other three families gets one.
options.why: Predicting the next sensation does happen in the pallium’s own circuitry, but prediction learning about the animal’s own output is the cerebellum’s. The pairing is with supervised learning.

items.stem: A lamprey has two of the three learning structures in Doya’s proposal. Which one is missing, and when did it arrive?

options.text: The structure specialized for errors delivered output by output, which arrived later, with the jawed fishes.
options.why: Correct. The cerebellum, in the form jawed vertebrates have it, arrived with the jawed fishes. The lamprey already has the other two.

options.text: The structure specialized for a broadcast verdict, which arrived later, with the first mammals.
options.why: A lamprey already has dopamine delivered to its striatum; a lamprey whose dopamine is depleted has trouble starting movements. The missing structure is the one for errors delivered output by output.

options.text: The structure specialized for learning with nothing delivered, which arrived later, with the first land animals.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the lamprey included. The missing structure is the one for errors delivered output by output.

options.text: The structure specialized for errors delivered output by output, which arose before any vertebrate and was then lost in the lamprey’s lineage.
options.why: The structure is right, but the history is not. The chapter says it arrived later, with the jawed fishes, not that the lamprey’s lineage lost it.

items.stem: A lamprey has two of the three learning structures. If Doya’s mapping holds, which families of learning have their structure in a lamprey, and which lack the structure specialized for them?

options.text: Unsupervised and reinforcement learning have theirs; prediction and supervised learning lack the one specialized for errors delivered to each output.
options.why: Correct. A lamprey has a pallium and a striatum reached by dopamine fibers. The cerebellum in its jawed form, which serves both error-driven families, is the one it lacks.

options.text: Prediction and supervised learning have theirs; unsupervised and reinforcement learning lack the ones specialized for them, which arrived with the mammals.
options.why: That reverses it. A lamprey has a pallium and a striatum reached by dopamine; the structure for errors delivered output by output is the later one.

options.text: Unsupervised, prediction and reinforcement learning all have theirs; only supervised learning lacks one, because a vertebrate almost never has a teacher.
options.why: Prediction and supervised learning share one structure, so they cannot come apart this way. The rarity of a teacher is a fact about the animal, not about which structures a lamprey has.

options.text: Reinforcement learning alone has its structure; the other three families lack theirs, because a lamprey has neither a pallium nor a cerebellum.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the lamprey included. The only one of the three a lamprey lacks is the structure for errors delivered output by output.

items.stem: Doya is careful about how much of the three-structure proposal is settled. What makes the cerebellar case the best supported of the three?

options.text: Its anatomy, what its climbing fibers fire for, and the loss of learning when those fibers are silenced all point the same way.
options.why: Correct. Three lines of evidence agree: the wiring of one fiber to one cell, the fibers’ firing for errors, and the learned blink never developing when they are silenced.

options.text: Reward-related activity has been recorded in it and nowhere else, so no other structure could be doing that kind of learning.
options.why: That confuses the cerebellum with the place where the pallium meets the striatum, and even there the chapter says reward-related activity also turns up in parts of the cortex.

options.text: It has no dedicated teaching pathway that anyone has found, so it can only be learning from the statistics of its own input.
options.why: That is the case for the pallium, which is the weakest of the three, not the strongest.

options.text: It is the oldest of the three structures, present in the lamprey as well as in every jawed vertebrate, so it has been studied longest.
options.why: The cerebellum in its jawed form is the newest of the three, arriving with the jawed fishes. Its support comes from the evidence, not from its age.

items.stem: The case for the pallium as the structure specialized for unsupervised learning rests on the weakest evidence of the three. Why does the chapter say that weakness is partly the point?

options.text: The case is made from an absence: this kind of learning needs nothing delivered, so there is no dedicated teaching pathway to find.
options.why: Correct. The other two cases can point to a delivery route and test it. The pallium’s case is that nothing arrives there but its own input, which leaves nothing to trace or silence.

options.text: The pallium has been studied in only a few kinds of fish, so the experiments that would support the case have simply not been done yet.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, and the chapter does not blame the weakness on missing experiments. The weakness is built into what unsupervised learning needs.

options.text: The pallium learns by every method at once, so no single family of learning could ever be shown to belong to it more than the others.
options.why: The chapter does say the mapping is not exclusive, but that is not why the pallium’s case is weak. The weakness is that there is no teaching pathway to find.

options.text: The pallium’s teaching pathway is too small to record from, so its signal can be inferred from behavior but never measured directly.
options.why: There is no teaching pathway to record from at all. That absence is the point, not a pathway too small to measure.

items.stem: A research team reports reward-related activity in part of the cortex, well away from where the pallium meets the striatum. Does that finding contradict the chapter’s mapping of four families of learning onto three structures?

options.text: No. The mapping says where each family’s signal is delivered, and reward-related activity is known to turn up in parts of the cortex as well.
options.why: Correct. The mapping is not exclusive. As the lecture puts it, the mapping assigns each family to where its signal is delivered, and does not say that nothing else can learn that way.

options.text: Yes. The mapping assigns each family to exactly one structure, so reward-related activity found anywhere outside the striatum would show the table to be wrong.
options.why: The chapter explicitly denies that the mapping is exclusive. Reward-related activity in the cortex is something it reports, not something it rules out.

options.text: No. Reward-related activity in the cortex is really the climbing fibers’ error signal, which is easily mistaken for a reward report in recordings.
options.why: Climbing fibers belong to the cerebellum and carry an error for one output cell. Nothing in the chapter reinterprets reward-related activity in the cortex this way.

options.text: Yes. The cortex is where unsupervised learning happens, which needs nothing delivered, so no reward signal of any kind could reach it.
options.why: The pallium is Doya’s candidate for unsupervised learning, but that does not rule out other learning there. The chapter reports reward-related activity in parts of the cortex.

items.stem: Suppose we traced every connection leaving the cerebellum, looking for a direct link to the basal ganglia. What would we find, and how do the two structures work together anyway?

options.text: No direct connections at all; each exchanges signals with the pallium by way of the thalamus, and the pallium is where their work meets.
options.why: Correct. The two cooperate without touching each other, and every route between them runs through the pallium and the thalamus.

options.text: A dense direct bundle between them, which lets the cerebellum pass its errors straight to the basal ganglia for use in choosing which program runs.
options.why: That is the intuitive guess, and the chapter says the opposite: there are no direct connections between the two at all.

options.text: No direct connections at all; the two never work together, since each learns by its own method and serves only its own behaviors.
options.why: There are no direct connections, but the chapter says no behavior uses one of the three structures alone. They cooperate by way of the pallium.

options.text: A single direct link, carried by the dopamine fibers, which reach both structures from the midbrain and so connect them.
options.why: Dopamine fibers arrive where the pallium meets the striatum. They are not a link between the cerebellum and the basal ganglia.

items.stem: The cerebellum and the basal ganglia both exchange signals with the pallium. What does the pallium supply to both of them?

options.text: The shared representation of the situation that both of them work on.
options.why: Correct. The pallium is the common ground: both structures work on the same representation, which the pallium supplies.

options.text: The error signal that tells each of them which one of its outputs was wrong.
options.why: Errors for each output arrive at the cerebellum on its climbing fibers. The pallium supplies a shared representation, not an error.

options.text: The verdict that tells each of them whether things went better than expected.
options.why: The verdict is carried by dopamine fibers from the midbrain. The pallium supplies what both structures work on.

options.text: The motor commands that each of them passes on, unchanged, to the spinal cord.
options.why: Neither structure is described as a relay for commands. The cerebellum learns from errors and the basal ganglia settle which program runs; the pallium supplies what both work on.

items.stem: A student sketches the actor in the basal ganglia and the critic in the cerebellum, on the grounds that one chooses actions and the other predicts. How does the chapter place them?

options.text: Both sit in the striatum, in two intermingled compartments, and both work through the loop that runs out to the pallium and back.
options.why: Correct. The actor and the critic share one structure, not two. Different jobs do not come with different addresses here.

options.text: The critic sits in the cerebellum, since prediction is the cerebellum’s kind of learning, and the actor sits in the striatum, where actions are released.
options.why: Predicting how well things will go is not an error for one output, so it is not the cerebellum’s kind of prediction. Both the actor and the critic sit in the striatum.

options.text: The actor sits in the striatum and the critic in the pallium, since the pallium supplies the shared representation that the actor works on.
options.why: The pallium does supply the shared representation, but the critic is not placed there. Both the actor and the critic sit in the striatum.

options.text: Both sit in the cerebellum, in two separate layers, and both work through the loop that runs out to the pallium by way of the thalamus.
options.why: The cerebellum has its own loop through the thalamus, but the actor and the critic are placed in the striatum, in intermingled compartments.

items.stem: A new driver figures out every lane change slowly and deliberately. A year later, lane changes happen smoothly while the driver holds a conversation. What is the chapter’s account of the change?

options.text: With practice, the mappings first worked out with effort were copied into the cerebellum, which now runs them as fast shortcuts.
options.why: Correct. A skill handed from one system to another is a second case of the structures working together, and it is part of why a practiced skill stops demanding attention.

options.text: With practice, the dopamine verdict for each lane change grew stronger, until the basal ganglia released the movement almost at once.
options.why: Dopamine sets how easily movements are released, but the chapter’s account of a practiced skill is a copy of the mappings into the cerebellum.

options.text: With practice, the pallium learned the skill so thoroughly that it no longer needs any of the other structures at all, and so it now has plenty of attention to spare.
options.why: The chapter says no behavior uses one structure alone. The practiced mappings are copied into the cerebellum rather than kept only in the pallium.

options.text: With practice, the spinal cord took over lane changes entirely, just as spinal circuits generate the swimming rhythm on their own in a lamprey.
options.why: Spinal circuits do generate a lamprey’s swimming rhythm, but a practiced skill is handed to the cerebellum, not to the spinal cord.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why four families of learning need only three structures in a vertebrate brain, and say why the chapter treats the resulting mapping as neither settled nor exclusive.
items.answer: Prediction learning and supervised learning both need an error computed separately for each output. They differ only in where the target comes from, the world or a teacher, and a climbing fiber does not report which supplied it. So both families share the cerebellum, and four families need only three structures. But Doya is careful about how much of this is settled. The cerebellar case is the best supported, by its anatomy, by what the climbing fibers fire for, and by the loss of learning when they are silenced. The pallium’s case is the weakest, because there is no teaching pathway to find. And the mapping is not exclusive: reward-related activity is well established where the pallium meets the striatum, but it also turns up in parts of the cortex.
rubric: Says prediction and supervised learning both need an error for each output, differing only in where the target comes from.
Concludes that the two share one structure, the cerebellum, so three structures serve four families.
Says the three cases are not equally strong, naming the cerebellum as best supported or the pallium as weakest.
Says the mapping is not exclusive, with reward-related activity in parts of the cortex as the example.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how the cerebellum and the basal ganglia can both take part in one behavior even though there are no direct connections between them, and give one of the chapter’s cases of the learning structures working together.
items.answer: No behavior uses one of the three structures alone. The cerebellum and the basal ganglia never connect to each other directly. Instead, each exchanges signals with the pallium by way of the thalamus, and the pallium supplies the shared representation that both of them work on, so their work meets there. One case is Module 5’s actor and critic: the critic learns to predict how well things will go from here, the actor adjusts its policy using the critic’s errors, and both sit in the striatum and work through the loop out to the pallium and back. Another is a skill handed from one system to another: something worked out slowly at first, like mental arithmetic, is copied with practice into the cerebellum, which runs it as a fast shortcut.
rubric: States that the cerebellum and the basal ganglia have no direct connections.
Says each exchanges signals with the pallium by way of the thalamus.
Says the pallium supplies the shared representation both work on.
Gives one case correctly: the actor and critic in the striatum working through the loop, or a practiced skill copied into the cerebellum.

pools.title: Wiring Plans, Choosing, and More Copies of the Same Unit
pools.covers: reading §6.2.8, §6.2.9, §6.2.10 · lecture 6.2 slides maps_and_loops, broadcasts_and_hierarchy, release_not_switch, copies_of_one_unit · lab Bench

items.stem: What is a topographic map?

options.text: An arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells, so the layout of the tissue mirrors the layout of what it represents.
options.why: Correct. The order of the tissue copies the order of what it represents, as the tectum copies the space around the animal.

options.text: A diagram that shows where each structure of the brain sits, drawn so that neighboring structures appear next to each other on the page.
options.why: That is a map of the brain, drawn by an anatomist. A topographic map is an arrangement inside the brain’s own tissue.

options.text: An arrangement in which each cell responds to one place in the world, with the cells for neighboring places scattered widely across the tissue.
options.why: Cells in a map do respond to places, but the defining feature is that neighboring places are handled by neighboring cells.

options.text: A pathway that carries one signal from a small cluster of cells to most of the rest of the brain, setting conditions for the whole animal.
options.why: That describes a broad projection, which sets global conditions rather than carrying an ordered copy of anything.

items.stem: The chapter names two things a topographic map buys. What are they?

options.text: Short wires, since cells comparing nearby points sit together, and easy comparison, since one sharpening circuit works everywhere on the sheet.
options.why: Correct. Both payoffs come from neighbors being next to each other: short connections between them, and one local circuit that can be repeated across the whole map.

options.text: Fast learning, because neighboring cells share their errors with each other, and stable memory, because a map keeps what it learned once it is laid down.
options.why: Maps are not credited with learning or memory in the chapter. Their two payoffs are about wiring length and comparison.

options.text: Global control, because one map can reach every part of the brain at once, and flexibility, because a map can be rearranged whenever the world changes.
options.why: Reaching most of the brain is what broad projections do. A map’s payoffs are short wires and easy comparison.

options.text: Selection, because a map picks one location and suppresses all the others, and speed, because a map skips the thalamus on its way to the pallium.
options.why: Picking one action and pressing the others down is the job of the basal ganglia. A map’s payoffs are short wires and easy comparison.

items.stem: Imagine a tectum with all the same cells and connections, but scrambled, so that each direction around the animal is handled by a randomly placed patch. According to the chapter’s account of maps, what would be lost?

options.text: Cells comparing nearby directions would no longer sit together, so wires would be long, and no single local circuit could sharpen differences everywhere.
options.why: Correct. Both payoffs of a map depend on neighbors in the world being neighbors in the tissue. Scrambling keeps the information but loses the short wires and the repeatable comparison.

options.text: Nothing at all would be lost, because the same cells still receive the same inputs, and the layout of the cells makes no difference to what the tectum computes.
options.why: The inputs would be the same, but the chapter says the layout is what keeps wires short and lets one circuit sharpen differences everywhere.

options.text: The tectum would lose its connections to the eyes, because a map can only receive input from sense organs that are laid out in the same order as it.
options.why: The scenario keeps every connection. What is lost is the ordered layout and the two payoffs that come with it.

options.text: The tectum would start carrying global conditions instead of positions, setting how strongly the whole animal responds instead of where it looks.
options.why: Setting global conditions is what broad projections do, and scrambling a map would not turn it into one.

items.stem: The chapter describes two loops that leave the pallium and return to it. What route do they take?

options.text: One runs through the basal ganglia and one through the cerebellum, and both return to the pallium by way of the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. The two loops pass through different structures on the way out and share the thalamus on the way back.

options.text: One runs through the basal ganglia and one through the cerebellum, and each returns to the pallium directly, without any relay on the way.
options.why: Both loops come back by way of the thalamus. Neither returns directly.

options.text: One runs through the hypothalamus and one through the amygdala, and both return to the pallium by way of the spinal cord.
options.why: The chapter’s two loops pass through the basal ganglia and the cerebellum, and return through the thalamus.

options.text: One runs from the basal ganglia to the cerebellum and the other runs back, so the two structures pass signals directly to each other in a circle.
options.why: The cerebellum and the basal ganglia have no direct connections to each other at all. Each loops through the pallium separately.

items.stem: The same loop through the basal ganglia serves movement and also something quite different from movement. How does the chapter say one arrangement can do both?

options.text: Each loop is really a bundle of parallel loops, and different ones serve different stretches of the pallium.
options.why: Correct. Because the loops run side by side, one stretch of pallium can use the arrangement for movement while another uses it for something else.

options.text: The loop switches between jobs many times a second, serving movement in one moment and something quite different in the next.
options.why: The chapter gives no time-sharing account. The loops run in parallel, each serving its own stretch of pallium.

options.text: The loop carries a single signal that every part of the pallium reads, and each part interprets that same signal in its own way.
options.why: One signal read by everyone is closer to a broad projection. The loops are many, each serving a different stretch of pallium.

options.text: The loop serves movement alone, and anything else it seems to do is a side effect of the movements it helps to produce.
options.why: The chapter says the same arrangement serves something quite different in another channel, not only movement.

items.stem: After drawing the two loops with the pallium at the top, the chapter adds a caution about the picture. What is the caution?

options.text: In a lamprey most basal ganglia output goes down to the brainstem, and in a mammal much of what returns to the pallium may be a copy of a command sent down.
options.why: Correct. A loop drawn with the pallium at the top is an incomplete mammal’s version of the story, since much of the action runs downward.

options.text: In a lamprey the loops run through the cerebellum alone, and in a mammal they run through the basal ganglia alone, so no single animal has both of the loops.
options.why: A lamprey lacks the cerebellum in its jawed form, so its loop could not run through the cerebellum. The caution is about which way the basal ganglia’s output goes.

options.text: In a lamprey there is no pallium at the top of the loop at all, so the loops begin and end in the thalamus, which does the pallium’s work in fishes.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the lamprey included. The caution is that most of the lamprey’s basal ganglia output goes down, not back up.

options.text: In a mammal the loops are drawn correctly, but in a lamprey they run backward, from the thalamus to the basal ganglia and then out to the pallium.
options.why: The caution applies to the mammal’s picture too: much of what returns to its pallium may be a copy of a command that went down.

items.stem: How do the broad projections differ from a map like the tectum in what they do?

options.text: A few thousand cells reach most of the brain and set global conditions, rather than carrying specific content about where something is.
options.why: Correct. They are the sources of Module 4’s modulators, and they set how strongly the whole animal responds and how readily it tries something new.

options.text: Millions of cells each carry one precise location, so together they hold a more detailed copy of the world than any map could manage to hold.
options.why: Broad projections come from a few thousand cells, and they carry no locations. Detailed positional content is what a map carries.

options.text: A few thousand cells each reach one small patch of the brain, and carry that patch’s own teaching signal, one output at a time.
options.why: An error for one output at a time is what climbing fibers deliver. Broad projections reach most of the brain and set global conditions.

options.text: A few thousand cells relay each sense into the pallium in turn, and carry signals back out from the pallium to the body afterward.
options.why: Relaying the senses into the pallium is the thalamus’s job. Broad projections set global conditions.

items.stem: Suppose the output of one of the broad projection systems is turned up across the whole brain. On the chapter’s account, what kind of change should that produce in the animal?

options.text: A change in how strongly the whole animal responds, or how readily it tries something new, rather than in what it perceives.
options.why: Correct. Broad projections set global conditions rather than carry specific content, so turning one up changes the animal’s overall state.

options.text: A change in where the animal looks, since every broad projection carries a map of the space around the animal to the whole brain.
options.why: A map of the space around the animal is in the tectum. Broad projections carry no positions.

options.text: A change in one particular movement’s timing, since broad projections deliver an error to each output cell that tells it when to fire.
options.why: An error for each output cell is the climbing fibers’ signal. Broad projections affect the whole animal’s responsiveness.

options.text: No change at all in behavior, since broad projections only relay copies of commands the pallium has already sent down to the body.
options.why: Returning copies of commands concerns the loops. Broad projections change how strongly and how readily the whole animal responds.

items.stem: A student writes that each modulator system is a broadcast, sending the same signal to every region of the brain. How does the chapter qualify that?

options.text: The word is only approximately right: most of these systems divide into subsystems with separate targets, and norepinephrine comes closest to everywhere.
options.why: Correct. Different regions get different signals from most of these systems. Norepinephrine is the nearest thing to a true broadcast.

options.text: The word is exactly right: every modulator system reaches every region equally, which is what lets it set global conditions for the whole animal all at once.
options.why: The chapter uses the word and withdraws most of it in the same breath. Most systems divide into subsystems with separate targets.

options.text: The word is wrong altogether: each modulator reaches only one structure, and none of them comes anywhere close to reaching most of the brain.
options.why: A few thousand cells do reach most of the rest of the brain. The qualification is that different regions get different signals.

options.text: The word is right only for dopamine, which reaches every region equally, while the other modulators each reach one structure alone.
options.why: Norepinephrine, not dopamine, comes closest to reaching everywhere, and dopamine fibers are described as arriving at particular places such as the striatum.

items.stem: A cat’s neocortex is removed, but its basal ganglia are left intact. What does the chapter report about its behavior?

options.text: It still walks, grooms and explores.
options.why: Correct. The result shows how much the lower levels of the hierarchy can do: whole behaviors still run, and the basal ganglia can still choose among them.

options.text: It lies still and cannot start any movement.
options.why: Movements that are hard to start come from too little dopamine, not from losing the neocortex. The cat still walks, grooms and explores.

options.text: It moves only in reflexes to touch.
options.why: The cat does far more than reflexes. Walking, grooming and exploring are whole behaviors, and they continue.

options.text: It walks, but only in a straight line.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter limits the cat’s walking. It also grooms and explores, so long as the basal ganglia are intact.

items.stem: Circuits in a lamprey’s spinal cord generate the swimming rhythm on their own. What, then, do the brainstem centers above them contribute to swimming?

options.text: They start the swimming, stop it, and steer.
options.why: Correct. The rhythm itself comes from below. The brainstem centers turn it on and off and set its direction, which is what an upper level of a hierarchy does.

options.text: They generate each stroke of the swimming wave.
options.why: The spinal circuits generate the strokes on their own. The brainstem centers start, stop and steer them.

options.text: They decide which of the animal’s programs is allowed to run.
options.why: Settling which program is allowed to run is the job of the basal ganglia, one level higher.

options.text: They deliver an error to each swimming muscle.
options.why: Delivering an error for each output is the climbing fibers’ job in the cerebellum, which a lamprey lacks in the jawed form.

items.stem: What is action selection?

options.text: Choosing which of the actions available to an animal is the one performed now.
options.why: Correct. In vertebrates the basal ganglia do it by releasing one motor program from inhibition.

options.text: Learning which actions led to reward in the past, so they are more likely to be repeated later.
options.why: That describes reinforcement learning, which can change what gets selected later. Action selection is the choosing itself.

options.text: Generating the rhythm of a repeated movement, such as swimming, without a rhythmic input.
options.why: That is what a central pattern generator does. Action selection chooses which program runs.

options.text: Adjusting the timing of a movement by the error delivered after each attempt at it.
options.why: That is the cerebellum’s error-driven learning. Action selection chooses which action is performed now.

items.stem: What is the name for choosing which of the actions available to an animal is the one performed now?

options.text: Action selection.
options.why: Correct. In vertebrates the basal ganglia carry it out, by releasing one motor program from inhibition.

options.text: Reverse inference.
options.why: Reverse inference is reasoning from brain activity to the process involved. It is not a job the brain does.

options.text: Homeostasis.
options.why: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within limits. It does not choose among actions.

options.text: Modularity.
options.why: Modularity describes a system built from units that can be copied. It is not the job of choosing one action.

items.stem: When an animal is at rest, what are the output cells of its basal ganglia doing, and what does choosing an action change?

options.text: They fire steadily, holding back the brainstem centers that run each program; choosing lifts that hold for a single action.
options.why: Correct. Everything is held back by default, and choosing is releasing the inhibition for one action.

options.text: They are silent, waiting for a command; choosing switches on the output cells for a single action so they can drive it.
options.why: That is the switch-on picture the chapter rejects. The output cells are busy at rest, inhibiting every program.

options.text: They fire steadily, driving every program at a low level; choosing turns the chosen program up and leaves the others as they are.
options.why: The steady firing is inhibition, not drive. Nothing runs at rest, and choosing releases one program from its hold.

options.text: They are silent, because nothing needs to be chosen at rest; choosing wakes the whole structure, which then drives all programs at once.
options.why: At rest the output cells fire steadily. And selection releases one program, not all of them.

items.stem: A student describes the basal ganglia as a switchboard that turns on the motor program the animal has chosen. What is wrong with that picture?

options.text: It runs the wrong way: every program is held back by default, and choosing is releasing the hold on one, not switching anything on.
options.why: Correct. The vertebrate answer is the reverse of what most people expect. The default is a hold, and selection is a release.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, except that the basal ganglia switch on several programs at a time and let the muscles sort out the conflict.
options.why: The chapter says a movement is produced by releasing a hold, and the whole point is to keep proposals from fighting over the muscles.

options.text: It gives the job to the wrong structure: the cerebellum switches on the chosen program, and the basal ganglia only adjust its timing.
options.why: The basal ganglia do carry out selection. What is wrong is the direction: selection releases a held program rather than switching one on.

options.text: It leaves out the teacher: a switchboard needs a signal naming the right program, and the basal ganglia receive one from the pallium.
options.why: No teacher names the right program. Selection releases one program from the inhibition that holds every program back.

items.stem: What is the direct pathway?

options.text: The route from the striatum to the output cells of the basal ganglia that silences the cells holding one program back, which releases it.
options.why: Correct. Silencing the cells that hold a program back is what frees that program to run.

options.text: The route from the striatum through two further stops that strengthens the inhibition on each of the competing programs, pressing them down.
options.why: That is the indirect pathway. The direct pathway releases one program; the indirect pathway holds the others down.

options.text: The route from the midbrain to the striatum that carries the dopamine signal reporting whether things went better than expected.
options.why: That is the dopamine projection, which carries a verdict. The direct pathway runs from the striatum to the output cells.

options.text: The route from the brainstem straight to the muscles that runs a motor program without any involvement of the basal ganglia at all.
options.why: The direct pathway is inside the basal ganglia’s circuitry, running from the striatum to its output cells.

items.stem: What is the indirect pathway?

options.text: The longer route from the striatum that strengthens the inhibition on competing programs, so that releasing one program presses the others down.
options.why: Correct. It runs through two further stops and ends by tightening the hold on everything except the program being released.

options.text: The shorter route from the striatum that silences the output cells holding back one program, so that the chosen program is free to run.
options.why: That is the direct pathway, which releases one program. The indirect pathway holds the competitors down.

options.text: The route from the pallium to the cerebellum and back by way of the thalamus, which serves movement in one channel and quite different work in another.
options.why: That is one of the two loops. The indirect pathway is a route within the basal ganglia’s selection circuitry.

options.text: The faster route that can stop a movement that is already underway, cutting it off before the movement has been completed.
options.why: The chapter names that as a third, faster route. The indirect pathway presses down the programs competing with the one released.

items.stem: When one motor program is released, the direct and indirect pathways do different things. What does each do?

options.text: The direct pathway frees the chosen program by silencing what holds it back; the indirect pathway tightens the hold on the competing programs.
options.why: Correct. The two are told apart by what each does to the competitors: one releases a single program, and the other presses the rest down.

options.text: The direct pathway switches the chosen program on; the indirect pathway switches it off again once the movement is complete.
options.why: Neither pathway switches anything on. And pressing competitors down, not ending the chosen movement, is the indirect pathway’s job.

options.text: The direct pathway carries the command for fast movements; the indirect pathway carries the command for slow movements, through two further stops.
options.why: The pathways are distinguished by what they do to the programs, not by the speed of the movement. The indirect pathway is longer, but it presses competitors down.

options.text: The direct pathway strengthens the hold on the competing programs; the indirect pathway silences what holds the chosen program back.
options.why: That swaps the two. The direct pathway releases one program, and the indirect pathway presses the others down.

items.stem: In Parkinson’s disease, movements are hard to start. Using the hold-and-release account, what does too little dopamine do?

options.text: Dopamine sets how easily anything is released at all, so with too little of it the hold on every program is harder to lift.
options.why: Correct. The same happens to a lamprey whose dopamine is depleted. The movements are there to be released; releasing them is what has become hard.

options.text: Dopamine is the command that switches each program on, so with too little of it there is simply no command left for the muscles to follow.
options.why: No program is switched on in this account. Dopamine sets how easily a held program is released.

options.text: Dopamine carries the error for each muscle, so with too little of it the timing of each movement is lost while starting it stays as easy as before.
options.why: An error for each output is the climbing fibers’ signal. Too little dopamine makes movements hard to start.

options.text: Dopamine releases the competing programs, so with too little of it every program runs at once and the movements cancel each other out.
options.why: That is closer to the opposite case. With too much dopamine, unwanted movements break through.

items.stem: There is no walking organ, no eating organ and no talking organ in a vertebrate brain. What is the chapter’s reason?

options.text: They all compete for the same muscles and body, so separate parts running them would pull in different directions; shared machinery with a selector works.
options.why: Correct. When one body has to do one thing at a time, shared machinery with something to settle which program is released is the arrangement that works.

options.text: Those actions are too complicated to fit into one organ each, so every one of them has to be spread across the whole brain with no particular order at all.
options.why: The chapter’s reason is competition for one body, not complexity. And the arrangement it describes is ordered: shared machinery with a selector.

options.text: Those actions are all learned, and learned behaviors never get organs of their own, since learning happens at synapses spread everywhere in the brain.
options.why: The reason is not that the actions are learned. It is that they compete for the same muscles and the same body.

options.text: Those actions each do have an organ, but the organs are in the spinal cord rather than the brain, where they run without any choosing at all.
options.why: The programs do run on shared brainstem and spinal circuitry, but not as one organ per action, and which program runs is still chosen.

items.stem: How are the basal ganglia organized, on the chapter’s account?

options.text: As one unit per motor program, such as locomotion, eye movements, posture and chewing, each with its own direct and indirect pathway.
options.why: Correct. The unit of selection is repeated, one per program, and every copy has both of its pathways.

options.text: As one unit for the whole body, with a direct pathway for movement and an indirect pathway for everything that is not movement.
options.why: The two pathways are not divided between movement and other work. Each unit has both, and there is one unit per motor program.

options.text: As one unit per sense, one each for vision, smell, touch and hearing, each deciding which of its own sensations is allowed to reach the pallium.
options.why: The units are organized by motor program, such as locomotion or chewing, not by sense.

options.text: As one unit per program, each with a direct pathway only, while a single shared indirect pathway serves all of the units at once.
options.why: Every unit has its own direct and indirect pathway. Neither pathway is shared across units.

items.stem: A mammal has many more motor programs than a lamprey, and some of its basal ganglia units serve parts of the pallium that are not about movement at all. What does the chapter conclude happened to the selection design between the two?

options.text: It was copied rather than improved: more units of the same kind, including units serving the pallium’s work that is not movement.
options.why: Correct. The design was not improved. It was copied, and the copies were put to work on more programs.

options.text: It was improved rather than copied: each unit became larger and faster, so that fewer units could handle many more programs at once.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite. The unit stayed nearly the same, and the number of copies grew.

options.text: It was replaced: a new selection system for work that is not movement grew alongside the old one, with different transmitters.
options.why: The further units use the same design. They are more copies, not a new system with different transmitters.

options.text: It was abandoned: mammals choose actions in the pallium, and the basal ganglia survive only as a leftover from the lamprey.
options.why: Mammals keep the basal ganglia and have more of its units, not fewer. Selection is still their job.

items.stem: What is modularity, as the chapter uses the term?

options.text: A system built out of units that each do their own job, connect to the rest through a limited set of connections, and can be copied or altered without redesigning everything else.
options.why: Correct. It is a claim about how a system is wired, as in the basal ganglia’s repeated selection units.

options.text: A mind built out of separate, independent faculties, such as one for language and one for faces, each with its own dedicated place in the brain.
options.why: The chapter explicitly declines that stronger claim. Modularity here is about wiring, not about faculties of mind.

options.text: A system in which every part connects richly to every other part, so that the whole network settles into the state that best satisfies all demands.
options.why: That is the rival answer to the separation question, one richly connected network. Modularity is about units with limited connections.

options.text: A system in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells, so that the layout of the tissue mirrors what it represents.
options.why: That describes a topographic map. Modularity concerns units that can be copied or altered on their own.

items.stem: What is the name for a system built out of units that each do their own job, connect to the rest through a limited set of connections, and can be copied or altered without redesigning everything else?

options.text: Modularity.
options.why: Correct. The basal ganglia, built from one repeated selection unit, are the chapter’s case of it.

options.text: Action selection.
options.why: Action selection is the job the basal ganglia units do. It is not the name for how a system is built.

options.text: Lateralization.
options.why: Lateralization is a difference between what the two sides of a brain do.

options.text: Reverse inference.
options.why: Reverse inference is a way of reasoning from activity to process, not a way of building a system.

items.stem: The chapter says three lines of evidence arrive at modularity independently. What are they?

options.text: The basal ganglia repeat one selection unit; copying circuitry and modifying the copy is a fast, often-taken route in evolution; Doya’s three systems are built from repeated pieces.
options.why: Correct. Each line points the same way from a different direction: repetition within one structure, how new arrangements arise, and repetition across the three learning systems.

options.text: Brain imaging finds a separate region for each faculty of mind; patients lose one faculty at a time after an injury; and each faculty develops on its own schedule during childhood.
options.why: That is evidence people give for separate faculties of mind, a claim the chapter explicitly does not make. Its evidence is about repeated wiring.

options.text: Every structure has its own transmitter; no two structures share any connections; and each structure can be removed without the others noticing it has gone.
options.why: None of those is claimed, and the chapter says no behavior uses one of the three learning structures alone. Its evidence is about repeated wiring.

options.text: The pallium is uniform across its whole surface; the cerebellum has one climbing fiber per cell; and dopamine reaches every region of the brain equally.
options.why: One climbing fiber per cell is true, but it is not one of the three lines. And dopamine does not reach every region equally.

items.stem: A magazine article says this chapter shows that the mind is built from separate, independent faculties, one for each capacity, just as the basal ganglia are built from repeated units. How would the chapter respond?

options.text: Modularity in its sense is a claim about wiring, not the stronger claim about faculties of mind, which the book does not make.
options.why: Correct. What the basal ganglia repeat is the selector, not a whole organ for each capacity. The chapter explicitly declines the faculty claim.

options.text: It would agree, since the repeated selection units are exactly the faculties of mind, one for locomotion, one for chewing, and so on.
options.why: The units select among motor programs; they are not faculties of mind, and the programs themselves run on shared circuitry.

options.text: It would agree about movement but not about thought, since the faculties of mind are found only in the pallium, which is not repeated.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about faculties anywhere, and it says the pallium’s own learning system is built from repeated pieces too.

options.text: It would say modularity is false, since the whole brain is one richly connected network with no repeated units anywhere in it.
options.why: The chapter gives good evidence for repeated units in the basal ganglia. It rejects the faculty claim, not modularity in its wiring sense.

items.stem: The chapter treats a large language model as a system in which both answers to the separation question are visible. What division is deliberately built into such a model, and how does it line up with the jobs the model has to get right?

options.text: It has many repeated layers of more than one kind; none of those designed divisions is a grammar part, a meaning part, or a part tracking who speaks.
options.why: Correct. The designed divisions are real, but none of them corresponds to what the model has to get right.

options.text: It is built with a separate grammar part, a meaning part and a speaker-tracking part; nothing else about its structure is decided by its designers at all.
options.why: That is exactly the division the chapter says the model does not have. What is built in is repeated layers of more than one kind.

options.text: It is built as one uniform layer repeated many times, with every layer the same; the grammar part and the meaning part are then added on top.
options.why: The layers are of more than one kind, each doing a different sort of work. And no grammar or meaning part is added.

options.text: It is built with no divisions of any kind; grammar, meaning and speaker tracking each get a layer of their own only after training is finished.
options.why: Some division is deliberate: repeated layers of more than one kind. And the jobs do not each end up in one layer.

items.stem: Researchers find a group of units in a trained language model that behave alike and seem to do one identifiable job. How does the chapter describe specialization like that?

options.text: It was not built in but emerged from training, and it is partial: the same units take part in many jobs, and most jobs are spread across many units.
options.why: Correct. One network meets competing demands at once, and what specialization appears is emergent and incomplete.

options.text: It was built in by the designers, who assigned that job to those units before training began, so that the group is a designed part, just like a layer is.
options.why: The designed divisions are the layers. Where something like specialization appears, the chapter says it emerged from training.

options.text: It was not built in, and it is complete: once a job emerges in a group of units, those units do that job and no other from then on.
options.why: The chapter stresses that emergent specialization is partial. The same units take part in many jobs.

options.text: It is proof that the model has separate structures for grammar, meaning and speaker tracking, each of which has now been found.
options.why: The chapter says the model has no such parts. What emerges is partial, and the research is active and contested.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how the basal ganglia choose one action out of several, including what happens at rest, what the direct and indirect pathways each do, and what dopamine sets.
items.answer: Nothing is switched on to produce a movement. At rest, the output cells of the basal ganglia fire steadily, and they inhibit the brainstem centers that would otherwise run each motor program, so everything is held back by default. Choosing an action is releasing that hold for a single program. The direct pathway, from the striatum to the output cells, silences the cells holding one program back, which frees it to run. That is disinhibition, inhibiting an inhibitor. The indirect pathway strengthens the inhibition on the competing programs, so releasing one presses the others down. Dopamine sets how easily anything is released at all.
rubric: Says every program is held back by default, with output cells firing steadily at rest.
Says choosing is releasing the hold on a single program, not switching it on.
Says the direct pathway silences the cells holding one program back.
Says the indirect pathway tightens the hold on competing programs.
Says dopamine sets how easily anything is released.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, define modularity as the chapter uses it, and explain two ways the chapter limits the claim, one about what kind of claim it is and one about how far the separation goes even in its best case.
items.answer: Modularity is a system built out of units that each do their own job, connect to the rest through a limited set of connections, and can be copied or altered without redesigning everything else. The basal ganglia are a case, built from one selection unit copied per motor program. First, the chapter limits the kind of claim. Modularity is a claim about wiring, not the stronger claim, which the book does not make, that a mind is built from separate independent faculties. Second, it limits the degree. Modularity is a matter of degree, and even in the basal ganglia the separation is partial: what is repeated is the selector, not a whole organ per behavior, and the programs it selects among run on shared brainstem and spinal circuitry.
rubric: Defines modularity as units with their own jobs, limited connections, and the ability to be copied or altered without redesigning the rest.
Says modularity is a claim about wiring, not about independent faculties of mind.
Says modularity is a matter of degree.
Says the basal ganglia repeat the selector rather than an organ per behavior, with programs on shared lower circuitry.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the chapter calls large language models an instructive case for the question of separate structures against one network, and state the cautions it attaches to the comparison.
items.answer: Both answers are visible in one system. Some division is deliberate: the model is built from many repeated layers of more than one kind. But none of those designed divisions corresponds to what the model has to get right, such as grammar, meaning or keeping track of who is speaking. Those demands compete, and one network meets all of them at once. Where something like specialization does appear, it was not built in but emerged from training, and it is partial, since the same units take part in many jobs. The cautions are that research on what the parts of these models do is active and contested, and that nothing here says brains and language models solved the problem in the same way. The comparison shows only that the same choice arises whenever one system must meet many demands at once.
rubric: Says the model has deliberate divisions, repeated layers of more than one kind, none matching grammar, meaning or speaker tracking.
Says one network meets the competing demands at once.
Says any specialization emerged from training and is partial.
Gives at least one caution: the research is contested, or brains and language models did not necessarily solve the problem the same way.
States that the comparison shows the same choice arises whenever one system meets many demands.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, lay out the hierarchy of control in a lamprey, say what makes it a hierarchy, and give the result from a cat that shows how much the lower levels can do.
items.answer: In a lamprey, circuits in the spinal cord generate the swimming rhythm on their own. Centers in the brainstem start those circuits, stop them, and steer. The basal ganglia settle which program is allowed to run, and the pallium sits above all of it. What makes this a hierarchy is not that the top gives every order. It is that the lower levels run whole behaviors by themselves, while the upper levels choose among them and adjust them. A cat whose neocortex is removed still walks, grooms and explores, so long as its basal ganglia are intact.
rubric: Places the swimming rhythm in spinal circuits that run on their own.
Gives the brainstem centers starting, stopping and steering, and the basal ganglia settling which program runs.
Says the lower levels run whole behaviors while the upper levels choose among and adjust them.
Gives the cat without a neocortex that still walks, grooms and explores with its basal ganglia intact.

pools.title: Hindbrain, Midbrain, and the Forebrain’s Old Core
pools.covers: reading §6.3.1, §6.3.2, §6.3.3 · lecture 6.3 slides running_the_body, the_midbrain, forebrains_old_core · lab Plan, Tree, Bench

items.stem: What is a central pattern generator?

options.text: A circuit that produces a rhythmic output without needing a rhythmic input to drive it.
options.why: Correct. The wave that travels down a swimming lamprey is made this way, by circuits in the spinal cord, segment by segment.

options.text: A circuit that copies a rhythm arriving from the senses and passes it on, beat for beat, to the muscles.
options.why: A relay of that kind needs a rhythmic input to drive it. What defines a pattern generator is that it makes the rhythm without one.

options.text: A small cluster of hindbrain cells whose fibers reach nearly the whole brain and set the pace of its activity.
options.why: That describes the norepinephrine cluster, which turns the arousal dial. A pattern generator is a circuit that makes a rhythm.

options.text: A loose network of cells along the brainstem that sets how awake an animal is and takes it into sleep.
options.why: That is the reticular formation. It sets arousal; it does not generate the rhythm of a movement.

items.stem: What is the name for a circuit that makes a rhythmic output with no rhythmic input driving it, such as the circuits in a lamprey’s spinal cord that produce its swimming wave?

options.text: Central pattern generator.
options.why: Correct. The lamprey’s swimming wave is made by pattern generators segment by segment along the cord.

options.text: Reticular formation.
options.why: The reticular formation runs the length of the brainstem and sets how awake an animal is. It makes no swimming rhythm.

options.text: Tectum.
options.why: The tectum is the roof of the midbrain. It holds maps of the space around the animal and turns the animal toward a position.

options.text: Basal ganglia.
options.why: The basal ganglia settle which proposed action is released. They select among actions rather than generating a rhythm.

items.stem: In an experiment, the connection between a lamprey’s spinal cord and its brain is cut. What happens to the swimming rhythm, and what does the result show?

options.text: The rhythm can still be produced, showing that circuits in the cord generate it without rhythmic drive from the brain.
options.why: Correct. This is the classic isolated-cord result. It is what makes the pattern generator more than a definition: the rhythm is made segment by segment in the cord itself.

options.text: The rhythm stops at once, which shows that the brain sends the swimming rhythm down the cord one beat at a time.
options.why: That is the expectation the experiment overturns. With the brain disconnected, the rhythm can still be produced.

options.text: The rhythm survives in the segments nearest the head, which shows that each wave is passed backward from the brain.
options.why: The wave is generated segment by segment along the cord, so no segment waits for a wave arriving from the head.

options.text: The rhythm turns into random twitching, which shows that the reticular formation must keep the cord awake for it to run.
options.why: The reticular formation sets how awake an animal is, but a cord cut off from the brain can still produce an orderly swimming rhythm.

items.stem: What is the reticular formation?

options.text: A loose network of cells running the length of the brainstem that sets how awake an animal is and takes it in and out of sleep.
options.why: Correct. The reticular formation is where arousal, a capacity met earlier without a location, gets part of its address.

options.text: A cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that quickly evaluates whether what has happened is good or bad.
options.why: That is the amygdala. It evaluates what matters; it does not set how awake the animal is.

options.text: A set of circuits in the spinal cord, one in each segment, that produce the rhythm of swimming with no rhythmic input.
options.why: Those are central pattern generators. They make rhythms like the swimming wave; they do not set arousal.

options.text: A dense bundle of fibers running between the two hemispheres of the forebrain, letting the two sides share what each of them has seen.
options.why: That describes a connection between the hemispheres, such as the corpus callosum of placental mammals. The reticular formation sets arousal.

items.stem: What is the name for the loose network of cells, running the length of the brainstem, that sets how awake an animal is and takes it in and out of sleep?

options.text: Reticular formation.
options.why: Correct. It runs the length of the brainstem, the midbrain and hindbrain together.

options.text: Central pattern generator.
options.why: A central pattern generator makes a rhythmic output, such as the swimming wave, without a rhythmic input. It does not set arousal.

options.text: Hypothalamus.
options.why: The hypothalamus keeps internal conditions such as temperature and water balance near their set points. It sits at the base of the forebrain, not along the brainstem.

options.text: Tectum.
options.why: The tectum is the roof of the midbrain. It holds maps of space and turns the animal toward a position.

items.stem: Module 4 treated norepinephrine as the vertebrate’s arousal dial but gave arousal no location in the brain. Where does the chapter say the dial is turned from?

options.text: A small cluster of hindbrain cells that makes most of the brain’s norepinephrine, with fibers reaching nearly the whole brain.
options.why: Correct. Arousal, left without an address in Module 4, has one here. The cluster’s reach is what lets one small place act on the whole brain.

options.text: Two clusters of cells in the midbrain, whose fibers run forward into the striatum and the pallium above them.
options.why: Those are the dopamine clusters. They are not where most of the brain’s norepinephrine comes from.

options.text: A series of clusters along the midline of the brainstem, sending norepinephrine back into the hindbrain and across the brain.
options.why: That is where the serotonin neurons sit. Most norepinephrine comes from one small cluster in the hindbrain.

options.text: The hypothalamus at the base of the forebrain, which regulates the internal states that set how a circuit treats the very same input.
options.why: The hypothalamus does regulate internal states, but the norepinephrine that turns the arousal dial comes mostly from one hindbrain cluster.

items.stem: A student has learned that there is no walking organ or eating organ, because behaviors that compete for one body share machinery with something to select among them. The student concludes that no part of the vertebrate nervous system is dedicated to a single behavior. What does the chapter say?

options.text: Near the bottom of the nervous system the conclusion fails: breathing, chewing, swallowing and locomotion each have their own pattern generator.
options.why: Correct. The chapter concedes that the shared-machinery answer holds near the top of the nervous system and fails near the bottom.

options.text: The conclusion holds all the way down: even breathing and swallowing are proposed by shared machinery and then released by the basal ganglia.
options.why: That carries the shared-machinery picture too far down. Breathing and swallowing have dedicated pattern generators of their own.

options.text: The conclusion fails in the forebrain, where the hypothalamus is dedicated to drinking and the amygdala to escaping from threats.
options.why: The chapter does not give forebrain structures single behaviors; one structure takes part in many capacities. Its dedicated circuits sit low in the nervous system.

options.text: The conclusion holds for the vertebrate nervous system, whose dedicated circuits were all replaced by shared machinery, and fails for invertebrates.
options.why: Vertebrates keep dedicated circuits of their own, in the hindbrain and spinal cord. Nothing in the chapter says those circuits were replaced.

items.stem: Breathing and swallowing each get a circuit of their own, while the choice between feeding and fleeing is settled by shared machinery. What reason does the chapter give for the difference?

options.text: Breathing and swallowing are stereotyped and must keep running while everything else changes; feeding and fleeing are chosen rather than generated.
options.why: Correct. Behaviors that are stereotyped and cannot stop are the keep-going half of the conflict with changing course, built into anatomy. Behaviors that are chosen share machinery with a selector.

options.text: Breathing and swallowing arose after the machinery for choosing between feeding and fleeing did, so they were added as separate circuits beside it.
options.why: The chapter gives no such timing. Its reason is what the behaviors are like: stereotyped, and unable to stop.
