options.text: Breathing and swallowing are learned from reward, and reward learning needs a separate structure for each of the behaviors that it learns to perform.
options.why: Learning from reward belongs to the basal ganglia, and it is not what makes these behaviors dedicated. They are stereotyped and must keep going.

options.text: Breathing and swallowing use muscles that feeding and fleeing leave alone, so there is nothing to compete over while the animal moves.
options.why: Swallowing is part of feeding, so the muscles are not left alone, and the chapter does not argue from muscles. Its reason is that these behaviors are stereotyped and must keep running.

items.stem: An animal whose tectum builds maps from hearing as well as from vision sees a flicker off to its left and, at the same moment, hears a splash from the same spot. How does the chapter say the roof of its midbrain handles the two signals?

options.text: Its maps of vision and hearing are in register, so the flicker and the splash mark the same position in each.
options.why: Correct. The tectum’s maps are built from the eyes and, in many animals, from hearing and touch as well, and a position in one is the same position in the others.

options.text: Its visual map turns the eyes toward the flicker, and the periaqueductal gray, also in the midbrain, turns the head toward the splash.
options.why: The periaqueductal gray organizes defensive responses, not orienting. The tectum’s maps are in register, so one position serves both signals.

options.text: Its maps of vision and hearing are laid out as mirror images, so a sound on the left marks a point on the right.
options.why: The maps are in register rather than mirrored: a position in one is the same position in the others.

options.text: Its maps keep vision and hearing apart, and the pallium has to work out afterward that the two positions match.
options.why: The point of maps in register is that no further step is needed to line them up. The tectum holds them already matched.

items.stem: Module 4’s worm and a vertebrate both steer toward things they sense. The lecture says the contrast between them is worth stating exactly. What is the difference?

options.text: The worm compares a signal now with a signal a moment ago; the vertebrate finds a place on a map. The difference is the map, not the accuracy.
options.why: Correct. The tectum solves Module 4’s problem of aiming again at a larger scale. What it adds is a map of positions, not a better score.

options.text: The vertebrate aims far more accurately, because it has millions of neurons to the worm’s few hundred. The difference is the accuracy.
options.why: The lecture says the opposite in so many words: the difference is the map, not the accuracy.

options.text: The worm aims by a map held in its head, and the vertebrate compares signals over time. The difference is which animal holds the map.
options.why: That reverses them. The worm’s aiming has no map anywhere in it; the vertebrate’s is built on one.

options.text: The worm drifts at random until it bumps into its food, while the vertebrate aims at a position. The difference is whether aiming happens at all.
options.why: The worm does aim, by comparing a signal against itself a moment earlier. Aiming is the shared problem, and the map is the difference.

items.stem: The dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine sources sit in different places. What does the chapter say the three have in common?

options.text: Each is small and old, and positioned to reach almost everything, so the brain’s broad projections start in a few little places.
options.why: Correct. The broad projections, modulator signals that reach almost the whole brain, start in a few small, old clusters.

options.text: Each is a large structure in the forebrain’s old core, so the broad projections start in the places where homeostasis and valence are handled.
options.why: The three sources sit in the midbrain and hindbrain, not in the forebrain’s old core, and each is small.

options.text: Each releases its molecule into the blood through the pituitary, so the broad projections reach the brain by way of the body.
options.why: Release into the blood is how the pituitary’s hormones travel. The modulator sources reach the brain through their own fibers.

options.text: Each sends its fibers to a single target, the striatum, so the broad projections are really one narrow projection repeated.
options.why: Only the dopamine fibers are singled out as running into the striatum, and even they reach the pallium too. The three sources reach almost everything.

items.stem: What kind of response does the periaqueductal gray organize?

options.text: Whole defensive responses: freezing, fleeing, and the dulled pain, or analgesia, that comes with either.
options.why: Correct. It organizes the whole defensive response, including the reduced sensitivity to pain that goes with freezing or fleeing.

options.text: Rhythmic behaviors that must keep going while everything else changes: breathing, chewing, swallowing and locomotion.
options.why: Those behaviors have pattern generators of their own, in the hindbrain and spinal cord.

options.text: Orienting responses: turning the eyes, the head, and in a fish the whole body toward a spot.
options.why: Orienting is the tectum’s job. The periaqueductal gray does the same kind of thing for defense.

options.text: Corrections to internal conditions: seeking out water, and releasing hormones into the blood.
options.why: Correcting drift in internal conditions is the hypothalamus’s job, behaviorally and through the pituitary.

items.stem: Three structures at the base and center of the forebrain give addresses to capacities met in earlier modules. Which pairing of structure and capacity matches the chapter?

options.text: The hypothalamus with internal states, the basal ganglia with choosing an action, and the amygdala with valence.
options.why: Correct. The hypothalamus regulates the internal states that set how a circuit treats an input, the basal ganglia select among actions, and the amygdala is part of the address of valence.

options.text: The hypothalamus with valence, the basal ganglia with internal states, and the amygdala with choosing an action.
options.why: Each structure has been given another’s capacity. Valence is the amygdala’s, and choosing an action is the basal ganglia’s.

options.text: The hypothalamus with choosing an action, the basal ganglia with valence, and the amygdala with internal states.
options.why: Each structure has been given another’s capacity. Internal states are regulated from the hypothalamus.

options.text: The hypothalamus with arousal, the basal ganglia with orienting, and the amygdala with learning from each of its errors.
options.why: Arousal is set from the brainstem, orienting is the tectum’s, and learning from errors is the cerebellum’s. None of those belongs to the forebrain’s old core.

items.stem: What is homeostasis?

options.text: Keeping the body’s internal conditions, such as temperature, water balance and blood sugar, within limits.
options.why: Correct. The hypothalamus does much of this work, with cells that detect drift and circuits that correct it.

options.text: Keeping the learned connections of a circuit stable, so that new learning does not overwrite what is already known.
options.why: Keeping what was learned while learning more is a real problem, but it is not homeostasis, which is about the body’s internal conditions.

options.text: Keeping the two halves of the brain in balance, so that neither side takes over a job that both of them should share.
options.why: A difference between what the two sides do is lateralization. Homeostasis is about internal conditions like temperature and water.

options.text: Keeping an animal awake enough to respond, raising and lowering its arousal over the course of a day.
options.why: Setting how awake an animal is belongs to the reticular formation. Homeostasis is about internal conditions like temperature and blood sugar.

items.stem: What is the general name for keeping the body’s internal conditions, such as temperature, water balance and blood sugar, within limits?

options.text: Homeostasis.
options.why: Correct. The hypothalamus holds these conditions near their set points, partly through behavior and partly through the pituitary.

options.text: Lateralization.
options.why: Lateralization is a difference between what the left and right sides of a brain do.

options.text: Action selection.
options.why: Action selection is choosing which available action is performed now, which the basal ganglia do.

options.text: Reverse inference.
options.why: Reverse inference is the move from “this region was active during the task” to “the task involved what this region does”.

items.stem: A lizard that has been in the sun too long moves into the shade, and a deer short of water walks to a stream. What does the chapter say produces behavior like this?

options.text: Hypothalamus cells detect how far a condition has drifted from its set point, and circuits act to correct it, here by driving behavior.
options.why: Correct. Some of the hypothalamus’s correction is behavioral, which is why an animal short of water looks for water.

options.text: The amygdala evaluates the heat or the thirst as bad, and the animal learns to avoid that bad outcome by moving away from what caused it.
options.why: The amygdala evaluates what matters, but correcting drift from a set point is the hypothalamus’s job, and no learning is needed for it.

options.text: The basal ganglia release a habit learned from reward, since the behavior of moving to shade or to water has paid off many times before.
options.why: The basal ganglia select actions, but the drive here comes from a condition drifting from its set point, which the hypothalamus detects.

options.text: The reticular formation raises arousal until the animal is awake enough to notice the heat or the thirst and move.
options.why: Arousal matters for any behavior, but detecting and correcting drift in temperature or water is the hypothalamus’s job.

items.stem: Module 5 separated habits, which run off automatically, from goal-directed actions, which depend on what the animal currently wants. How does the chapter map the two onto the striatum?

options.text: They map onto different parts of it, with habits leaning toward one end and goal-directed action toward the other.
options.why: Correct. The distinction drawn in Module 5 has an address: two ends of the same input stage.

options.text: They share one part of it, and differ in how much dopamine arrives in that part while each of them is being performed.
options.why: The chapter maps habits and goal-directed action onto different parts of the striatum, not onto one part with different dopamine levels.

options.text: Habits map onto the striatum, while goal-directed action is handled entirely in the pallium, outside the basal ganglia.
options.why: Both map onto the striatum, at different ends of it.

options.text: Goal-directed action maps onto the striatum, while habits move out to the cerebellum once they become automatic.
options.why: Habits are not moved to the cerebellum. Both kinds of action map onto the striatum, at its two ends.

items.stem: What is the amygdala?

options.text: A cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that evaluates what matters, quickly, before much else has happened.
options.why: Correct. Part of the address of valence is here: some of its neurons respond to good outcomes and others to bad ones.

options.text: A cluster of cells at the base of the forebrain that keeps temperature, water balance and blood sugar near each of their set points.
options.why: That describes the hypothalamus. The amygdala evaluates what matters rather than holding internal conditions near set points.

options.text: The input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium arrive and the dopamine fibers meet them.
options.why: That is the striatum. The amygdala is a separate cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain.

options.text: A structure deep in the forebrain that stores frightening memories and produces the feeling of being afraid.
options.why: This is a common belief, but the chapter describes quick evaluation of what matters, good or bad. The circuits that produce a defensive response are not the ones that produce the feeling of fear.

items.stem: What is the name for the cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that quickly evaluates what matters, with some of its neurons tuned to good outcomes and others to bad ones?

options.text: Amygdala.
options.why: Correct. Its good-tuned and bad-tuned neurons are intermingled in the same tissue.

options.text: Hypothalamus.
options.why: The hypothalamus sits at the base of the forebrain too, but it keeps internal conditions near their set points.

options.text: Striatum.
options.why: The striatum is the input stage of the basal ganglia, where signals from the pallium and the dopamine fibers arrive.

options.text: Thalamus.
options.why: The thalamus sits above the hypothalamus, and almost everything that reaches the pallium passes through it.

items.stem: Researchers record from many neurons in one small patch of a rat’s amygdala, first while the rat receives a sweet reward and then while it receives a mild shock. What does the chapter lead us to expect?

options.text: Some neurons respond selectively to the reward and others to the shock, intermingled in the same patch of tissue.
options.why: Correct. That is the literal form of the valence claim: populations tuned to good outcomes and to bad ones, mixed together in the same tissue.

options.text: The reward neurons and the shock neurons sit in separate subregions of the patch, one for good outcomes and one for bad ones.
options.why: This is the picture the chapter’s wording rules out. The two populations are intermingled in the same tissue, not divided into a good region and a bad one.

options.text: Nearly all the neurons respond to the shock, since the amygdala is the part of the brain concerned with threats rather than rewards.
options.why: The amygdala is part of the address of valence, good as well as bad. Some of its populations respond selectively to good outcomes.

options.text: Nearly all the neurons respond to both outcomes equally, since the amygdala tracks how strong an event is and not whether it is good.
options.why: Responding to whatever is salient is one job the amygdala has been credited with, but the chapter’s valence claim is that separate populations respond selectively to good and to bad outcomes.

items.stem: What can the chapter say about a lamprey’s amygdala, and how does that compare with what it can say about the lamprey’s selection circuitry?

options.text: Whether it has an amygdala-like region is not settled, so the amygdala claim covers jawed vertebrates; its selection circuit matches a mammal’s part for part.
options.why: Correct. The two claims carry different weight. Reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have an amygdala-like region; for the lamprey the question is open, while its selection circuit is not in doubt.

options.text: It clearly lacks both, since an amygdala and a selection circuit each arose with the jawed fishes, after the lamprey’s lineage had split from theirs.
options.why: The lamprey has basal ganglia matching a mammal’s part for part, and whether it lacks an amygdala-like region is not settled.

options.text: It has both, each matching a mammal’s part for part, since reptiles, birds and jawed fishes all have an amygdala-like region with similar circuitry of their own.
options.why: What reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have does not settle the lamprey. The chapter restricts its amygdala claim to jawed vertebrates.

options.text: It has an amygdala-like region matching a mammal’s, but whether it has selection circuitry of the mammalian kind is not settled.
options.why: That swaps the hedge. The selection circuit is the part that matches a mammal’s, and the amygdala is the part that is not settled.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the vertebrate nervous system has circuits dedicated to single behaviors near its bottom but shares machinery among behaviors higher up. Name at least two of the dedicated behaviors.
items.answer: In the hindbrain and spinal cord, dedicated circuitry for a particular behavior really does exist. Breathing has its own pattern generator, and so do chewing, swallowing and locomotion. Each of these behaviors is stereotyped, and each has to keep running while everything else changes, so it pays to give each a circuit of its own. That is the keep-going half of the conflict between keeping going and changing course, built into anatomy. Higher up, actions are chosen rather than generated. Behaviors like walking and eating compete for the same body, so there the arrangement is shared machinery, with something to select which action is released.
rubric: Names at least two of breathing, chewing, swallowing and locomotion as having pattern generators of their own.
Says these behaviors are stereotyped.
Says they must keep running while everything else changes, as the keep-going half of the conflict with changing course.
Says that higher up actions are chosen rather than generated, by shared machinery with something to select among the options.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say where the dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine that reach so much of the brain come from, and what the three sources have in common.
items.answer: The dopamine neurons sit in two clusters in the midbrain, and their fibers run forward into the striatum and the pallium. The serotonin neurons sit in a series of clusters along the midline of the brainstem, reaching back into the hindbrain. Most of the norepinephrine comes from one small cluster of cells in the hindbrain, whose fibers reach nearly the whole brain. All three sources are small and old, and positioned to reach almost everything. So the brain’s broad projections start in a few little places.
rubric: Places the dopamine neurons in two clusters in the midbrain, with fibers to the striatum and the pallium.
Places the serotonin neurons in clusters along the midline of the brainstem.
Places most of the norepinephrine in one small hindbrain cluster whose fibers reach nearly the whole brain.
Says the three sources are small and old and reach almost everything, so the broad projections start in a few small places.

items.stem: On a hot day, a dog pants less once it has had a long drink and lain down in the shade. In a short paragraph, use the chapter’s account of the hypothalamus to say what is being regulated and the two ways it is corrected, and name the general term for this.
items.answer: The dog’s body temperature and water balance are internal conditions that the hypothalamus keeps near their set points. The hypothalamus has cells that detect how far each condition has drifted and circuits that act to correct it. Some of the correction is behavioral: the drift drives the dog to look for water and to move into the shade. Some is physiological, working through the pituitary gland below the hypothalamus, which releases hormones into the blood that reach the rest of the body. Keeping internal conditions within limits like this is homeostasis.
rubric: Identifies temperature or water balance as an internal condition held near a set point by the hypothalamus.
Says the hypothalamus detects drift and acts to correct it.
Gives the behavioral correction, such as seeking water or shade.
Gives the physiological correction, through pituitary hormones released into the blood.
Names the general term, homeostasis.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say what the amygdala does, what makes the chapter’s valence claim about it “more literal than one might expect”, and why the chapter’s claim about the amygdala is narrower than its claim about the lamprey’s selection circuitry.
items.answer: The amygdala is a cluster of nuclei at the front and base of the forebrain that evaluates what matters, quickly, before much else has happened. Its valence claim is literal because populations of amygdala neurons respond selectively to good outcomes and other populations to bad ones, intermingled in the same tissue. Reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have an amygdala-like region with similar circuitry, but whether a lamprey has one is not settled, so the claim is about jawed vertebrates. The lamprey’s selection circuitry, by contrast, matches a mammal’s part for part, so that claim needs no such restriction.
rubric: Says the amygdala evaluates what matters quickly.
Says separate populations respond to good and to bad outcomes.
Says those populations are intermingled in the same tissue, not in separate regions.
Says whether a lamprey has an amygdala-like region is not settled, so the claim covers jawed vertebrates.
Contrasts the lamprey’s selection circuitry, which matches a mammal’s part for part.

pools.title: The Pallium, What Came Later, and Two Halves
pools.covers: reading §6.3.4, §6.3.5, §6.3.6 · lecture 6.3 slides pallium_and_thalamus, what_came_later, two_halves · lab Specimens, Tree

items.stem: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the roof of the forebrain. How does a lamprey’s pallium compare with a mammal’s?

options.text: The lamprey’s is thin, with three layers; the mammal’s grew enormously and acquired six layers, which is the neocortex.
options.why: Correct. The structure is the same one, and what it is made of differs. Its six-layered mammalian form is what the word neocortex names.

options.text: The lamprey has none; a pallium first appears in mammals, where it grew enormously and acquired its six layers, the neocortex.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the lamprey included. What arrived with the mammals is the six-layered form.

options.text: The lamprey’s has six layers like the mammal’s, but it is far smaller, and so the name neocortex is kept for the mammal’s.
options.why: A lamprey’s pallium has three layers. The six layers are the mammalian form.

options.text: The two are built alike, three thin layers in each, and differ in size, the mammal’s having grown enormously larger.
options.why: The mammalian pallium did grow enormously, but it also acquired six layers. The difference is in what it is made of, not only in size.

items.stem: Recent experiments suggest that a lamprey’s pallium has output cells reaching the basal ganglia, the tectum, the brainstem and the spinal cord, much as a mammal’s does. How firmly does the chapter hold that resemblance?

options.text: As a promising result rather than a settled one, since the evidence is recent and comes largely from one laboratory.
options.why: Correct. The chapter hedges its most attention-getting lamprey claim at once. The resemblance may well hold, but it has not yet been confirmed widely enough to be treated as settled.

options.text: As settled beyond reasonable doubt, since the same result has been found in lampreys, hagfishes and every jawed fish that has been tested.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite about the evidence: it is recent and comes largely from one laboratory.

options.text: As disproved, since a lamprey’s pallium is too thin to contain output cells and receives smell alone, with no other input.
options.why: A lamprey’s pallium is thin, with three layers, but the chapter does not treat the result as disproved. It holds it as promising.

options.text: As settled for the lamprey’s inputs but doubtful for its outputs, since recent work confirms its visual signals and not its output cells.
options.why: The chapter’s hedge covers the arrangement as a whole, inputs and outputs alike. It does not split them.

items.stem: Three words are in play for the roof of the forebrain. How does the chapter use pallium, neocortex and cortex?

options.text: Pallium is the structure in any vertebrate, neocortex is its six-layered mammalian form, and cortex alone is loose usage for the neocortex.
options.why: Correct. The convention keeps one word for the structure every vertebrate has and another for its mammalian form.

options.text: Cortex is the structure in any vertebrate, pallium is its six-layered mammalian form, and neocortex is loose usage for the pallium of birds.
options.why: That scrambles the three words. Pallium is the general word, and neocortex is the mammalian six-layered form.

options.text: Neocortex is the structure in any vertebrate, pallium is the three-layered form in fishes, and cortex is the six-layered form in mammals.
options.why: Neocortex is the mammalian form, not the general one. Pallium is the word for the structure in any vertebrate.

options.text: Pallium, neocortex and cortex are three names for one structure, and the chapter uses them interchangeably for every vertebrate.
options.why: The chapter separates the words deliberately, and it does not apply cortex to a fish.

items.stem: A student’s lab report describes stimulating “the cortex of a trout”. How would the chapter’s convention phrase the same thing?

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s pallium, since the chapter keeps the word cortex for the neocortex and does not apply it to a fish.
options.why: Correct. A trout has a pallium, as every vertebrate does. Cortex on its own is loose usage for the mammalian neocortex.

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s neocortex, since every vertebrate’s pallium becomes a neocortex once it has more than three layers.
options.why: The neocortex is the six-layered mammalian form. A fish’s pallium is not a neocortex.

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s tectum, since a fish has no forebrain roof and handles everything in the roof of its midbrain instead.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium. The tectum is a different structure, the roof of the midbrain.

options.text: Stimulating the trout’s cortex, since the chapter treats cortex as loose usage for the forebrain roof of any vertebrate, fishes included.
options.why: The chapter’s convention says cortex is loose usage for the neocortex, and this chapter does not apply it to a fish.

items.stem: Where is the thalamus, and what passes through it?

options.text: It sits above the hypothalamus, in the middle of the forebrain, and almost everything that reaches the pallium passes through it.
options.why: Correct. The thalamus is the gate on the way into the pallium, for nearly all of what arrives there.

options.text: It sits below the hypothalamus, at the very base of the forebrain, and the hormones of the pituitary pass through it into the blood.
options.why: The pituitary hangs below the hypothalamus. The thalamus sits above the hypothalamus, and signals bound for the pallium pass through it.

options.text: It sits in the roof of the midbrain, and the maps of the space around the animal pass through it on their way to the eyes.
options.why: The roof of the midbrain is the tectum. The thalamus is in the forebrain, above the hypothalamus.

options.text: It sits deep in the forebrain, wrapped around its sides, and every proposed action passes through it to be released or held back.
options.why: Releasing one action and holding back the others is the basal ganglia’s job. The thalamus is where their output returns on its way back up.

items.stem: Because almost everything that reaches the pallium passes through the thalamus, a student calls the thalamus a passive relay station, a switchboard that forwards signals unchanged. What does the chapter say?

options.text: The thalamus is not a passive relay station, although what it does to the signals it passes is left to later modules.
options.why: Correct. The chapter denies the passive picture and defers the positive account, so it says what the thalamus is not before saying what it is.

options.text: The student is right: the thalamus is a relay station that forwards signals unchanged, which is why the chapter says nothing more about what it does to them.
options.why: The chapter says outright that a thalamus is not a passive relay station. It defers what the thalamus does, not whether it does anything.

options.text: The thalamus is not a relay at all, since almost every signal bound for the pallium reaches it directly and never passes through the thalamus.
options.why: Almost everything that reaches the pallium does pass through the thalamus. The correction is to “passive”, not to “relay”.

options.text: The thalamus is a passive relay for vision and an active one for smell, since smell is the one sense the thalamus reshapes on its way to the pallium.
options.why: Smell reaches a lamprey’s pallium directly, without passing through the thalamus. The chapter makes no sense-by-sense split.

items.stem: Set a lamprey’s brain beside a mouse’s. What does the chapter say has changed between the two?

options.text: The same parts are there in the same order, with one exception, and what changed is mostly proportion and number.
options.why: Correct. One plan runs through both brains. The differences are mostly in how big each part is and how many copies of it there are.

options.text: The mouse’s brain has a different set of parts in a different order, since half a billion years of change rebuilt it from scratch.
options.why: The parts and their order are the same, with a single exception. What changed is mostly proportion and number.

options.text: Nothing has changed: the two brains have the same parts in the same proportions, and differ only in their overall size.
options.why: The proportions differ markedly, and one part is missing from the lamprey in the form jawed vertebrates have it.

options.text: The same parts are there, but their order along the brain is reversed, with the forebrain at the back in the lamprey.
options.why: The order is the same in both, from the hindbrain at the back to the forebrain at the front.

items.stem: Across living vertebrates, brain size for a given body size varies about thirtyfold. Where does the chapter say the increases in relative brain size happened?

options.text: Independently, in some members of every major group: in sharks, in bony fishes, in birds and in mammals.
options.why: Correct. The thirtyfold range and the independent increases are one fact in two parts. Brains got bigger more than once.

options.text: Once, in the lineage leading to mammals, so that every mammal has a larger brain for its size than any other vertebrate.
options.why: Relative brain size increased independently in several groups, not once, and not only in mammals.

options.text: Once, in the common ancestor of birds and mammals, whose descendants all inherited the enlarged brain from it.
options.why: Sharks and bony fishes include large-brained members too. The increases happened separately in each group.

options.text: Gradually along a single line, from lampreys to fishes to amphibians to reptiles, and then to birds and mammals at the top.
options.why: That is the ladder the chapter rejects. The plan was elaborated many times over, in parallel.

items.stem: A lineage evolves a larger brain for its body size. What does the chapter say such a brain generally has more of?

options.text: More distinct parts, rather than simply more of the same tissue.
options.why: Correct. Larger brains generally have more distinct parts, as in the front of the forebrain, where six cell groups became sixty-six.

options.text: More of the same tissue, with the same number of parts, each one scaled up to the new size.
options.why: That is the picture the chapter corrects. Larger brains generally have more distinct parts, not just more of the same.

options.text: Larger neurons, with the number of neurons and parts left unchanged.
options.why: The chapter’s point is about parts, not about the size of individual neurons.

options.text: More folding of its surface, with the number of parts left unchanged.
options.why: Folding is a matter of how a sheet is packed, not how many parts there are. Larger brains generally have more distinct parts.

items.stem: A museum case lines up brains from a lamprey, a shark, a frog, a lizard, a bird and a mouse, labeled as steps from “primitive” to “advanced”. What does the chapter say is wrong with that arrangement?

options.text: The vertebrate plan was elaborated many times over, in parallel, rather than climbed once toward mammals.
options.why: Correct. Size increased independently in sharks, bony fishes, birds and mammals, and birds built a large pallium in their own way. There is no single climb for the case to show.

options.text: Nothing, since each group in the case descends from the one before it, adding one new part at each step on the way to mammals.
options.why: Living groups do not descend from one another; they share common ancestors. And the additions came in parallel, not one step at a time.

options.text: The order is wrong, since birds have larger brains than mammals and belong at the top of the case instead of the mouse.
options.why: Reordering the case keeps the ladder. The chapter’s objection is to the ladder itself.

options.text: The case should show one brain only, since every vertebrate brain is identical in its parts and in their proportions.
options.why: The parts are the same, but the proportions differ markedly. What the chapter rejects is reading those differences as steps on one ladder.

items.stem: Crows and parrots solve problems with a flexibility that rivals some mammals’. How is the bird pallium that supports this organized?

options.text: It is large, and organized in clusters rather than in layers.
options.why: Correct. The bird pallium is the clearest case of independent elaboration: large, supporting flexible behavior, and built in clusters.

options.text: It is large, and organized in six layers like the mammalian neocortex.
options.why: The six layers are the mammalian form. The bird pallium is organized in clusters rather than in layers.

options.text: It is thin, with the three layers of a lamprey’s pallium, and simply spread over a larger area.
options.why: The bird pallium is large and clustered, not a stretched three-layered sheet.

options.text: It is small, and the flexible behavior is handled instead by an enlarged cerebellum at the back of the brain.
options.why: The forebrain roof grows largest in birds and mammals. The bird pallium itself is large.

items.stem: Researchers have argued for decades over whether particular parts of the bird pallium correspond to particular parts of the mammalian neocortex. Why is the question so hard to settle?

options.text: Homology is hard to establish when two lineages have been separate for three hundred million years, and here they are also organized differently.
options.why: Correct. The bird pallium is a good illustration of how hard homology can be to establish across such a long separation, with clusters on one side and layers on the other.

options.text: It is not hard to settle; the matter was decided long ago, and the bird pallium is known to be a six-layered neocortex in another shape.
options.why: The chapter says the question has been argued for decades, and the bird pallium is organized in clusters, not six layers.

options.text: Birds have no pallium at all, so the comparison is between a mammalian structure and a bird structure that is not part of the forebrain roof.
options.why: Every vertebrate has a pallium, birds included. The dispute is about which parts of it correspond to which parts of the neocortex.

options.text: Birds and mammals are so closely related that their pallia are hard to tell apart, which makes any difference between them difficult to measure.
options.why: The difficulty runs the other way. Birds and mammals have been separate for three hundred million years, and their pallia look very different.

items.stem: What is lateralization?

options.text: A difference between what the left and right sides of a brain do.
options.why: Correct. The departures from symmetry that it names are real, widespread across vertebrate groups, and old.

options.text: A difference between what the front and back of a brain do.
options.why: The front-to-back plan is the one the chapter lays out part by part. Lateralization is about left and right.

options.text: The bundle of fibers that connects the two sides of a brain.
options.why: That describes a connection between the hemispheres, such as the corpus callosum. Lateralization is a difference in what the two sides do.

options.text: The mirror-image match between the two sides of most brain structures.
options.why: Most paired structures are near mirror images, but lateralization is the name for the departures from that symmetry.

items.stem: What is the general name for a difference between what the left and right sides of a brain do?

options.text: Lateralization.
options.why: Correct. The domestic chick is the case of it worked out in most detail.

options.text: Corpus callosum.
options.why: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres in placental mammals. It is a bridge between the sides, not a difference between them.

options.text: Modularity.
options.why: Modularity is a system built from units that each do their own job and connect through a limited set of connections.

options.text: Reverse inference.
options.why: Reverse inference is the move from “this region was active” to “the task involved what this region does”.

items.stem: A student says that left-right differences in the brain are a recent, human specialty, and that other animals’ brains are simply symmetrical. What does the chapter say?

options.text: Nearly every structure comes in two, mostly near mirror images, but the departures from symmetry are real, widespread across vertebrates, and old.
options.why: Correct. The brain is paired and mostly symmetrical, and its asymmetries are found across vertebrate groups and are old.

options.text: The student is right: outside human beings, the two sides of every vertebrate brain are exact mirror images of each other.
options.why: The chapter says departures from symmetry are widespread across vertebrate groups. The chick is its detailed case.

options.text: The student is half right: left-right differences are old, but they are confined to the mammals with a corpus callosum joining their two halves.
options.why: The chick, the chapter’s detailed case of lateralization, has no corpus callosum at all.

options.text: The student is wrong the other way: a vertebrate brain is not paired, and most structures sit singly along the midline of the brain.
options.why: A vertebrate brain is paired. Nearly every structure comes in two, one on each side.

items.stem: A domestic chick pecks for grain scattered among pebbles while also watching for a hawk overhead. Which eye, and mainly which hemisphere, does it use for each job?

options.text: The right eye and mainly the left hemisphere for the grain; the left eye and mainly the right hemisphere for the hawk.
options.why: Correct. Picking grain from pebbles takes a fine visual discrimination, and the chick gives it to the right eye and left hemisphere.

options.text: The left eye and mainly the right hemisphere for the grain; the right eye and mainly the left hemisphere for the hawk.
options.why: That reverses the two jobs. The right eye, and so mainly the left hemisphere, handles the grain.

options.text: The right eye and mainly the right hemisphere for the grain; the left eye and mainly the left hemisphere for the hawk.
options.why: Each eye works mainly with the hemisphere on the opposite side. The right eye goes with the left hemisphere.

options.text: Both eyes and both hemispheres for each job in turn, switching between the grain and the hawk from one moment to the next.
options.why: The chick divides the two jobs between its two sides, which is exactly what makes it the detailed case of lateralization.

items.stem: How do chicks from lit eggs and chicks from dark eggs compare on the grain task and the hawk task?

options.text: Lit-egg chicks do better at both at once; dark-egg chicks do as well at either alone but get worse at the grain when they must also watch for the hawk.
options.why: Correct. The dark-egg chicks are not worse at either job; they are worse at doing the two together. That is interference between two jobs.

options.text: Lit-egg chicks do better at each task alone; dark-egg chicks do worse at each task alone, whether or not they are also watching for the hawk.
options.why: Dark-egg chicks do just as well on either task alone. Their trouble shows up only when both jobs have to be done at once.

options.text: Lit-egg chicks do better at spotting the hawk, and dark-egg chicks do better at finding the grain, whether the two tasks are done alone or together.
options.why: Lit-egg chicks do better at both jobs at once. The dark-egg chicks lose the grain discrimination when they must watch for the hawk.

options.text: The two kinds of chick do equally well at both tasks, alone and together, since light before hatching changes only which eye is used.
options.why: Light before hatching strengthens the asymmetry, and it changes how well the chicks do both jobs at once.

items.stem: Why does it matter that chicks from dark eggs do just as well as lit-egg chicks on either task alone?

options.text: It shows their trouble is interference between two jobs done at once, the argument about competing demands with an experiment attached.
options.why: Correct. The dark-egg chicks lose nothing on either job alone, so the cost appears only when one side must do both. That is the argument about competing demands at a smaller scale, with an experiment attached.

options.text: It shows that keeping the eggs dark damages the chicks’ eyesight, so the dark-egg chicks see less well in whatever task they happen to be given.
options.why: If their eyesight were damaged, they would do worse on each task alone. They do not.

options.text: It shows that lateralization brings no advantage at all, since chicks with a weaker asymmetry manage each of the jobs just as well.
options.why: The advantage appears when both jobs must be done at once, which is exactly the situation the dual task sets up.

options.text: It shows that most chicks favor the same side because of their neighbors, since chicks raised together learn which eye to use.
options.why: Why chicks favor the same side is a separate question the dual-task result says nothing about.

items.stem: The chick dual-task result is often taken to explain lateralization. What does the chapter say it explains, and what does it leave unexplained?

options.text: It explains why an individual chick is lateralized, and says nothing about why most chicks are lateralized the same way.
options.why: Correct. How well one animal divides its own work has nothing to do with which side its neighbors favor, so the two questions are independent.

options.text: It explains why most chicks are lateralized the same way, and says nothing about why any individual chick is lateralized at all.
options.why: That reverses the two. The dual-task advantage is an advantage to the individual, and it is silent on alignment across the population.

options.text: It explains both, since a chick that divides its work well will favor the same side its neighbors favor, and so the whole flock lines up.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: one animal’s division of work has nothing to do with which side its neighbors favor.

options.text: It explains neither, since the result was found only in chicks from dark eggs, which are not lateralized in the first place.
options.why: The advantage appears in the chicks from lit eggs, whose asymmetry is stronger. It explains why an individual is lateralized.

items.stem: Species A lives in large groups whose members must coordinate their movements, and Species B lives alone. What does the proposed social explanation predict about their lateralization?

options.text: Population-level alignment can be stable in Species A and absent in Species B, even if individuals of both are lateralized.
options.why: Correct. When animals must coordinate, matching the majority is worth more than being unpredictable. The explanation is contested, but this is what it predicts.

options.text: Population-level alignment should be stable in Species B and absent in Species A, since animals living alone need not fear being predictable.
options.why: That reverses the prediction. It is coordination with others that makes matching the majority worthwhile.

options.text: Both species should align as populations equally, since the individual advantage from dividing two jobs is the same whether an animal lives alone or not.
options.why: The individual advantage explains why an animal is lateralized, not which way its neighbors lean. The social account ties alignment to coordination.

options.text: Neither species should be lateralized at all, since being unpredictable to predators is worth more than any benefit of favoring one side.
options.why: The social account concerns alignment across a population. It does not predict that individual lateralization disappears.

items.stem: Across sixteen fish species, the schooling ones were lateralized as populations and several solitary ones only as individuals. What status does the chapter give the social explanation in light of that evidence?

options.text: A proposal with support, not a settled result: it is contested, and several researchers have proposed other explanations.
options.why: Correct. The sixteen-species comparison is evidence for the social proposal, not proof of it, and the chapter says so.

options.text: A settled result, since the sixteen fish species show that schooling is the cause of population-level alignment across vertebrates.
options.why: The chapter marks the social explanation as contested. A correlation across sixteen species supports it without settling it.

options.text: A refuted proposal, since several solitary species were lateralized too, which the social account says should not happen at all.
options.why: The social account concerns alignment across a population. Solitary species being lateralized as individuals is what it allows.

options.text: An untested idea, since schooling and solitary species have yet to be compared for how they are lateralized.
options.why: The sixteen-species comparison is exactly such a study, and it counts as support.

items.stem: What is the corpus callosum?

options.text: The great bundle of fibers connecting the two hemispheres in placental mammals, roughly two hundred million of them.
options.why: Correct. It is the largest bridge between the halves, and it is found in placental mammals only.

options.text: The great bundle of fibers connecting the two hemispheres in every vertebrate, from the lamprey to human beings.
options.why: Other vertebrates, including birds, fishes and mammals that are not placental, connect their hemispheres through smaller commissures.

options.text: The loose network of cells running the length of the brainstem, setting how awake an animal is and taking it into sleep.
options.why: That is the reticular formation. The corpus callosum is a bridge of fibers between the two hemispheres.

options.text: The difference between what the left and right sides of a brain do, which the fibers between the halves make possible.
options.why: A difference between the two sides’ jobs is lateralization, and the chick shows it without any corpus callosum.

items.stem: What is the name for the great bundle of fibers, roughly two hundred million strong, that connects the two hemispheres in placental mammals?

options.text: Corpus callosum.
options.why: Correct. Birds, fishes and mammals that are not placental use smaller commissures instead.

options.text: Reticular formation.
options.why: The reticular formation is a loose network of cells in the brainstem that sets how awake an animal is.

options.text: Thalamus.
options.why: The thalamus is the structure above the hypothalamus through which almost everything reaching the pallium passes.

options.text: Lateralization.
options.why: Lateralization is a difference between what the two sides of a brain do, not a connection between them.

items.stem: An online quiz sorts people into “left-brained” logical thinkers and “right-brained” creative ones. What does the chapter say about the claims behind it?

options.text: The familiar claims about logical and creative hemispheres are not supported by the evidence.
options.why: Correct. The human case is the one most students have heard about, and usually in this form. Human lateralization, and what language has to do with it, is taken up separately.

options.text: The claims about logical and creative hemispheres are well supported in humans, although they have not been tested in other vertebrates.
options.why: The chapter says the evidence does not support these claims.

options.text: The claims are well supported in the chick, whose left hemisphere handles the grain and whose right hemisphere handles the hawk.
options.why: The chick does divide its work between its sides, but that division is about grain and predators, not logic and creativity.

options.text: The claims hold for placental mammals alone, since they are the animals with a corpus callosum to keep the two halves apart.
options.why: The corpus callosum connects the two halves rather than keeping them apart, and the chapter says the logical-creative claims are unsupported.

items.stem: Lateralization raises two questions that look like one. In a short paragraph, state the two questions, say why the chick dual-task result answers only one of them, and say what has been proposed for the other and how firmly.
items.answer: The first question is why an individual animal is lateralized. The second is why most animals in a population are lateralized the same way. The chick result answers the first: a chick that divides its work between its two sides does better at two jobs at once. But how well one animal divides its own work has nothing to do with which side its neighbors favor, so the result says nothing about the second. Population alignment is a separate puzzle, and it even has a cost, since a predator can learn which way a population escapes. The proposed answer is social: when animals must coordinate, matching the majority is worth more than being unpredictable. There is support for it, in schooling fish, but it is contested, and it is a proposal rather than a settled result.
rubric: Distinguishes why an individual is lateralized from why a population is lateralized the same way.
Says the chick result explains individual lateralization only, because one animal’s division of work is independent of its neighbors’ side.
Mentions the cost of alignment: a predator can learn which way a population escapes.
Gives the social proposal: coordinating animals gain by matching the majority.
Says the social proposal is contested, supported but not settled.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the experiment in which chick eggs are left in the light or kept dark, give its result, and explain why the result on each task alone is what makes the experiment convincing.
items.answer: A chick embryo lies turned so that only its right eye gets light through the shell. Eggs left in the light develop a stronger asymmetry than eggs kept dark. When the chicks hatch, those from lit eggs do better at two jobs at once: finding grain among pebbles and spotting a hawk overhead. Chicks from dark eggs do just as well on either task alone, but get worse at the grain discrimination when they must watch for the predator at the same time. Because the dark-egg chicks are fine on each task by itself, their trouble is not poor eyesight or poor skill but interference between two jobs done at once. So the experiment tests the argument that one mechanism struggles to do two incompatible things, and shows a benefit from giving the jobs to two sides.
rubric: Says only the right eye gets light through the shell, and light strengthens the asymmetry.
Says lit-egg chicks do better at both jobs at once.
Says dark-egg chicks do as well on either task alone.
Says dark-egg chicks do worse at the grain when also watching for the predator.
Explains that the single-task result shows the deficit is interference between two jobs, not a general loss.

items.stem: A classmate writes that “lampreys have a cortex just like ours”. In a short paragraph, correct the wording using the chapter’s convention for pallium, neocortex and cortex, say how a lamprey’s pallium differs from a mammal’s, and say how firmly the chapter holds the resemblance between them.
items.answer: Every vertebrate has a pallium, the roof of the forebrain, so the lamprey has one. But the chapter keeps neocortex for the six-layered mammalian form, and uses cortex on its own only as loose usage for the neocortex, never for a fish. A lamprey’s pallium is thin, with three layers, while a mammal’s grew enormously and acquired six. Recent experiments suggest the lamprey’s pallium already has output cells reaching the brainstem and spinal cord and receives visual signals through the thalamus, much as a mammal’s does. But that evidence is recent and comes largely from one laboratory, so the resemblance is a promising result, not a settled one.
rubric: Replaces cortex with pallium for the lamprey, and says cortex is not used for a fish.
Gives the convention: pallium for any vertebrate, neocortex for the six-layered mammalian form.
Contrasts the lamprey’s thin three-layered pallium with the mammal’s enlarged six-layered one.
Says the resemblance rests on recent evidence largely from one laboratory, and is promising rather than settled.

pools.title: A Sheet Becomes a Tube, Position Before Identity, and Layers
pools.covers: reading §6.3.7, §6.3.8, §6.3.9 · lecture 6.3 slides title, rules_not_a_blueprint, made_moved_steered_culled

items.stem: A classmate argues that the genome must contain a complete wiring diagram of the brain, stored in a very compact code. What does the chapter say against this?

options.text: A human brain has some eighty-six billion neurons and trillions of connections, and a genome holds nowhere near enough information to list them.
options.why: Correct. Nothing could specify that many cells and connections one at a time. There is no list anywhere of which cell goes where, and not remotely enough information in a genome to hold one.

options.text: A genome does hold a complete wiring list, but only for the forebrain; the hindbrain and spinal cord are wired later by experience.
options.why: No part of the brain is wired from a list in the chapter’s account. The same small set of local rules builds every part, the hindbrain included.

options.text: A genome holds the wiring list, but the list is lost when the neural tube closes, so the cells must rebuild the wiring from the old plate’s layout.
options.why: Nothing is lost when the tube closes, because no list ever existed. Cells respond only to their immediate surroundings, following a small set of rules.

options.text: A wiring list would not work because the brain keeps changing after birth, so any list written in the embryo would soon be out of date.
options.why: Change through experience after birth is real, but it is not the chapter’s reason. The reason is scale: billions of cells and trillions of connections, with far too little information in a genome to list them.

items.stem: In place of a list of which cell goes where, what does the chapter say a genome holds?

options.text: A small set of rules, applied over and over by cells that can respond only to their immediate surroundings.
options.why: Correct. Read a gradient, listen to the neighbors, follow a cue, and compete for a limited supply. Run in the right order, those rules build the brain.

options.text: A map of the adult brain at reduced scale, which each cell consults to find its own place in the finished structure.
options.why: A map that each cell consults would still be a blueprint. The chapter’s cells cannot see the whole; they respond only to their immediate surroundings.

options.text: A separate address for every neuron, carried as a chemical label that matches a label on the neuron’s target.
options.why: One address per cell was Sperry’s interpretation of how axons find their targets, and the chapter calls it a blueprint. What was found instead was gradients.

options.text: A record of the ancestral adult brain, which the embryo passes through stage by stage on its way to the modern form.
options.why: Development is not a replay of ancestral adults, a warning Module 2 gave. The genome holds local rules, not a record of ancestors.

items.stem: About eighteen days after conception, the tissue beneath the midline of the embryo’s outermost layer starts the nervous system. What does that tissue do?

options.text: It releases molecules that block the skin-making signal, so the cells above are left to become neural.
options.why: Correct. Neural is what the outer layer becomes when the skin-making signal is blocked. The nervous system is, in this sense, a default.

options.text: It releases a neural-making signal that instructs the cells above to stop being skin and become neurons instead.
options.why: The molecules the tissue releases do not instruct cells to become neural. They block the signal that would otherwise have made those cells skin.

options.text: It sends its own cells up into the outer layer, where they settle along the midline and become the neural plate.
options.why: The neural plate is made from cells already in the outer layer. The tissue beneath changes what those cells become; it does not replace them.

options.text: It fuses with the outer layer above it, so the two layers together fold into the hollow neural tube.
options.why: Folding and fusion come afterward, and they involve the edges of the neural plate, not the tissue beneath it.

items.stem: Suppose a patch of the embryo’s outer layer, well away from the midline, were kept from receiving the skin-making signal at all. On the chapter’s account, what should the cells of that patch become?

options.text: Neural tissue, since neural is what the outer layer becomes when nothing tells it to make skin.
options.why: Correct. The chapter frames the nervous system as the outer layer’s default, reached when the skin-making signal is blocked. Nothing further is needed to make the cells neural.

options.text: Skin anyway, since skin is the outer layer’s default and would form even without any signal to make it.
options.why: That reverses the default. Skin needs a signal; left without one, cells of the outer layer become neural.

options.text: Nothing at all, since cells that receive no signal have no fate to follow and so die off early.
options.why: The chapter gives these cells a fate without the signal: they become neural. Lacking the skin signal is exactly how the neural plate forms.

options.text: Neural tissue only if a second, neural-making signal were added, since blocking one signal cannot give cells a fate.
options.why: No neural-making signal is needed in the chapter’s account. Blocking the skin-making signal is enough, because neural is the default.

items.stem: What is the neural plate?

options.text: The strip of cells on the back of an early embryo that becomes the nervous system, formed where the skin-making signal is blocked.
options.why: Correct. Signals from the tissue beneath block the skin-making signal, and the strip of cells above becomes the neural plate.

options.text: The hollow structure formed when raised folds lean in and fuse, from which every vertebrate brain and spinal cord is built.
options.why: That is the neural tube, which the neural plate becomes once its edges rise into folds and fuse.

options.text: The stiff rod that runs along the back beneath the embryo’s midline, shared by vertebrates and their closest invertebrate relatives.
options.why: That is the notochord. The neural plate is the strip of the outer layer that becomes the nervous system.

options.text: The cells at the very edges of the folds that leave as the folds meet and migrate out through the body along several routes.
options.why: That is the neural crest, which is made from the edges of the folds as the plate closes into a tube.

items.stem: What is the neural tube?

options.text: The hollow tube formed when the edges of the neural plate rise and fuse, from which every vertebrate brain and spinal cord is built.
options.why: Correct. Every vertebrate nervous system is built from the neural tube, and its hollow interior becomes the ventricles and the canal of the spinal cord.

options.text: The canal running down the center of the adult spinal cord, which carries fluid and is lined with the cells that once made its neurons.
options.why: That canal is what the tube’s hollow interior becomes. The neural tube is the whole embryonic structure, walls as well as hollow.

options.text: The strip of cells on the back of an early embryo that will become the nervous system once signals from beneath block skin.
options.why: That is the neural plate, which becomes the neural tube once its edges rise and fuse.

options.text: The long fiber of a progenitor cell, stretching from the hollow center to the surface, which newborn neurons climb.
options.why: That describes a radial glial fiber, which spans the wall of the tube rather than being the tube itself.

items.stem: What is the name for the hollow structure formed when the edges of the neural plate rise and fuse, from which every vertebrate brain and spinal cord is built?

options.text: The neural tube.
options.why: Correct. The neural tube is the hollow structure every vertebrate nervous system is built from.

options.text: The neural plate.
options.why: The neural plate is the flat strip that comes before the tube, before its edges rise and fuse.

options.text: The neural crest.
options.why: The neural crest is a population of cells that leaves the edges of the folds as they fuse, not the tube they form.

options.text: The notochord.
options.why: The notochord is a stiff rod along the back. It is not hollow, and the nervous system is not built from it.

items.stem: A section through an embryo shows a flat neural plate. Which sequence describes how the plate becomes the neural tube?

options.text: Its edges rise into folds, a groove deepens between them, and the folds lean in and fuse above the groove.
options.why: Correct. Folds, a groove, and fusion convert the flat plate into the hollow neural tube.

options.text: Its edges curl downward, away from the back, and meet beneath the plate to enclose a space below it.
options.why: The edges rise, not fall. The folds lean in above the groove and fuse there.

options.text: It sinks beneath the outer layer as a flat sheet, and the sheet then curls into a tube once it is covered.
options.why: The plate does not sink as a flat sheet first. Its edges rise into folds that lean in and fuse.

options.text: Its cells leave the plate one at a time and gather beneath the midline, where they arrange themselves around a space.
options.why: The plate is converted into the tube as a sheet, by folding and fusion. Cells leaving one at a time describes the neural crest, not the tube.

items.stem: Spina bifida and anencephaly are two birth defects of the nervous system. How does the chapter distinguish them?

options.text: Both are failures of neural tube closure; spina bifida occurs at the tail end and anencephaly at the head end.
options.why: Correct. The two ends of the tube close last, and a failure at the tail end gives spina bifida, at the head end anencephaly.

options.text: Both are failures of neural tube closure; anencephaly occurs at the tail end and spina bifida at the head end.
options.why: That reverses the two. Anencephaly is a failure at the head end, where the brain would form.

options.text: Spina bifida is a failure of neural tube closure, while anencephaly is a failure of the neural crest cells to migrate.
options.why: Both are failures of closure. The neural crest is not involved in the difference between them; the end of the tube is.

options.text: Both occur at the head end; spina bifida is a failure of closure and anencephaly a failure of the three bulbs to form.
options.why: Spina bifida occurs at the tail end. Both conditions are failures of the tube to close, at opposite ends.

items.stem: Just as the neural folds meet, a cell at their very edge loses its attachments to its neighbors. What does the chapter say happens to cells like this one next?

options.text: They leave the tube and migrate out through the body along several routes, as the neural crest.
options.why: Correct. The neural crest is made at the moment the folds meet, from the cells at their edges.

options.text: They stay in the lining of the neural tube’s hollow center and become the progenitors of the brain’s neurons.
options.why: The progenitors of the brain’s neurons line the hollow center of the tube. Cells at the edges of the folds leave the tube instead.

options.text: They climb the long fiber of a parent cell outward until a signal at the surface tells them to stop.
options.why: Climbing a fiber is how newborn cortical neurons reach their layers. Crest cells leave the tube altogether.

options.text: They die in an orderly way, since cells that lose their attachments cannot receive a survival signal.
options.why: Losing attachments is how crest cells become free to migrate, not a step toward dying.

items.stem: The chapter says the vertebrate head is assembled by cells that leave the nervous system on their way to becoming it. What does that description mean?

options.text: Neural crest cells begin at the edges of the forming neural tube, then leave the tube and build much of the face and skull.
options.why: Correct. The crest starts as part of the nervous system and leaves it, and much of the new vertebrate head is built from those departing cells.

options.text: Neurons of the brain migrate out through the skull after birth and become the bone and cartilage that surround the brain.
options.why: Brain neurons do not become bone. The departing cells are neural crest cells, and they leave in the embryo, as the tube closes.

options.text: Cells of the outer layer begin as skin, then leave the skin behind to become the nervous system lying under the embryo’s midline.
options.why: The neural plate’s cells never become skin; they become neural when the skin-making signal is blocked. And the paradox is about the head, not the brain.

options.text: Radial glia build the brain and are then largely gone from it, so the finished head is left without its builders.
options.why: Radial glia do largely disappear, but that is a different point: some of what builds a brain is not in the brain it builds.

items.stem: Early in development the front of the neural tube swells into three bulbs. What do those three bulbs become?

options.text: The forebrain, the midbrain and the hindbrain, the three main divisions of every vertebrate brain.
options.why: Correct. The three bulbs are the three main divisions already met in the lamprey’s brain.

options.text: The left and right hemispheres of the forebrain, and the brainstem that joins them to the cord.
options.why: The hemispheres are parts of the forebrain, not bulbs of their own. The three bulbs are forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

options.text: The pallium, the thalamus and the cerebellum, the three largest structures of the adult brain.
options.why: Each of these comes from a later division of the bulbs. The three bulbs themselves are forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

options.text: The cortex, the spinal cord and the sensory ganglia, each of which later divides into smaller parts.
options.why: The spinal cord is the rest of the tube, and sensory ganglia come from the neural crest. The bulbs are the three main brain divisions.

items.stem: Along the neural tube from the belly side to the back, what decides which kind of cell a given cell becomes?

options.text: Where it sits, since signals from the floor and the roof fall off with distance and the mixture it receives depends on its position.
options.why: Correct. Position comes before identity: a cell’s place between the two sources sets the mixture of signals it reads.

options.text: When it was born, since the earliest-born cells take the fates nearest the floor and later ones the fates nearer the roof.
options.why: Birthday sets a cortical neuron’s layer, which is a different rule. Belly-to-back identity is set by position between two signals.

options.text: Which parent cell it came from, since each progenitor along the tube passes one fixed identity down to every cell it goes on to produce.
options.why: Identity is not inherited as a fixed label from a parent. It is read off the mixture of signals where the cell sits.

options.text: Which neighbors it outcompetes, since cells that win the most survival signal take the fates nearest the floor.
options.why: Competition for survival signals decides which neurons live, not what kind of cell each becomes.

items.stem: What is a morphogen?

options.text: A molecule that carries positional information by spreading from its source and falling off with distance.
options.why: Correct. Because a morphogen falls off with distance, the amount a cell receives tells it where it sits.

options.text: A molecule released by target cells in small amounts that arriving neurons need in order to stay alive.
options.why: That is a neurotrophic factor, which decides which neurons survive, not where a cell sits.

options.text: A molecule fixed on a surface that the growing tip of an axon is drawn toward or repelled by as the tip passes.
options.why: That is a guidance cue fixed on a surface. A morphogen spreads, and its amount carries position.

options.text: A gene switched on in one of the overlapping bands that mark position along the length of the hindbrain.
options.why: Those banded genes mark position a second way, along the tube’s length. A morphogen is a spreading molecule, not a gene.

items.stem: Position from the belly side to the back of the neural tube is read off signals from the floor and the roof. How does the chapter say position along the length of the hindbrain is marked?

options.text: A family of genes is switched on in overlapping bands, in the same order along the body as along the chromosome.
options.why: Correct. The order of the genes on the chromosome matches the order of the bands they are switched on in along the body.

options.text: The same two signals from the floor and the roof, which also vary from the head end of the tube to the tail end.
options.why: The floor and roof signals mark position from belly to back. Position along the length is marked a second way, by banded genes.

options.text: The birthdays of its neurons, since the hindbrain is built from the front to the back, one wave of new neurons after another.
options.why: Birthday sets layer in the cortex. The chapter marks position along the hindbrain with banded genes, not with birth order.

options.text: A separate chemical label on each segment along the hindbrain, which the segment’s axons carry with them as they grow toward their targets.
options.why: Per-segment labels carried by axons echo Sperry’s one-address idea. The chapter describes overlapping bands of gene activity.

items.stem: The same family of position-marking genes is switched on in bands along the body in flies and along the hindbrain in fish. A classmate concludes that a fish embryo passes through an insect-like stage. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: What a fly and a fish share is a mechanism for marking position, not a stage of ancestry being re-run in the embryo.
options.why: Correct. This is the warning from Module 2 against reading development as a replay of ancestral adults. The genes are a shared way of marking position.

options.text: Flies and fish do not share this gene family at all; the resemblance lies only in the pattern of bands, not the genes.
options.why: The chapter says the same gene family marks position along the body in insects. The sharing is real; the replay is not.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since an embryo passes through an adult stage of each of its ancestors on the way to its own form.
options.why: That is the replay view Module 2 warned against. Development does not pass through ancestral adult forms.

options.text: The shared genes do the marking of position in flies but of cell birthdays in fish, so the two uses have nothing in common.
options.why: The genes mark position in both. What they share is a mechanism for marking position.

items.stem: In a mouse, researchers weaken one of the two signals whose gradients run across the future cortex. According to the chapter, what happens to the cortical areas?

options.text: Every areal boundary moves together, so some areas shrink and others expand, with the whole map shifting as one.
options.why: Correct. Changing one gradient moves every boundary together, which is the evidence that the gradients set the map.

options.text: Only the area lying nearest the weakened signal’s source changes size, and all of the other areas stay exactly as they were.
options.why: A change confined to one area is what a list of separate areas would allow. The finding is that every boundary moves.

options.text: The areas fail to form at all, and the cortex ends up as one undivided and scrambled sheet of cells.
options.why: A scrambled cortex is what happens to the layers without the surface stop signal. Weakening one gradient shifts the areas instead.

options.text: Nothing changes, since each area’s size is fixed by its own gene and does not depend on any gradient.
options.why: The chapter rejects a gene per area. The boundaries depend on the gradients, so changing one moves them.

items.stem: Consider two accounts of cortical areas: a list in the genome with one entry per area, or two opposing gradients that cells read. Why does the finding that changing one gradient moves every boundary together favor the gradients?

options.text: Every boundary is set by the same two signals, so shifting one signal shifts them all; a list would let areas change one at a time.
options.why: Correct. Boundaries that move together are what gradients predict and a list does not. There is no list of areas; the areas fall out of two gradients.

options.text: Under gradients the areas are set after birth by experience, so a change made in the embryo could not have left any boundary in place.
options.why: The gradients act in the embryo, before experience. The finding favors them because all the boundaries share the same two signals.

options.text: Under a list the boundaries would move together too, so the finding favors the gradients only because gradients are simpler to describe.
options.why: A list gives each area its own entry, so it does not predict boundaries moving together. The finding really does tell the two accounts apart.

options.text: Under gradients every area has the same size, so any change must spread across all of them equally rather than resting on one.
options.why: The areas are not equal in size, and the change is not equal: some areas shrink while others expand.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the chapter calls the patterning of the cortex the clearest case of a rule standing in for a blueprint, and describe the evidence that supports the rule.
items.answer: Two signals form opposing gradients across the sheet of cells that will become the cortex, one strongest at the back and inner edge and the other at the front and outer edge. Where a cell sits in that pair of gradients decides whether it will belong to motor, somatosensory or visual cortex. The evidence is that changing one of the gradients in a mouse moves every areal boundary together, shrinking some areas and expanding others. That is what gradients predict, since every boundary depends on the same two signals, and it is not what a list of areas with one entry each would predict. So there is no list of areas anywhere. There are two gradients, and the areas fall out of them.
rubric: Names two opposing gradients across the future cortex.
Says a cell’s position in the pair of gradients determines which area it joins.
Gives the mouse evidence: changing one gradient moves every boundary together, some areas shrinking and others expanding.
Explains why boundaries moving together favor gradients over a list of areas.
Concludes that no list of areas exists; the areas fall out of the gradients.

items.stem: What are radial glia?

options.text: Progenitor cells lining the hollow center of the tube, whose long fibers span the growing wall and serve as a path neurons climb.
options.why: Correct. Radial glia are glial cells, the source of the neurons, and the scaffold the neurons climb, all at once.

options.text: The cells at the edges of the neural folds that leave the tube as it closes and migrate out through the body along several routes.
options.why: That is the neural crest. Radial glia stay in the tube, lining its hollow center.

options.text: The support cells of the adult cortex, which hold its neurons in their layers after the neurons have finished climbing.
options.why: Radial glia are largely gone from the adult brain. They are a developmental scaffold, not an adult support structure.

options.text: The inhibitory neurons of the cortex, which are born at the base of the forebrain and travel sideways into the cortex.
options.why: Those neurons are the exception that does not climb a radial fiber. Radial glia are progenitors, not neurons.

items.stem: What is the name for the progenitor cells lining the hollow center of the neural tube, whose long fibers span the wall of the growing brain and serve as the path that newborn neurons climb?

options.text: The radial glia.
options.why: Correct. Radial glia are both the source of the neurons and the scaffold they climb.

options.text: The neural crest.
options.why: The neural crest leaves the tube and migrates through the body. It does not line the hollow center.

options.text: The growth cones.
options.why: A growth cone is the tip of a growing axon. It does not make neurons or span the wall.

options.text: The neural plate.
options.why: The neural plate is the flat strip that comes before the tube. The progenitors line the tube once it has formed.

items.stem: A classmate describes brain development as needing two separate cell populations: one that makes the neurons and another that lays down tracks for them to climb. How does the chapter’s account differ?

options.text: One population does both jobs: radial glia are the progenitors that make the neurons, and their fibers are the tracks the neurons climb.
options.why: Correct. A newborn neuron attaches to the fiber of its own parent and climbs. Source and scaffold are the same cells.

options.text: The chapter agrees with it: progenitors at the lining make the neurons, and a separate population of glia later grows fibers across the wall.
options.why: The progenitors are themselves the glia with the long fibers. There is no separate track-laying population in the chapter’s account.

options.text: No tracks are needed, since each newborn neuron reads a gradient and moves to its layer without anything to climb.
options.why: Most cortical neurons do climb a guide, the fiber of a radial glial cell. Gradients set identity and area, not the route to a layer.

options.text: The tracks are laid by the neural crest, whose cells stretch from the lining to the surface before migrating away.
