options.why: Neural crest cells leave the tube altogether. The fibers that span the wall belong to the radial glia.

items.stem: What is neurogenesis, and when is nearly all of it finished in a human being?

options.text: The production of new neurons, nearly all of it finished before birth.
options.why: Correct. Neurogenesis is the production of new neurons, and in a human being nearly all of it is done before birth.

options.text: The production of new neurons, nearly all of it finished by the end of adolescence.
options.why: The definition is right, but the timing is not. Nearly all neurogenesis in a human being is finished before birth.

options.text: The death of surplus neurons in competition, nearly all of it finished before birth.
options.why: The death of surplus neurons is programmed cell death, the opposite process. Neurogenesis is the making of neurons.

options.text: The formation of the neural tube from the plate, nearly all of it finished by the fourth week.
options.why: The tube closes by the fourth week, but that is the building of the tube, not the production of neurons.

items.stem: What is the name for the production of new neurons, which in a human being is nearly all finished before birth?

options.text: Neurogenesis.
options.why: Correct. Neurogenesis is the making of neurons, and the progenitors lining the tube do it.

options.text: Programmed cell death.
options.why: Programmed cell death removes neurons that do not get enough survival signal. It is the opposite of making them.

options.text: Gastrulation.
options.why: Gastrulation is the earlier stage at which the embryo becomes three layers of cells, before any neurons exist.

options.text: Radial glia.
options.why: Radial glia are the cells that carry out neurogenesis. The process itself has its own name.

items.stem: Two neurons are headed for the same patch of cortex. Neuron A was born early in neurogenesis and neuron B much later. Where does each most likely end up?

options.text: A in a deeper layer and B in a layer nearer the surface, since each later wave climbs past the waves already in place.
options.why: Correct. The cortex is built from the inside out, deepest layer first, so an early birthday means a deep layer.

options.text: A in a layer nearer the surface and B in a deeper layer, since the earliest neurons have the longest time to climb.
options.why: That reverses the order. Later waves climb past earlier ones, so the earliest-born neurons end up deepest.

options.text: Both in the same layer, since a neuron’s layer is set by where it sits in the gradients across the cortex, not by its birthday.
options.why: The gradients across the cortex set area, not layer. Birthday is what determines layer.

options.text: Both in the deepest layer, since every neuron settles just above the lining and the layers form later by sorting.
options.why: Only the earliest wave settles just above the lining. Later waves climb past it, which is what builds the layers.

items.stem: Where are the inhibitory neurons of the cortex born, and how do they get into the cortex?

options.text: At the base of the forebrain, a different region entirely, and they travel sideways into the cortex.
options.why: Correct. Most neurons are not made where they end up, and these are the extreme case: they arrive among cells that came by a different route.

options.text: At the lining beneath the cortex, and they climb radial glial fibers straight up into their layers.
options.why: That is the route most other cortical neurons take. Inhibitory neurons arrive sideways, from elsewhere.

options.text: In the neural crest, and they migrate forward into the head before entering the cortex from its surface.
options.why: The neural crest builds structures outside the brain. Cortical inhibitory neurons come from the base of the forebrain.

options.text: In the cortex itself after birth, since neurogenesis for inhibitory neurons continues into adulthood.
options.why: Nearly all neurogenesis in a human being is finished before birth. These neurons are born at the base of the forebrain.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the chapter says a genome holds rules for building a brain rather than a list of its wiring, name the rules, and say what they produce.
items.answer: A human brain has on the order of eighty-six billion neurons and many trillions of connections, and nothing could specify them one at a time. There is no list of which cell goes where and what it connects to, and a genome does not hold nearly enough information for one. What it holds instead is a small set of rules, applied over and over by cells that respond only to their immediate surroundings: read a gradient, listen to the neighbors, follow a cue, and compete for a limited supply. Run in the right order, the rules produce a brain whose overall structure is reliable enough that its parts can be named, and whose details differ from one individual to the next.
rubric: Says there is no list of which cell goes where, and not enough information in a genome to hold one.
Says the genome holds a small set of rules applied by cells responding only to their immediate surroundings.
Names at least three of the four rules: read a gradient, listen to the neighbors, follow a cue, compete for a limited supply.
Says the rules produce a reliable overall structure whose parts can be named.
Says the details differ from one individual to the next.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how a cortical neuron’s birthday comes to determine which layer it ends up in.
items.answer: A newborn neuron attaches to the fiber of the radial glial cell that made it and climbs outward from the hollow center toward the surface. Neurons are made in waves, and each new wave climbs past the waves already in place. So the cortex is built from the inside out: the deepest layer is laid down first and the outermost layer last. A signal released by cells at the surface tells arriving neurons where to stop. The result is that an early-born neuron ends up deep and a late-born one ends up nearer the surface, so a neuron’s birthday determines its layer.
rubric: Says newborn neurons climb the fiber of a radial glial cell outward.
Says each later wave climbs past the waves already in place.
States the inside-out order: deepest layer first, outermost last.
Mentions the surface signal that tells neurons where to stop.
Concludes that early-born neurons end up deeper and late-born ones nearer the surface.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what the chapter means by saying the vertebrate head is assembled by cells that leave the nervous system on their way to becoming it.
items.answer: The neural crest is made as the neural folds meet. The cells at the folds’ very edges leave the tube, lose their attachments to one another, and migrate out through the body along several routes. What each one becomes is settled by the signals it meets along the way. They build most of the peripheral nervous system, including the sensory and autonomic ganglia and the nervous system of the gut, along with pigment cells and much of the face and skull. So cells that began as part of the forming nervous system leave it, and much of the new vertebrate head is built from them.
rubric: Says neural crest cells come from the edges of the neural folds as they meet.
Says the cells leave the tube and migrate through the body.
Says each cell’s fate is settled by the signals it meets along the way.
Names at least two things the crest builds, including part of the face and skull.

items.stem: In a developing neural tube, cells near the roof receive a lot of a molecule released there, and cells closer to the floor receive less of it. Each cell switches on a different set of genes depending on how much it receives. What is the molecule acting as?

options.text: A morphogen, carrying positional information by spreading and falling off with distance, so the amount tells a cell where it sits.
options.why: Correct. The amount a cell receives depends on its position, and the cell reads that amount to settle what it becomes.

options.text: A neurotransmitter, released across a synapse to tell a receiving cell that the sending cell has just fired.
options.why: A transmitter acts between two cells already connected. Here no connection is involved, and the amount marks position.

options.text: A survival signal, released by a target so that only the cells receiving enough of it go on living.
options.why: Survival signals settle which cells live once they have been made. Here the signal settles what each cell becomes.

options.text: A neuromodulator, broadcast widely to change what an existing circuit does with the same input.
options.why: A neuromodulator changes how an existing circuit behaves. Here the signal sets the identity of each cell.

pools.title: Finding the Way, Competition, and Sex Differences

items.stem: What is a growth cone?

options.text: The tip of a growing axon, a flattened, restless structure that extends fine processes, samples what it touches, and steers toward some things and away from others.
options.why: Correct. The growth cone samples its surroundings and pulls itself toward some molecules and away from others.

options.text: The long fiber of a progenitor cell, stretching from the hollow center of the tube to its surface, which newborn neurons climb on their way outward.
options.why: That is a radial glial fiber, which carries whole neurons to their layers. A growth cone is the steering tip of one neuron’s growing axon.

options.text: The joint structure formed where an arriving axon meets its target, with release machinery on one side and receptors on the other.
options.why: That is a synapse, which is assembled once a growth cone arrives. The growth cone is what gets the axon there.

options.text: A molecule released by target cells in small amounts, which arriving neurons need to take up in order to stay alive.
options.why: That is a neurotrophic factor. A growth cone is a structure at the tip of an axon, not a molecule.

items.stem: What is the name for the flattened, restless tip of a growing axon, which extends fine processes, samples its surroundings, and steers toward some molecules and away from others?

options.text: The growth cone.
options.why: Correct. The growth cone is the part of a growing axon that responds to guidance cues.

options.text: The radial glia.
options.why: Radial glia are progenitor cells whose fibers newborn neurons climb. They do not sit at the tip of an axon.

options.text: The neural crest.
options.why: The neural crest is a population of migrating cells, not the tip of a single axon.

options.text: The topographic map.
options.why: A topographic map is an arrangement of cells that mirrors the layout of the world. The steering tip of an axon is the growth cone.

items.stem: In a dish, two growth cones meet the same guidance molecule at the same concentration. One turns toward it and the other turns away. What best explains the difference?

options.text: The two growth cones carry different receptors, and the same molecule can attract or repel depending on the receptor.
options.why: Correct. Which way a cue works depends on the receptor the growth cone carries, which is one reason a small set of cues can do a great deal of wiring.

options.text: The two growth cones sit at different distances from the source, and a molecule attracts when it is weak and repels when it is strong.
options.why: The case holds the concentration the same for both. The chapter locates the difference in the receptors, not in the dose.

options.text: One growth cone has already found its target and stopped responding, so only the other one is still reading the cue at all.
options.why: Both growth cones respond, just in opposite directions. The same molecule can do either job, depending on the receptor.

options.text: One growth cone carries a matching chemical label for the molecule, and the other carries a label that does not match it.
options.why: Matched labels were Sperry’s interpretation, which the chapter rejects. Receptors decide whether a shared cue attracts or repels.

items.stem: Why can a small set of guidance molecules produce a large amount of wiring?

options.text: The same molecule can attract one growth cone and repel another, depending on which receptor each growth cone carries.
options.why: Correct. One cue can do different jobs for different axons, so the number of cues does not have to match the number of connections.

options.text: Each molecule is used only once, at one target, so a small set of molecules can be spent in sequence across the brain.
options.why: Using each cue once would need as many cues as targets. The economy comes from one cue doing different jobs.

options.text: Most wiring is done by activity rather than by molecules, so just a handful of molecules are needed to start the process.
options.why: Activity sharpens a map once it is roughly in place. The economy the chapter names is the receptor-dependent effect of a single cue.

options.text: Each molecule marks one target cell uniquely, and a few molecules can be combined into a label for every cell in the target.
options.why: A label per target cell is still one address per cell, the blueprint the chapter refuses. The economy comes from receptors.

items.stem: Roger Sperry rotated a frog’s eye in its socket and let the cut optic nerve regrow. What happened?

options.text: The axons returned to their original targets, restoring the old map, so the frog struck to the wrong side of a fly.
options.why: Correct. The regrown map matched the eye’s old position, not its new one, so the frog’s strikes were misdirected.

options.text: The axons grew to new targets that matched the eye’s new position, so the frog struck at the fly as accurately as it had before.
options.why: That is what a system wired by use might do. The axons went back to their original targets, and the frog struck to the wrong side.

options.text: The axons failed to regrow at all, so the frog was left blind in that eye and ignored flies on that side of its body.
options.why: The axons did regrow, and they reached their original targets. The frog saw the fly and struck to the wrong side of it.

options.text: The axons connected at random, so the tectum’s map was scrambled and the frog struck in unpredictable directions at the fly.
options.why: The map was not scrambled. It was restored in its original orientation, which is why the error was systematic.

items.stem: The lecture sums up Sperry’s rotated-eye experiment by separating his result from his interpretation. Which part still stands, and which part was replaced?

options.text: The result stands, since the axons really did return to their original targets; his inference to one chemical label per cell does not.
options.why: Correct. The frog really did strike to the wrong side. What failed was the claim that each cell carries its own label; opposing gradients were found instead.

options.text: The interpretation stands, since each target cell does carry its own label; the result does not, as the axons in fact found new targets.
options.why: That reverses the verdict. The axons really did return to their original targets, and the per-cell label is what was replaced.

options.text: Both stand, since opposing gradients are simply the chemical labels Sperry proposed, given a newer name by later researchers.
options.why: Gradients are not labels renamed. A label gives each cell an address; a gradient gives each axon a position.

options.text: Neither stands, since later work showed the frog had learned to strike correctly and the original map had never been restored.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter or the lecture says the result was overturned. The map was restored, and the frog struck to the wrong side.

items.stem: What was found in place of Sperry’s one label per cell, as the way optic axons reach their places in the tectum?

options.text: A pair of opposing gradients, one across the arriving axons and one across the tectum, giving each axon a position.
options.why: Correct. Each axon has a position rather than an address: it ends where its level in one gradient matches the level in the other.

options.text: A set of labels for large regions of the tectum, each shared by many cells, with the finer placement left to chance alone.
options.why: Regional labels would still be addresses, just coarser ones. The finding is a pair of opposing gradients.

options.text: A single gradient across the tectum alone, which every arriving axon climbs until it reaches the gradient’s highest point.
options.why: A single gradient climbed to its peak would send every axon to the same place. There are two gradients, one on each side.

options.text: Random growth of the axons across the tectum, followed by the death of every axon that happened to land in the wrong place.
options.why: Competition and death do shape numbers later, but the map is set by opposing gradients, not by random growth and culling.

items.stem: Two species differ only in the size of the tectum, one having ten times as many target cells as the other. Why does a gradient account of the map suit both species better than one label per cell?

options.text: A gradient takes little information to specify and scales, so the bigger tectum needs no more information than the smaller.
options.why: Correct. That is one of the two advantages the chapter gives a gradient: it scales.

options.text: A gradient is more precise than a label, so the bigger tectum gets a sharper map with no help from activity.
options.why: The chapter does not claim gradients are more precise. Activity sharpens the map after the gradients have set it roughly.

options.text: A label account would need ten times fewer labels in the bigger tectum, since its cells are grouped into larger regions.
options.why: Labels come one per cell, so ten times the cells would need ten times the labels. That cost is why gradients scale better.

options.text: A gradient account gives the bigger tectum ten times as many gradients, one for each of its extra groups of target cells to read.
options.why: The bigger tectum needs no extra gradients. The same pair covers a small tectum and a large one.

items.stem: A classmate says that each axon has exactly one correct partner, and that the two fit together like a key in a lock. What does the chapter say instead?

options.text: Partners have graded preferences rather than a lock-and-key fit, and a good deal of what forms at first is provisional.
options.why: Correct. Preferences are graded rather than all-or-nothing, and much of what forms at first is provisional.

options.text: The classmate is right, and every synapse that forms at first is the permanent one the animal keeps for life.
options.why: The chapter rejects lock and key. Much of what forms first is provisional.

options.text: Axons have no preferences at all, and they connect to whichever cell happens to be nearest when they stop growing.
options.why: Partners do have preferences; they are graded rather than all-or-nothing.

options.text: Each axon carries a chemical label for one partner, but the labels can be misread, so errors are later corrected by death.
options.why: A label for one partner is the lock-and-key picture again. The chapter describes graded preferences instead.

items.stem: How many of the neurons made during development survive, according to the chapter?

options.text: Far fewer than are made, since in many regions half or more of the neurons produced go on to die.
options.why: Correct. Most of what development builds is destroyed, and in many regions half or more of the neurons die.

options.text: The great majority of them, since destroying a neuron once it is made would waste what went into building it.
options.why: Overproduction is how development works, not waste to be avoided. Half or more die in many regions.

options.text: Far fewer than are made in the spinal cord, but nearly all of those made elsewhere in the nervous system survive.
options.why: The losses are not confined to the spinal cord. In many regions, half or more of the neurons produced die.

options.text: Every one of them, since the number of neurons made is matched in advance to the number each target needs.
options.why: Nothing matches numbers in advance. Far more are made than survive, and the target settles the final count.

items.stem: What decides which of the neurons arriving at a target survive?

options.text: Competition for survival molecules that the target releases in small amounts; neurons that get enough persist.
options.why: Correct. The supply is limited, so survival is a competition, and the neurons that get enough of the molecules live.

options.text: Their birthdays, since the neurons that arrive first claim the target and the later arrivals are turned away to die.
options.why: Birthday sets a cortical neuron’s layer. Survival depends on how much of the target’s survival molecules each neuron gets.

options.text: Their positions in the gradients across the target, since neurons whose position matches no target cell are removed.
options.why: Gradients guide axons to positions. Which neurons live is settled by competition for survival molecules.

options.text: A count kept in the genome, since each target is assigned a number of neurons and the extra ones are told to die.
options.why: No count is kept anywhere. The supply of survival molecules sets the number.

items.stem: In chick embryos, one experiment removes a developing limb and another grafts on an extra limb. What happens to the motor neurons in each case?

options.text: With the limb removed, far fewer survive than normal; with an extra limb, more survive than usual.
options.why: Correct. The size of the target moves the number of surviving motor neurons in both directions.

options.text: With the limb removed, more survive than normal, since fewer targets leave more survival signal for each neuron.
options.why: Removing the limb removes the source of the survival signal, so the neurons that would have supplied it die.

options.text: With the limb removed, far fewer survive; with an extra limb, the number is unchanged, since it is fixed in advance.
options.why: The number is not fixed in advance. An extra limb supplies more survival signal, and more neurons survive.

options.text: In both cases the number is unchanged, since motor neurons survive whether or not a limb is there for them.
options.why: Motor neurons depend on their target to survive. Both manipulations change the number that survive.

items.stem: Grafting an extra limb onto a chick embryo leaves more motor neurons than usual. Why does it matter that the extra neurons turned out to be cells that would otherwise have died, rather than newly made cells?

options.text: It shows the extra limb rescued doomed neurons, so a supply of survival signal sets the number, not extra production.
options.why: Correct. If the graft had caused new neurons to be made, the result would fit a limb that induces production. Rescued cells point to a supply, not a count.

options.text: It shows the extra limb made the progenitors divide more often, so the target sets the final number by ordering up new neurons.
options.why: That is the alternative the control rules out. The extra survivors were not new cells.

options.text: It shows the survivors were in the wrong place, so the graft experiment tells us nothing about normal development.
options.why: The control does the opposite: it is what lets the experiment support the chapter’s conclusion about a supply.

options.text: It shows that a count kept in the genome was exceeded, so the embryo must have corrected its count upward.
options.why: No count is kept anywhere. The supply of survival signal, not a stored number, sets how many neurons remain.

items.stem: How does an organizational effect of a hormone differ from an activational effect?

options.text: An organizational effect is a permanent early change in how a circuit is built; an activational effect is a reversible adult change in how it runs.
options.why: Correct. Early hormones build; adult hormones switch what was built on and off.

options.text: An organizational effect is a reversible change in how a circuit runs, made early; an activational effect is a permanent adult change in how it is built.
options.why: That reverses the two. Organizational effects are early and permanent; activational effects are adult and reversible.

options.text: An organizational effect is produced by genes on the sex chromosomes; an activational effect is produced by a hormone at any time in life.
options.why: Both effects in the classic account are produced by hormones. They differ in timing and in whether the change lasts.

options.text: An organizational effect acts on the whole brain at once; an activational effect acts on a single cluster of cells at a time.
options.why: The difference is not scope. It is early and permanent against adult and reversible.

items.stem: In an adult songbird, a seasonal rise in a hormone switches a song circuit on each spring, and its fall switches the circuit off again each autumn. What kind of effect is this?

options.text: An activational effect: a reversible change in how a circuit runs, produced by a hormone in adulthood.
options.why: Correct. The change comes and goes with the hormone in an adult animal, which is the mark of an activational effect.

options.text: An organizational effect: a permanent change in how a circuit is built, produced by a hormone early in life.
options.why: The switching is reversible and happens in an adult, so it is not a permanent early change.

options.text: Programmed cell death: an orderly process in which cells of the circuit die when their hormone supply falls each year.
options.why: Nothing in the case says cells die. The circuit is switched off and on again, which is a change in how it runs.

options.text: A mosaic effect: a mixture of features toward either end of the range, in a combination unique to that one bird.
options.why: The mosaic describes how features combine across a whole brain. The case describes a hormone switching one circuit.

items.stem: Two adult animals of the same species receive the same dose of a hormone. A circuit switches on in one animal and nothing happens in the other. On the classic account, what is the likeliest explanation?

options.text: Only the first animal’s circuit was organized by hormone exposure early in life, and later hormones act only on organized circuits.
options.why: Correct. A circuit organized early can be switched on and off for life by hormones that would do nothing to a circuit that had not been organized.

options.text: The second animal’s circuit had already been switched on too often earlier in adulthood, and activational effects wear out with use.
options.why: Activational effects are reversible, not used up. The difference lies in whether the circuit was organized early.

options.text: The second animal received the hormone too late in life, since activational effects can only be produced during the first months after birth.
options.why: Activational effects are produced in adulthood by definition. The early event that matters is organization.

options.text: The second animal has a mosaic brain and the first does not, since only brains at one end of every feature respond to hormones.
options.why: The mosaic is a claim about how features combine, and almost every brain is a mosaic. It does not explain this difference.

items.stem: A hormone is found to promote new synapses in one brain region. A student predicts it must also promote cell survival in a second region, since it did so in the rat preoptic cluster. Why is that prediction unsafe?

options.text: Each region has its own mechanism, so one hormone can promote survival in one place, death in another, and synapses in a third.
options.why: Correct. What a hormone does depends on the region it acts on, so its effect in one place predicts little about another.

options.text: The hormone promotes new synapses only in adults and cell survival only in embryos, so the two effects can never be found together.
options.why: The chapter does not divide the effects by age this way. Its point is that each region responds in its own way.

options.text: The hormone’s effects are the same everywhere, so it cannot promote synapses in one region unless it promotes them in every region.
options.why: That is exactly what the chapter denies. The same hormone has different effects in different regions.

options.text: A hormone that promotes synapses is a different molecule from one that promotes survival, so the student has mixed up two hormones.
options.why: The chapter’s point is that one hormone can have all three effects, depending on where it acts.

items.stem: Males and females of a species show identical parenting behavior. A researcher concludes that the brain machinery producing the behavior must be the same in both sexes. What does the chapter say against this conclusion?

options.text: Some sex-specific mechanisms exist to cancel differences, so the two sexes can reach the same behavior by different routes.
options.why: Correct. Sameness of outcome does not imply sameness of mechanism, and equal behavior is not evidence of equal machinery.

options.text: Identical behavior shows the brain machinery is the same, so the conclusion is sound as it stands.
options.why: The chapter’s finding is that mechanisms can differ in order to produce the same result. Equal behavior does not establish equal machinery.

options.text: Identical behavior shows there are no sex differences anywhere in the brain, which is a stronger conclusion than the researcher drew.
options.why: Sex differences in the brain are real and common. A matched behavior says nothing about the absence of differences elsewhere.

options.text: Identical behavior is impossible between the sexes, so the measurement of parenting in this species must have been mistaken.
options.why: The chapter treats identical behavior as possible, and sometimes produced by mechanisms that differ in order to cancel a difference.

items.stem: Suppose each region of the brain is shaped by its own mix of developmental signals. What does that predict about whole brains?

options.text: A whole brain should be a mosaic, some features toward one end of the range and others toward the other, in a unique combination.
options.why: Correct. Features set one region at a time need not line up, so a whole brain should be a mixture rather than one of two kinds.

options.text: A whole brain should come in one of two versions, since the regions respond alike to the same hormones and so end up at the same end.
options.why: Two versions would follow only if every region responded alike. The premise is that each region responds in its own way.

options.text: A whole brain should sit at one point on a single scale, consistently toward one end or the other across every one of its features.
options.why: A single consistent position across features is what the mechanism does not predict. Region-by-region shaping lets features diverge.

options.text: A whole brain should show no differences between the sexes at all, since each region’s signals cancel out across the brain as a whole.
options.why: Region-by-region shaping produces real differences in individual features. It predicts that they do not line up, not that they vanish.

items.stem: The mosaic prediction was tested on more than fourteen hundred human brains, using the features that showed the largest average difference between females and males. Which two questions did the researchers ask of each brain?

options.text: Whether the two sexes’ distributions were separate, and whether that brain was consistently at one end across features.
options.why: Correct. The first question asks about overlap; the second asks whether any one brain lines up at one end.

options.text: Whether male brains were larger than female brains, and whether brain size predicted the person’s abilities.
options.why: Neither question was asked. The study asked about overlap and about internal consistency across features.

options.text: Whether each brain’s features had been set by genes or by hormones, and at what age each feature had been set.
options.why: Neither question was asked. The study asked about overlap between the sexes and about consistency within each brain.

options.text: Whether each brain matched the average for its sex, and whether the brains that did not match had been measured wrongly.
options.why: Matching an average was not the question. The study asked whether the distributions overlapped and whether single brains were consistent.

items.stem: One headline says “Men and women have two different kinds of brain”. Another says “There are no sex differences in the brain”. How does the chapter’s summary of the evidence relate to the two headlines?

options.text: It rejects both: the differences are real and matter for medicine, but they do not add up to two kinds of brain.
options.why: Correct. Mechanism predicts a mosaic, and the mosaic is what we find. Both halves of the summary have to be said together.

options.text: It endorses the first: the differences are real, so there are two kinds of brain, one of them typical of each sex.
options.why: The differences are real, but they do not add up to two kinds of brain. Almost every brain is a mixture.

options.text: It endorses the second: the distributions overlap extensively, so there are no real differences to speak of.
options.why: Overlap is not absence. The average differences are real, and ignoring them has done harm in medicine.

options.text: It declines to judge either one, since no study of human brains has ever measured differences between the sexes.
options.why: The chapter reports a study of more than fourteen hundred human brains and draws a clear summary from it.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say that ignoring sex differences in the brain has done harm?

options.text: The differences matter for medicine, and a great deal of research has studied males only.
options.why: Correct. Findings drawn from males alone may not hold for females, and the differences are real enough to matter.

options.text: The differences are large enough to sort people by sex, and ignoring them hides who is suited to which work.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: the differences license nothing about any individual’s abilities.

options.text: The differences are the cause of most sex differences in behavior, so ignoring them hides the source of behavior.
options.why: The chapter makes no such causal claim, and it notes that biological sex and social experience are intertwined in humans.

options.text: The differences prove there are two kinds of brain, and treating all brains as one kind has misled neuroscience.
options.why: The differences do not add up to two kinds of brain. The harm the chapter names is research done on males only.

items.stem: A company proposes to screen job applicants by comparing their brain scans with features that differ on average between the sexes. What does the chapter’s account imply for this plan?

options.text: Sex differences license nothing about any individual’s abilities, and almost every person’s scan shows a mixture of features.
options.why: Correct. Average differences sit inside overlapping distributions, and single brains rarely line up at one end.

options.text: The plan is sound, since features with the largest average difference sort individuals reliably into two groups.
options.why: Even the features with the largest average difference overlapped extensively, so they do not sort individuals.

options.text: The plan is sound only for the reproductive circuits, since the sex differences there are the largest and the most reliable ones.
options.why: Those differences are the largest, but the chapter still says sex differences license nothing about an individual’s abilities.

options.text: The plan fails only because sex differences do not exist, so there is nothing in any scan for it to measure.
options.why: Sex differences are real. The plan fails because they license nothing about any individual.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe Sperry’s rotated-eye experiment, say which part of his conclusion was later replaced and by what, and give the chapter’s reasons the replacement is better.
items.answer: Sperry rotated a frog’s eye in its socket and let the cut optic nerve regrow. The axons found their original targets in the tectum, so the map was restored in its original orientation and the frog struck to the wrong side of a fly. That result stands. Sperry concluded that each target cell carries its own chemical label and each axon a matching one, which amounts to one address per cell, a blueprint. What was found instead was a pair of opposing gradients, one across the arriving axons and one across the tectum, so each axon has a position rather than an address. A gradient takes very little information to specify, and it scales, so a bigger tectum needs no more information than a small one.
rubric: Describes the experiment: eye rotated, optic nerve regrows, axons return to their original targets, frog strikes to the wrong side.
Says the result stands while the interpretation of one label per cell was replaced.
Names the replacement: opposing gradients giving each axon a position rather than an address.
Gives at least one advantage of gradients: little information to specify, or scaling to a bigger tectum.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the chick limb experiments in both directions, explain why one control is essential to the conclusion, and state the principle the chapter draws.
items.answer: When a developing limb is removed from a chick embryo, the motor neurons that would have supplied it die, leaving far fewer than normal. When an extra limb is grafted on, more motor neurons survive than usual. The essential control is that the extra survivors are not newly made cells but cells that would otherwise have died. Without that control, the extra limb might simply have caused more neurons to be made. With it, the conclusion follows that the supply of survival signal from the target, not a count kept somewhere, sets the final number. The principle is to overproduce and let the target settle it, so a population ends up matched to what it serves without anything counting either one.
rubric: Describes limb removal leading to fewer surviving motor neurons.
Describes an extra limb leading to more surviving motor neurons.
Names the control: the extra survivors are cells that would otherwise have died, not new cells.
Explains that the control rules out the limb causing extra neurons to be made.
States the principle: the supply of survival signal, not a count, sets the number; overproduce, then let the target settle it.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why the developmental mechanism behind sex differences predicts that whole brains will be mosaics rather than two kinds, and say what the study of more than fourteen hundred human brains found.
items.answer: Each region of the brain responds to developmental signals in its own way. The same hormone saves cells in one rat cluster and kills them in a neighboring one, and elsewhere it builds new synapses. If each region is shaped by its own mix of signals, its features are set one at a time, so there is no reason for them all to fall toward the same end. A whole brain should therefore be a mosaic, with some features toward one end of the range and others toward the other, in a combination unique to the individual. The human study bore this out. Even the features with the largest average difference overlapped extensively between the sexes, and almost no brain was consistently at one end; between nothing and about a tenth were, depending on the dataset. Mechanism predicts a mosaic, and the mosaic is what we find.
rubric: States that each region responds to signals in its own way, with an example such as the same hormone saving cells in one place and killing them in another.
Reasons that features set region by region need not line up, so a brain should be a mixture rather than one of two kinds.
Reports extensive overlap between the sexes even for the features with the largest average difference.
Reports that almost no brain was consistently at one end across features.
Does not conclude either that there are no differences or that there are two kinds of brain.

items.stem: In a few sentences, give both halves of the chapter’s summary of sex differences in the brain, and state the one limit it places on human evidence.
items.answer: First, sex differences in the brain are real, they matter for medicine, and ignoring them has done harm, since a great deal of research has used males only. Second, those differences do not add up to two kinds of brain, and they license nothing about any individual’s abilities. The limit is that in any human measurement, biological sex and a lifetime of different social experience are intertwined, and no imaging study separates them.
rubric: States that the differences are real and matter for medicine.
Names the harm: much research has used males only.
States that the differences do not add up to two kinds of brain.
States that they license nothing about any individual’s abilities.
States that in human measurements, sex and social experience are intertwined and no imaging study separates them.

pools.title: An Address Is Not an Account, and What the Chapter Concludes
pools.covers: reading §6.3.13, §6.C (the Close) · lecture 6.3 slides address_not_account, old_problems_new_parts · lab Bench

items.stem: Module 1 described a small structure buried in the brain, the amygdala, driving the whole cascade of a frightening moment: the heart rate, the freezing, the turn of attention. Given what the chapter now reports about the amygdala, what is the status of that description?

options.text: It still holds, because it described a cascade of responses to a threat rather than the feeling of being afraid.
options.why: Correct. The amygdala does drive the threat cascade. The new findings break later steps taken from that description, and Module 1 was careful never to take them.

options.text: It has been withdrawn, because the amygdala turns out to be needed for learning about rewards, so the cascade was described too narrowly.
options.why: Reward learning breaks the step from one region to one function. It does not undo the claim that the amygdala drives the threat cascade.

options.text: It holds only for rats, because the human amygdala turns out to take no part in the responses to a threat.
options.why: The chapter makes no such species split. The description of the cascade holds as it was given.

options.text: It has been strengthened, because the amygdala turns out to be the place where the feeling of fear is produced.
options.why: That is the step the chapter rejects. The circuits that produce a defensive response are not the circuits that produce the feeling of being afraid.

items.stem: The chapter keeps the claim that the amygdala drives the threat response, but it rejects two steps that people often take from that claim. What are the two steps?

options.text: From driving the threat response to being where fear lives, and from one region to one function.
options.why: Correct. Both steps go beyond the evidence. The first confuses a response with a feeling, and the second assumes a structure has a single job.

options.text: From being active during a threat to being active during every task, and from jawed vertebrates to the lamprey.
options.why: Whether a lamprey has an amygdala-like region is a real open question in the chapter, but it is not one of these two steps. The steps are about fear and about one function.

options.text: From a recording in rats to a claim about human beings, and from a lesion to a claim about what stimulation would do.
options.why: These are general cautions about method. The two steps the chapter rejects are from response to feeling and from one region to one function.

options.text: From a cascade of responses to a single reflex, and from one side of the brain to both sides of the brain.
options.why: Neither step is one the chapter discusses. The rejected steps are from the threat response to where fear lives, and from one region to one function.

items.stem: A skeptic grants that damage to the amygdala impairs learning about rewards, but suggests that the damage also struck a separate neighboring structure, and that this neighbor does the reward learning. What finding does the chapter give that closes off this explanation?

options.text: Neurons tuned to reward and neurons tuned to threat are intermingled, mixed together in the same tissue of the amygdala.
options.why: Correct. Because the two populations are intermingled, the result cannot be two adjacent structures mistaken for one.

options.text: Neurons tuned to reward sit in one part of the amygdala and neurons tuned to threat sit in another part.
options.why: Two separate clusters would help the skeptic, not refute the skeptic. The chapter reports the opposite: the two populations are intermingled.

options.text: Damage to the amygdala also impairs learning about threats, so the same damage affects both kinds of learning.
options.why: That damage affects threat learning too is true, but it leaves the skeptic’s explanation open: damage that spread to a neighbor could still account for the reward result. What closes it off is that the two kinds of neurons share the same tissue.

options.text: The amygdala is active during reward tasks, and that activity by itself shows that the amygdala is doing the reward learning.
options.why: Activity alone licenses very little, which is the chapter’s whole point about reverse inference. The decisive finding is where the neurons sit.

items.stem: After learning that defensive responses and the feeling of fear run on different circuits, a student concludes that the account of the amygdala driving the cascade of a frightening moment was simply wrong. What is the flaw in the student’s conclusion?

options.text: That account described the heart rate, the freezing and the turn of attention, not a feeling, so the new finding does not contradict it.
options.why: Correct. A finding about where the feeling comes from cannot overturn an account that was only ever about the responses.

options.text: That account was about human beings and the new finding comes from studies of rats, so the two cannot be compared with each other at all.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter turns on that species contrast. The account survives because it described responses, not a feeling.

options.text: That account was right about the feeling of fear, and only its claims about freezing and heart rate need to be revised.
options.why: That reverses the case. The claims about the responses stand, and the account never made a claim about the feeling.

options.text: The new finding concerns learning about rewards, which has nothing to do with the cascade of a frightening moment.
options.why: Reward learning is a separate finding. The one the student is reacting to is about defense and feeling, and it leaves the cascade intact.

items.stem: The chapter says structures and functions map “many to many”. Which pair of observations shows both halves of that claim?

options.text: The amygdala takes part in threat learning, reward learning and attention; and learning from reward draws on both the amygdala and the striatum.
options.why: Correct. The first observation is one structure taking part in many capacities. The second is one capacity drawing on many structures. The claim needs both.

options.text: The amygdala takes part in threat learning, reward learning and attention; and the striatum takes part in selecting actions, habits and reward learning.
options.why: Both observations show one structure with many jobs, so this pair shows only one half. The other half is one capacity drawing on several structures.

options.text: Each structure does one job and each job has one structure; but the same job can be done by differently shaped structures in different species.
options.why: That is a one-to-one mapping inside each brain, which is what the chapter denies. Variation across species is a different point.

options.text: Many structures sit in the forebrain and many others sit in the brainstem; so the capacities are spread along the whole length of the brain.
options.why: Where the structures sit says nothing about how structures and capacities map onto each other. The claim is about one-to-many in both directions.

items.stem: What does the chapter conclude that naming the address of a capacity amounts to?

options.text: The beginning of an account of the capacity, not the end of one, however firm the address.
options.why: Correct. An address is where an explanation starts. Every capacity in the book now has one, and none of them is explained by it.

options.text: The end of an account of the capacity, once a lesion has confirmed that the address is right.
options.why: Even a confirmed address is only a start, since one structure takes part in many capacities and one capacity draws on many structures.

options.text: Nothing of any use, since the addresses of capacities in the brain turn out to be arbitrary.
options.why: The addresses are real and worth knowing. The chapter’s point is that they begin an account rather than complete it.

options.text: A complete account at the implementational level, though not yet at the other two levels.
options.why: An address is not a complete account even at the implementational level. It says where, and leaves how and why open.

items.stem: Compare the demands on a Cambrian animal, on a lamprey and on a mouse with the machinery each one uses to meet them. What pattern does the chapter find across half a billion years?

options.text: The demands have barely changed, while the machinery meeting them has been rebuilt several times over.
options.why: Correct. The computational level has barely moved and the implementational level has been remade repeatedly. A problem can stand still while its machinery changes.

options.text: The demands have grown steadily harder, and the machinery has been enlarged step by step to keep pace with them.
options.why: The demands on the three animals are the same. The chapter also rejects a single ladder of enlargement.

options.text: The demands and the machinery have both stayed nearly fixed, differing among the three only in overall brain size.
options.why: The machinery changed a great deal, with a cerebellum arriving, an output nucleus dividing and a pallium acquiring layers.

options.text: The machinery has barely changed, while the demands on it have been rebuilt several times over as the world changed.
options.why: That reverses the two levels. The demands are what stood still, and the machinery is what was rebuilt.

items.stem: A researcher finds two separate structures in a newly studied fish and concludes that they must exist because the fish faces two conflicting demands. Why does the chapter say this inference is not safe?

options.text: One demand can be met by many arrangements, so finding an arrangement does not tell us which demand it answers.
options.why: Correct. The inference runs from arrangement to demand, which is the direction that fails. The structures might answer other demands, or the same demands might be met another way.

options.text: Separate structures never answer conflicting demands, so the two structures must be doing something else entirely.
options.why: Separate structures are one real solution to conflicting demands. The problem is that finding them does not show which demand they answer.

options.text: Fish face no conflicting demands, since conflicts between demands arose only with the larger brains of mammals.
options.why: The demands are old and shared by every animal moving among other animals. A fish faces them as a mouse does.

options.text: The inference runs in the right direction, from arrangement to demand, but it needs recordings from both structures before it can be trusted.
options.why: That is the direction that fails. Recordings would not repair it, since activity alone licenses very little.

items.stem: What is the thesis the chapter was built around?

options.text: The structures are new, but the parts they are built from are not.
options.why: Correct. Vertebrates added structures given over largely to one job, built from material already in place before there were vertebrates.

options.text: The parts are new, but the structures they make up are ancient.
options.why: That reverses the thesis. The structures are the new thing, and the parts are old.

options.text: Both the structures and the parts are new, arising together with the first vertebrates.
options.why: The parts, from genes that mark position to learning rules, were in place before there were vertebrates.

options.text: Both the structures and the parts are ancient, and vertebrates only enlarged the brain that held them.
options.why: Vertebrates did add structures, such as a cerebellum with the jawed fishes. What is old is what they were built from.

items.stem: The cerebellum and the basal ganglia are vertebrate structures, yet the chapter says the learning rules they use are old. What, then, do those two structures add?

options.text: A way of getting a particular signal delivered to a synapse, not a new kind of synapse.
options.why: Correct. The rules at the synapse were already there. What is new is the route that brings an error or a reward signal to it.

options.text: A new kind of synapse that can change its strength, which no earlier nervous system had.
options.why: Synapses that change with experience are much older than vertebrates; the worm of earlier modules learns.

options.text: A separate new learning rule for each structure, which is why the two structures learn differently.
options.why: The structures differ in what signal reaches their synapses, not in having new rules. The rules are old.

options.text: Nothing to do with learning at all, since both structures only relay signals between the pallium and the brainstem.
options.why: Both structures are sites of learning. What they add is delivery of a particular signal to the synapses there.

items.stem: Of all the parts of the vertebrate brain, which grew the most, and what did it become in mammals?

options.text: The pallium, which became a large, nearly uniform sheet running one kind of circuit, with the same six layers throughout.
options.why: Correct. The mammalian pallium runs one kind of circuit over and over across its whole extent.

options.text: The cerebellum, which became a large, folded structure running a different circuit for each kind of movement.
options.why: The cerebellum did enlarge in several lineages, but the part that grew most is the pallium.

options.text: The basal ganglia, which became a stack of many copies, one copy for each action a mammal can perform.
options.why: More basal ganglia units were added, but they are not one per action, and they are not what grew most.

options.text: The pallium, which became a patchwork of different circuits, each one built separately for the particular kind of signal that reaches it.
options.why: The right structure, but the wrong result. The striking thing about the mammalian sheet is that it is nearly uniform.

items.stem: A piece of mammalian cortex that receives signals from the eyes is compared with a piece that receives signals from the skin. What does the chapter lead us to expect about how the two pieces are built?

options.text: Both have the same six layers and run the same kind of circuit, although the signals arriving differ.
options.why: Correct. The sheet is nearly uniform, with the same six layers whether its signals come from the eyes, the skin or the ears.

options.text: Each has a layered structure suited to its own sense, with more layers where the arriving signals are more complex.
options.why: That is what one might expect, and it is not what the chapter reports. The layers are the same whatever the signals.

options.text: The piece for vision has six layers and the piece for touch has three, like the pallium of a lamprey.
options.why: Three layers describes the pallium of a lamprey or a reptile. Across the mammalian sheet the count is six.

options.text: Neither has layers, since the mammalian pallium is organized in clusters in the way a bird’s pallium is.
options.why: Clusters describe the bird pallium. The mammalian pallium is the six-layered form.

items.stem: The mammalian cortical sheet does the same thing everywhere, to whatever signals reach it. What dilemma does that uniformity pose?

options.text: It is either doing something very general or doing nothing in particular, and what such a structure extracts from its signals is still open.
options.why: Correct. Both horns are live, and the chapter does not choose between them. The question it leaves is what a uniform sheet can extract from its input.

options.text: It is either a single structure or many separate structures, and imaging has now shown that it is really many structures working side by side.
options.why: The sheet is one structure with areas staked out by gradients. The dilemma is about what its one circuit does, not about how many structures it is.

options.text: It either learned its job or was built for its job, and its six uniform layers show that it was built for one job only.
options.why: Uniform layers are what make the sheet’s job puzzling. They do not settle it in either direction.

options.text: It either handles signals from the eyes or signals from the skin, and each area chooses between the two before birth by its layers.
options.why: Areas are staked out by gradients, and every area has the same six layers. The dilemma is about generality, not about which sense.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe how the computational and implementational levels behaved differently across vertebrate history, give two examples of the implementational change, and say what the pattern implies about inferring a demand from a brain’s arrangement.
items.answer: The computational level has barely moved. The demands on a Cambrian animal are the demands on a lamprey and on a mouse, and they would be the demands on anything that moves through a world with other animals in it. The implementational level, meanwhile, has been rebuilt over and over. A cerebellum arrived with the jawed fishes, and the output nucleus of the basal ganglia divided in two. The pallium acquired six layers in one lineage and clusters in another, and the whole plan was scaled up independently in sharks, bony fishes, birds and mammals. So a problem can stand still for half a billion years while the machinery that answers it is remade several times. It follows that one demand can be met by many arrangements. Finding an arrangement therefore does not tell us which demand it answers.
rubric: States that the computational level, the demands, has barely changed from the Cambrian to the mouse.
States that the implementational level has been rebuilt repeatedly.
Gives two correct examples of that rebuilding, such as the cerebellum arriving, the output nucleus dividing, six layers against clusters, or independent enlargement.
Concludes that finding an arrangement does not reveal which demand it answers, keeping the direction from arrangement to demand.

items.stem: A friend calls the amygdala “the brain’s fear center”. In a short paragraph, explain what is right in the idea behind that phrase and what is wrong with the phrase itself, using the two findings the chapter gives.
items.answer: What is right is that the amygdala drives the cascade of a frightening moment: the heart rate, the freezing, the turn of attention. That still holds. What is wrong is two steps taken beyond it, from driving the threat response to being where fear lives, and from one region to one function. First, the amygdala is also needed for learning about rewards. Its reward-tuned and threat-tuned neurons are mixed together in the same tissue, so this is one structure with more than one job, not two neighboring structures. Second, the circuits that produce a defensive response are not the circuits that produce the feeling of being afraid. For that reason the researcher who did most to establish the amygdala’s role in threat rejects the phrase.
rubric: Keeps the claim that the amygdala drives the threat cascade, without calling it withdrawn.
Names the amygdala’s role in learning about rewards.
Says the reward and threat neurons are intermingled in the same tissue, so this is not two neighboring structures.
Says the circuits for a defensive response are not those for the feeling of being afraid.
Identifies at least one failing step: response to feeling, or one region to one function.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain the chapter’s claim that the vertebrate brain’s structures are new but its parts are old. Give at least two examples of old parts, and say what the cerebellum and the basal ganglia add.
items.answer: Vertebrates added structures given over largely to one job, but they built those structures from material that was already there. The genes that mark position along a body, the kinds of cells that neurons are, the rules by which a growth cone finds its way, and the rules by which too many neurons are made and then reduced were all in place before there were vertebrates. Even the learning rules are old. What the cerebellum and the basal ganglia add is not a new kind of synapse but a way of getting a particular signal delivered to one.
rubric: States that the structures are new and the parts are old.
Gives at least two correct old parts: position genes, neuron cell types, growth-cone rules, overproduce-and-compete rules, or learning rules.
Says these parts were in place before there were vertebrates.
Says the cerebellum and basal ganglia add delivery of a particular signal to a synapse, not a new kind of synapse.

items.stem: A news story reports that a brain-imaging study has found “the region for regret”, which becomes active whenever people regret a choice. What does a finding like that give us?

options.text: The beginning of an account of regret: an address, which leaves open how the region contributes and what else it does.
options.why: Correct. Naming where a capacity happens is where an explanation starts. One region takes part in many capacities, and one capacity draws on many regions.

options.text: A complete account of regret at the implementational level, so the other two levels are what remain to be worked out.
options.why: An address is not a complete account even at the implementational level. It says where, and leaves how open.

options.text: Nothing worth having, since activity in a region during a task is never evidence about anything the region does.
options.why: Activity alone is weak evidence, but an address is real and worth knowing. It begins an account rather than completing it.

options.text: A full account of regret, since a region active whenever regret occurs must be the place where regret is produced.
options.why: That step is reverse inference. The region may be active during many other things, and regret may draw on many regions.

items.stem: With the lab’s specimens redrawn at their true sizes, compare where the marmoset, a primate, falls with where the dolphin falls, each against the human. What does the comparison show about using a brain’s size to judge how closely its owner is related to us?

options.text: Size is a poor guide to relatedness: the primate’s brain is about a rat’s size and the dolphin’s about the human’s, since size evolved more than once.
options.why: Correct. The line under the true-scale drawings says size and folding evolved more than once, so neither is a reliable clue to descent.

options.text: Size is a good guide to relatedness: the primate’s brain comes out close to the human’s, while the dolphin’s comes out about the size of a rat’s.
options.why: That reverses the result. The marmoset’s brain is in the rat’s range, about 3 to 4 centimeters, and the dolphin’s is about the human’s.

options.text: Size is a good guide to relatedness: the marmoset’s and the dolphin’s brains both come out far smaller than the human’s, as their distance from us predicts.
options.why: The dolphin’s brain comes out about as wide as the human’s, roughly 15 centimeters, even though dolphins are not primates.

options.text: Size is a poor guide only for sea animals: the dolphin’s brain is unusually small, while the marmoset’s matches the human’s as its relatedness predicts.
options.why: The dolphin’s brain is not small; it is about the human’s width. And the marmoset’s is in the rat’s range, so size misleads on land too.

items.stem: In the lab, the same schematic brain model was drawn twice, once from a lamprey’s settings and once from a mammal’s. Set side by side, how do the two models differ?

options.text: Mostly the same parts in both, but the mammal’s forebrain roof is taller and longer, its hindbrain shorter, and its cerebellum solid.
options.why: Correct. The mammal’s roof is labeled pallium (neocortex), and the lamprey’s model has only a dashed outline where a cerebellum would sit. What changed is mostly proportion.

options.text: The mammal has several parts the lamprey lacks altogether, such as a pallium, a tectum and basal ganglia, while its hindbrain stays the same.
options.why: The lamprey model has a pallium, a tectum and basal ganglia too. The mammal’s differ in proportion and in labels such as neocortex.

options.text: The two models are identical in their proportions, and the only difference between them is that the mammal’s regions carry different labels.
options.why: The proportions do differ: the mammal’s forebrain roof is taller and longer, and its hindbrain shorter.

options.text: The lamprey’s forebrain roof is the larger of the two, and the mammal’s is reduced to make room for a much longer hindbrain.
options.why: That reverses the proportions. The mammal’s forebrain roof is the larger, and its hindbrain the shorter.

items.stem: In the lab, recordings were taken from a generic mammal’s brain while it learned to freeze to a tone paired with a shock, and while it learned to approach a light that predicted food. What did the recordings show for the amygdala across those two tasks?

options.text: It recorded high in both of them, in the task about a threat and in the task about food alike.
options.why: Correct. A structure recorded high during a threat task and during a food task is not selective for threat, which is the first crack in a recording-only table.

options.text: It recorded high during the tone and shock and low during the light and food, as a structure for threat would.
options.why: That is the pattern a structure dedicated to threat would show, and it is not what the recording showed. The amygdala was high during the food task too.

options.text: It recorded high during the light and food and low during the tone and shock, as a structure for reward would.
options.why: This reverses the threat-only reading but keeps the idea of one job. The recording was high during both tasks.

options.text: It showed no result for either task, since the chapter reports nothing about the amygdala in a learning task.
options.why: Gray cells did appear on the bench wherever the chapter supports no result, but not for the amygdala in these two tasks. It recorded high during both.

items.stem: In the lab’s record-only step, the basal ganglia were recorded at their input stage, the striatum, during each of six tasks. What pattern did the striatum show?

options.text: Activity in several quite different tasks, from orienting toward a flash to approaching a cue that predicted food.
options.why: Correct. Like the recordings the chapter describes, the striatum was active across tasks, so a job assigned from its row alone was a reverse inference.

options.text: Activity during the lever task alone, since that is the one task in which the animal worked for a reward.
options.why: The striatum was not confined to the lever. It was active while the animal oriented to a flash and while it approached a food cue.

options.text: Activity only in the tasks that were trained, and none at all while the animal oriented toward a flash.
options.why: Orienting is not a trained task, and the striatum still recorded activity during it. Its activity was not restricted to learning.

options.text: No activity in any task until the dopamine clusters were stimulated, since the striatum waits on dopamine before it can act at all.
options.why: The striatum recorded activity in the record-only step, before any stimulation. The row was broad, not empty.

items.stem: In the lab, a table of what each structure is for was filled in using recordings alone. In a short paragraph, explain why every entry in that column was a reverse inference, and use one structure’s recorded pattern from the lab as the example.
items.answer: Each entry went from “this structure was active during these tasks” to “so it is for the process those tasks involve”, which is the definition of reverse inference. The inference is only as good as the structure’s selectivity, and most structures were not selective. The amygdala, for example, recorded high during the tone paired with a shock and also during the light that predicted food, so writing that it is for fear or threat ignored half of its own row. The striatum was active in tasks as different as orienting to a flash and approaching a food cue. A recording shows that a structure is active, not what it is for, and a structure active during many different things licenses very little on its own.
rubric: Identifies each entry as a move from activity during a task to the process the structure performs.
Gives a structure’s recorded pattern from the lab accurately, such as the amygdala high in both the threat task and the food task.
Explains why that pattern undercuts a single-job entry, since the structure was not selective.
States that a structure active during many different things licenses very little on its own.

items.stem: In the lab, the climbing fibers to the cerebellum were silenced during training only, and the animal was then trained and tested on the tone followed by a puff to the eye. What did the two blink readouts show?

options.text: The learned, timed blink never developed, while the reflex blink to the puff itself was unaffected.
options.why: Correct. Showing the two separately is the point: the cerebellum was needed to learn the timing, not to blink at all.

options.text: Both blinks were lost, the timed blink never developing and the reflex blink to the puff failing as well.
options.why: The reflex blink to the puff survived. Losing it would suggest a problem with blinking itself rather than with learning.

options.text: The timed blink was learned normally, while the reflex blink to the puff itself was slowed down.
options.why: This reverses the result. The timed blink failed to develop and the reflex blink was unaffected.

options.text: Both blinks were normal, since the climbing fibers were restored before the test was run.
options.why: The fibers were restored before the test, but the learning had been missed during training. The timed blink never developed.

items.stem: In the lab, the dopamine fibers to the striatum were silenced during training only and restored before the test. How did the lever task and the timed blink come out?

options.text: At test the animal moved normally but pressed no more than an untrained animal, and the timed blink was learned normally.
options.why: Correct. Cutting the verdict’s route stopped the learning that depends on a verdict and spared the learning that depends on an error.

options.text: At test the animal moved slowly and pressed very little, and the timed blink could not be scored at all in that animal either.
options.why: Slowed movement across tasks came from removing the dopamine clusters. With only the fibers silenced during training, movement at test was normal.

options.text: The lever was learned normally, and the timed blink never developed, while the reflex blink was unaffected.
options.why: That pattern belongs to silencing the climbing fibers. Silencing the dopamine fibers stopped the lever and spared the blink.

options.text: Neither was learned, since both the lever task and the timed blink depend on a dopamine signal reaching the striatum.
options.why: The timed blink depends on an error delivered by climbing fibers, not on dopamine. It was learned normally.

items.stem: On the lab bench, one delivery route at a time was silenced during training only and restored before the test, and the timed blink and the lever were each trained and then tested. What pattern did the two silencings produce?

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no timed blink, lever learned. Dopamine fibers silenced: blink learned, and the animal moved normally at test but pressed no more than an untrained one.
options.why: Correct. Each route was needed for one task and not the other, and the dopamine result is not a movement problem, since the animal moved normally at test. That is why prediction learning, and supervised learning with it, go in the climbing-fiber row, and reinforcement learning in the dopamine row.

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no timed blink, lever learned. Dopamine fibers silenced: blink learned, but every movement at test was slow and hard to start, so the lever could not be scored.
options.why: Slow movements that are hard to start are what removing the dopamine clusters produced. With the fibers silenced only during training, the animal moved normally at test and simply had not learned the lever.

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no timed blink and no lever. Dopamine fibers silenced: no lever and no timed blink, since both are learned movements that need every learning structure.
options.why: No behavior uses one structure alone, but that is not what the silencings showed. Each route was needed for one task and not the other.

options.text: Climbing fibers silenced: no lever, blink learned. Dopamine fibers silenced: no timed blink, and the animal moved normally at test but pressed as much as a trained one.
options.why: That reverses the result. The timed blink depends on an error delivered to each output cell, and the lever press on a broadcast verdict.

items.stem: The lab bench labels each result either as an experiment the reading reports, naming the animal it was found in, or as a result that only follows from what the reading says a structure does. How were the two silencing results labeled, and how does that fit the chapter’s grading of the evidence?

options.text: The climbing-fiber result was reported, in the rabbit, and the dopamine-fiber result only followed. That fits the cerebellar case being the best supported.
options.why: Correct. The loss of the timed blink with the climbing fibers silenced is an experiment the reading describes. The dopamine silencing is an inference from the mapping, and the bench says so.

options.text: The dopamine-fiber result was reported, in the rat, and the climbing-fiber result only followed. That fits the reinforcement learning case being the best supported.
options.why: That reverses the labels. The bench reports the climbing-fiber experiment, in the rabbit, and marks the dopamine silencing as following from the reading.

options.text: Both results were reported, each in its own animal. That fits the chapter’s view that the three cases are all about equally well supported.
options.why: The chapter says the three cases are not equally strong, and the bench agrees: only the climbing-fiber silencing is an experiment the reading reports.

options.text: Neither result was reported, since both only followed from what the reading says. That fits the chapter’s view that none of the three pairings has been tested.
options.why: The chapter counts silencing the climbing fibers as part of the evidence for the cerebellar case, and the bench reports that experiment, in the rabbit.

items.stem: Filling in Doya’s table from the lab bench, each family of learning gets the pathway whose silencing stopped it. What goes in the unsupervised learning row, and why?

options.text: None, because there is no route to cut: it needs nothing delivered, so no dedicated teaching route exists for it.
options.why: Correct. The bench can silence only the climbing fibers and the dopamine fibers. Unsupervised learning uses the activity of the two cells a connection joins, which is already there.

options.text: The dopamine fibers, because unsupervised learning is how the animal learned to approach the food cue, and dopamine fibers carry news about food.
options.why: Dopamine fibers carry a verdict, which is the signal reinforcement learning needs. Unsupervised learning needs nothing delivered.

options.text: The climbing fibers, because unsupervised learning is how the animal learned the timing of the blink, and climbing fibers carry that timing.
options.why: The timing of the blink is prediction learning, which needs an error for one output. Unsupervised learning needs nothing delivered.

options.text: Both pathways, because unsupervised learning happens at synapses everywhere, and so it is stopped by silencing any route into the brain.
options.why: Co-occurrence-sensitive synapses are everywhere, which is exactly why no single delivery route serves them and there is nothing to silence.

items.stem: On the lab bench, a single point on the tectum was stimulated, and the point was moved step by step from one end of the tectum to the far end. What did the animal’s head do?

options.text: It turned in order as the point moved: from far left, through straight ahead, all the way to far right.
options.why: Correct. Neighboring points on the tectum turned the head to neighboring directions, in order along its length, which is what makes the tectum a topographic map.

options.text: It turned to the same side every time, more strongly as the point moved further along, since stimulation only sets how strongly the animal responds.
options.why: Setting how strongly the animal responds is what broad projections do. Moving the point on the tectum changed where the head turned, not how hard.

options.text: It jumped between directions with no order to them, since each point on the tectum is wired to a direction chosen at random during development.
options.why: The directions came in order. Neighboring points turned the head to neighboring directions, which is the defining feature of a map.

options.text: It did not move at all, since stimulating a structure can show only that it is active, not that it is enough on its own to produce a movement.
options.why: Stimulation tests sufficiency, and here it was sufficient: each point produced a turn of the head toward its own direction.

items.stem: On the lab bench, the neocortex was removed and the animal was first run in the open field and then tested on the lever. What did the bench report for each?

options.text: In the open field walking, grooming and exploring continued, found in the cat; for the lever it reported nothing, as the chapter describes only the open field.
options.why: Correct. The open field result is the decorticate cat, with its basal ganglia intact. The bench left the lever blank rather than invent a result the reading does not support.
