options.text: In the open field the animal lay still, found in the cat; for the lever it showed pressing had stopped, since without the neocortex nothing voluntary is left at all.
options.why: Without a neocortex the animal still walked, groomed and explored in the open field. And the bench reported nothing at all for the lever.

options.text: In the open field walking, grooming and exploring continued, found in the cat; for the lever it showed pressing was normal, since lower levels run everything.
options.why: The open field result is right, but the bench reported no result for the lever. A blank is not the same as a normal result.

options.text: In the open field every movement was slow and hard to start, found in the lamprey; for the lever it showed pressing had fallen to almost nothing.
options.why: Slow movements that are hard to start come from removing the dopamine clusters, not the neocortex. Without a neocortex, walking and grooming continued.

items.stem: On the lab bench, the dopamine clusters were removed and each of the six tasks was then run or tested. What did the bench show?

options.text: Every movement was slow and hard to start, in every task, a result found in a lamprey whose dopamine was depleted and in Parkinson’s disease.
options.why: Correct. The effect was not limited to learned tasks. Removing the dopamine clusters made every movement slow and hard to start, which is why the learned tasks were hard to score.

options.text: Only the lever task failed, since dopamine carries the reward signal, and every other task was run with normal movement, a result found in the rat.
options.why: The lever did fail, but so did movement in every other task. That is what makes the lever result hard to interpret.

options.text: Unwanted movements broke through in every task, since without the dopamine clusters nothing was left to hold the competing programs back.
options.why: Unwanted movements breaking through is the result of raising dopamine. Removing the dopamine clusters made movements slow and hard to start.

options.text: Nothing changed in any task, since the dopamine clusters had already done their work during training and were no longer needed afterward.
options.why: Removal changed every task. Every movement became slow and hard to start.

items.stem: With the dopamine clusters removed, a trained animal on the lab bench pressed the lever far less than before. Why does that result, on its own, fail to show that the animal had lost what it learned?

options.text: Every movement in every task was slow and hard to start, so the animal might remember the lever perfectly well and still be unable to press it.
options.why: Correct. Failing to learn and failing to move predict the same low pressing. Removing the dopamine clusters cannot separate the two explanations.

options.text: The lever is not a learned task, so a change in pressing could never show anything about learning, whichever structure was removed from the animal.
options.why: The lever is one of the learned tasks, trained and then tested. The problem is that every movement was slowed, not that nothing was learned.

options.text: The dopamine clusters grow back within a few trials, so any loss of pressing would disappear if the animal were tested again a little later.
options.why: Nothing on the bench shows regrowth. The problem is that the animal’s movements were slow and hard to start in every task.

options.text: The pressing dropped only because the animal was frightened by the removal, which the bench reports as a change in its response to pain.
options.why: The bench reports slow movements that are hard to start, in every task. Fear is not the explanation it offers.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe what the animal on the lab bench did as the stimulated point was moved along the tectum from one end to the other, name the kind of arrangement that result reveals, and give the two things the chapter says that arrangement buys.
items.answer: As the stimulated point moved along the tectum, the animal’s head turned in order, from far to the left, through straight ahead, to far to the right. Neighboring points on the tectum turned the head toward neighboring directions. That makes the tectum a topographic map: neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells, so the tissue is an ordered copy of the space around the animal, which is what lets the eyes and head be aimed from it. A map keeps wires short, because cells that compare nearby points sit near each other. And it makes comparison easy, because the circuitry that sharpens a difference between neighbors can be the same everywhere on the sheet.
rubric: Reports that the head turned in order, from one side through straight ahead to the other, as the point moved.
Names the arrangement as a topographic map, with neighboring points in the world handled by neighboring cells.
Gives short wires as one payoff, because cells comparing nearby points sit together.
Gives easy comparison as the other, because the same sharpening circuitry works everywhere on the sheet.

items.stem: On the lab bench, a student tries to remove the generic mammal’s hindbrain, and the bench refuses. What reason does the refusal give?

options.text: The animal would not survive, because the hindbrain runs breathing and heart rate.
options.why: Correct. The bench removes nothing and cites the hindbrain’s role in the jobs that keep an animal alive. It is the one removal the scene will not perform.

options.text: The reading reports no experiment in which a hindbrain was removed, so there is no result to show.
options.why: A missing experiment is what the bench’s gray “no result reported” marks, and it is shown as a gap rather than a refusal. The refusal gives survival as its reason.

options.text: The animal would stay asleep, because the reticular formation that sets arousal runs through the hindbrain.
options.why: The reticular formation does run the length of the brainstem, but the refusal does not cite arousal. It cites breathing and heart rate.

options.text: The spinal cord’s pattern generators would keep the animal moving, so the tasks would look just as before.
options.why: The cord does run locomotion by itself, but that is not the bench’s reason. The refusal says the animal would not survive without breathing and heart rate.

items.stem: On the lab bench, a student records from the generic mammal’s brain while it turns toward a flash, and again while it learns that a tone predicts a shock. How does the norepinephrine cluster’s recorded activity compare between the two tasks?

options.text: It is low while the animal turns toward the flash and high in the task where a tone predicts a shock.
options.why: Correct. The arousal dial is turned up when a shock is coming and barely moves for a simple orienting turn, which fits a source that sets how aroused the whole animal is.

options.text: It is high in both tasks, since the cluster’s fibers reach nearly the whole brain and any task needs the animal awake.
options.why: Reach is not the same as activity. The cluster records low during the orienting turn and high when a tone predicts a shock.

options.text: It is high while the animal turns toward the flash and low in the task where a tone predicts a shock, since orienting is arousal.
options.why: That reverses the result. The orienting turn is the tectum’s job, and the tectum is the structure that records high there.

options.text: It is grayed out in both tasks, since the reading describes norepinephrine as a dial and reports no recordings of it.
options.why: The cluster does have results on the bench, low for the orienting turn and high for tone and shock. The rows grayed out in both are other structures.

items.stem: On the lab bench, a student stimulates the periaqueductal gray. What result does the bench give, and how is it labeled?

options.text: The whole defensive pattern, freezing or fleeing with a reduced response to pain, labeled as reported and found in the rat.
options.why: Correct. The reading describes this experiment, so the result is labeled reported and names the rat. It is the entire pattern rather than a fragment.

options.text: Freezing by itself, with the response to pain unchanged, labeled as following from the reading rather than as reported.
options.why: Freezing by itself would be a fragment. The bench shows the whole pattern, with a reduced response to pain, and marks it as reported from the rat.

options.text: Fleeing by itself, with a stronger response to pain, labeled as reported and found in a cat with its basal ganglia left intact.
options.why: The cat with its basal ganglia intact belongs to the removal of the neocortex. Stimulating the periaqueductal gray gives the whole defensive pattern, found in the rat.

options.text: A gray “no result reported”, since the reading describes recordings of the periaqueductal gray but not stimulation of it.
options.why: The reading does describe stimulating the periaqueductal gray in a rat, so the bench reports a result.

items.stem: In the lab’s tree activity, a student places the card for an amygdala-like region at the root of all the vertebrates, the lamprey included. How does the reveal treat that placement?

options.text: As neither right nor wrong: the key’s ring is solid on the jawed-vertebrate branch and dashed at the root, as the question is open.
options.why: Correct. The dashed ring marks a question that is not settled, which is why the root placement is shown in amber rather than struck out.

options.text: As wrong: the key places the card with the mammals, since an amygdala-like region is a late mammalian addition to the forebrain.
options.why: Reptiles, birds and jawed fishes have an amygdala-like region too, so the card does not belong with the mammals.

options.text: As right: the key places the card at the root, since the lamprey has an amygdala-like region matching a mammal’s part for part.
options.why: Matching a mammal’s part for part is true of the lamprey’s selection circuit. Whether it has an amygdala-like region is not settled.

options.text: As wrong: the key places the card on the jawed-vertebrate branch alone, since the lamprey is known to lack an amygdala-like region altogether.
options.why: The key’s solid ring is on the jawed-vertebrate branch, but the lamprey is not known to lack one. The question is open, so the root placement is not marked wrong.

items.stem: In the lab’s tree activity, one card reads “a pallium” and another reads “a six-layered pallium (neocortex)”. Where does the key place the card that reads “a pallium”?

options.text: On the branch at the root of the vertebrates, the lamprey included, since every vertebrate has a pallium.
options.why: Correct. The lamprey has a pallium, thin and three-layered, so the card belongs where the lamprey joins the rest. The six-layered card is the one that belongs with the mammals.

options.text: On the branch leading to the mammals, since the pallium is the part of the forebrain that grew enormously in them.
options.why: This is the trap the activity is built around. The mammals’ card is the six-layered pallium, the neocortex; a pallium itself is in every vertebrate.

options.text: On the branch leading to the jawed vertebrates, since the pallium arrived with the jawed fishes, together with the cerebellum.
options.why: The cerebellum arrived with or shortly before the jawed fishes. The pallium is older, and the lamprey already has one.

options.text: On the branches leading to the birds and the mammals separately, since the forebrain roof grows largest in those two lineages.
options.why: The forebrain roof does grow largest in birds and mammals, but growing large is not arising. The lamprey already has a pallium.

items.stem: The lab’s true-scale view carries one line: size and folding evolved more than once. What does that mean for a strategy of identifying a brain by how large and how folded it is?

options.text: Size and folding are poor guides to relatedness, since distantly related lineages with big brains can arrive at similar size and folding on their own.
options.why: Correct. A feature that evolved more than once tells us about size or lifestyle rather than about descent, so it can make unrelated brains look alike.

options.text: Size and folding are the best guides to relatedness, since a feature shared by two brains was most likely inherited from their common ancestor.
options.why: The common-ancestor inference applies to parts shared by descent. A feature that evolved more than once can be shared without being inherited.

options.text: Size and folding show how old a lineage is, since lineages that split from ours earlier have had less time to grow and fold their brains.
options.why: Every living lineage has been evolving for exactly as long as ours. Size and folding do not measure age.

options.text: Size and folding pick out the primates, since a large, folded brain arose once in the primate lineage and nowhere else.
options.why: Large, folded brains arose in several lineages, including the dolphin’s, far from the primates. The line under the view says as much.

items.stem: In the lab’s tree activity, the card for a corpus callosum has to be placed among the mammals, which include a platypus, a kangaroo, a dolphin, a rat, a chimpanzee and a human. What fixes the card’s branch?

options.text: The platypus and the kangaroo lack one, so the card goes on the branch leading to the placental mammals, the dolphin, rat, chimpanzee and human.
options.why: Correct. The platypus and the kangaroo are mammals that are not placental, and they connect their hemispheres through smaller commissures. Their lack is what keeps the card off the branch for all mammals.

options.text: The chimpanzee and the human alone have one, so the card goes on the branch leading to the primates, the lineage with the largest and most folded brains.
options.why: The dolphin and the rat have a corpus callosum too. The callosum belongs to placental mammals, not to primates alone.

options.text: Every mammal on the tree has one, so the card goes on the branch leading to all the mammals, the platypus and the kangaroo included.
options.why: The platypus and the kangaroo are not placental mammals, and they have no corpus callosum.

options.text: The dolphin and the rat lack one, so the card goes on the branch shared by the platypus, the kangaroo, the chimpanzee and the human.
options.why: The dolphin and the rat are placental mammals and have a corpus callosum. The two mammals without one are the platypus and the kangaroo.

items.stem: On the lab’s bench, the amygdala was removed, and the animal was then trained and tested on the tone-and-shock task, the cue-and-food task and the lever task. What did the bench report?

options.text: Freezing to the tone and approach to the food cue both failed to be learned, and no result was reported for lever pressing.
options.why: Correct. Both cue tasks failed, one about a threat and one about food, in results found in the rat. The lever cell was gray, because the chapter reports no result for it.

options.text: Freezing to the tone failed to be learned, but approach to the food cue and lever pressing were both learned normally.
options.why: That is what calling the amygdala a fear center would predict. The food-cue approach failed too, because the amygdala is needed for learning about rewards.

options.text: Freezing to the tone and lever pressing both failed to be learned, while approach to the food cue was learned normally all the same.
options.why: The food task that failed was approach to the cue. The lever task produced no result at all, not a failure.

options.text: All three were learned, but the animal moved slowly and was hard to start in every task it was given.
options.why: Slow movement that is hard to start is what the bench showed after the dopamine clusters were removed, not the amygdala.

items.stem: After the amygdala was removed on the bench, the lever task showed a gray cell. A lab partner writes that the amygdala is therefore not involved in lever pressing. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: The gray cell means the chapter reports no experiment for that case, which is a gap in the evidence, not a finding that the amygdala plays no part.
options.why: Correct. A gray cell is an honest gap. Since one capacity can draw on many structures, silence about a structure is not evidence that it is uninvolved.

options.text: The gray cell means the lever was pressed only at the untrained rate, which shows that the amygdala is needed for lever pressing after all, rather than uninvolved.
options.why: A gray cell carries no number and no result. Reading it as a failure is the same mistake as reading it as uninvolvement.

options.text: The gray cell means the animal could not survive the removal, so no task at all could be tested after the amygdala was gone.
options.why: The refusal on grounds of survival was for the hindbrain, and it was shown in red. The animal without an amygdala was tested on the two cue tasks.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since a structure the bench reports nothing for was recorded as inactive during that task.
options.why: A gray cell is not an inactive structure, whether in a recording or after a removal. It marks a case the chapter does not report.

items.stem: On the lab’s bench, the periaqueductal gray was stimulated. What did the result show, and what could it not show?

options.text: The whole defensive pattern appeared, freezing or fleeing with a reduced response to pain, but nothing in it could show that the animal felt afraid.
options.why: Correct. The bench reads out behavior, activity and pain response, and nothing on it measures what the animal feels. The circuits for a defensive response are not those for the feeling.

options.text: Freezing appeared alone, as a fragment of the defensive pattern, which showed that the structure handles only one part of defense.
options.why: The stimulation produced the whole pattern, not a fragment of it. That is what makes the result striking.

options.text: The whole defensive pattern appeared, and the reduced response to pain, coming along with the freezing or the fleeing, showed that the animal also felt afraid.
options.why: A reduced pain response is a readout of behavior, not of feeling. Nothing on the bench, and no method from Module 2, measures what the animal feels.

options.text: The head and eyes turned toward one point in space, which showed that the structure holds a map of the space around the animal.
options.why: Turning toward a point is what stimulating the tectum produced, with the direction set by where the tectum was stimulated.

items.stem: On the lab’s bench, the pallium was recorded during the open-field task, and then the neocortex was removed and the open field was run again. What did the two results show, taken together?

options.text: The pallium was active in the open field, yet the animal walked, groomed and explored without it: its activity was a correlation, not a sign of need.
options.why: Correct. Recording is correlational and removal tests necessity, so the two results answer different questions and do not conflict. The removal result was found in the cat, with the basal ganglia intact.

options.text: The pallium was silent in the open field, and removing it stopped the walking and grooming: the two methods agreed that it is needed for movement in general.
options.why: The pallium was recorded active in every task, and the animal kept moving without it. Neither half of this matches the bench.

options.text: The pallium was active in the open field, and removing it stopped all exploring: the recording and the removal agreed that it is what runs exploration in that task.
options.why: The recording was right, but the removal left exploring intact. That mismatch is the lesson about reading a job off a recording.

options.text: The pallium was silent in the open field, and removing it left behavior unchanged: the two methods agreed that it takes no part in any of the bench’s tasks.
options.why: The pallium was active in every task. Activity without necessity is not the same as taking no part.

items.stem: The lab’s bench offered four methods: recording from a structure, removing it, stimulating it, and silencing one delivery route during training only. In a short paragraph, say what kind of claim each method supports, and illustrate at least two of them with a result the bench gave.
items.answer: Recording is correlational: it shows that a structure is active during a task, not that the task needs it. The pallium was recorded active in every task, yet removing the neocortex left walking, grooming and exploring in the open field intact. Removing a structure tests necessity: without an amygdala, the animal learned neither to freeze to a tone paired with shock nor to approach a light paired with food. Stimulating tests sufficiency: stimulating the periaqueductal gray produced the whole defensive pattern, freezing or fleeing with a reduced response to pain. Silencing a route only during training separates learning from the ability to perform. With the dopamine fibers to the striatum silenced during training and restored for the test, the animal moved normally but pressed the lever no more than an untrained animal. Removing the dopamine clusters outright could not show that, because it made every movement slow and hard to start.
rubric: Says recording is correlational, showing activity but not need.
Says removal tests necessity and stimulation tests sufficiency.
Says silencing a route during training only separates what was learned from the ability to move or perform at test.
Gives at least two correct bench results, each matched to its method.
